Trump laying groundwork to impose national emergency by sowing election distrust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:29 UTC
19:00:29 KST

A series of moves by Donald Trump’s administration to sow doubt in the integrity of US elections have intensified concern among voting experts – and sparked hope among election deniers – that it could declare a national emergency.
The White House and US federal agencies have released a string of documents this summer – including disputed analyses of alleged voting by noncitzens and historical intelligence memos – stoking expectations that the US president could move to exert greater control over November’s US midterm elections.
Trump used a primetime television address in July to claim – again – that US elections were vulnerable to foreign manipulation, and repeat the lie that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen.
Trump’s speech prompted Steve Bannon, his former political strategist, to predict the US president will declare a state of emergency on national security grounds to “protect” elections.
“Take your No 2 pencil out,” Bannon, a rightwing commentator, said on his War Room video podcast on 29 July. “It’s coming. It’s coming. Just block the last week of August out. It’s coming.”
While Trump and his allies could try to use a national emergency declaration to delegitimize results of November’s results, experts say such a declaration would not supersede the constitutional restrictions on executive power on election administration. No president has ever attempted to invoke an emergency to assert control over voting.
Asked earlier this month by Wayne Allyn Root, a rightwing broadcaster, if he would “declare a national security emergency for elections”, Trump notably did not shoot down the idea.
“Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” the president told Real America’s Voice, a rightwing cable channel. “I’ll leave it at that.”
The administration is “trying to lay the groundwork to declare some sort of emergency to nationalize elections”, said Aria Branch, a partner at the Elias Law Group, who led a lawsuit blocking Trump’s previous executive orders on election administration. “I think the president is looking for any opportunity to do that.”
‘We need to be prepared for everything’
“I mean, listen, I think it is quite obvious that the man is losing his grip in reality, so I think we need to be prepared for everything,” said Santiago Mayer, president of Voters of Tomorrow, a gen Z-led voter advocacy organization. “We have spent a long time thinking and preparing for any eventuality and anything that he might attempt. I think our focus at the end of the day is to turn out enough voters where, no matter what he pulls, it won’t succeed.”
Democratic members of US congress have been wargaming strategies to respond to executive provocations in recent months, considering scenarios such as AI-generated disinformation videos and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents being dispatched to polls. Progressive organizations in the democracy space have also been preparing for something to happen before the election.
The presence of Tulsi Gabbard, Trump’s former director of national intelligence, at an FBI raid in Fulton county, Georgia, raised questions earlier this year. Gabbard later testified before Congress that she had been leading an investigation into claims of foreign interference in US elections. Gabbard’s team was involved in the seizure and examination of voting equipment in Puerto Rico, and spent months scrutinizing potential vulnerabilities in voting machines and the possibility of foreign interference.
When Gabbard resigned on 30 June, Trump named his longstanding ally Bill Pulte as her acting replacement, a widely criticized move by members of both parties, who pointed to Pulte’s lack of intelligence experience. While Jay Clayton later took up the post permanently, Pulte is said to have pushed the election interference narrative in a less-visible role.
“This is why Pulte is so important,” Bannon said in July. “So, ah, Jay has got to – Clayton – has big shoes to fill. Every day we’re going to be dogging him on, like, where’s the next release on this.”
On the night of Trump’s July address, Bannon texted CNN: “We need a National Security Emergency about the midterm elections immediately – this is a powerful predicate for that.”
Ty Cobb, a former White House attorney, now a sharp Trump critic, warned of the same while speaking to PBS following the president’s July TV address. “Well, I think tonight’s speech is intended to add the predicate that he needs to declare an emergency at or about the time of the elections,” he said.
ICE agents at polls is “a virtual certainty”, said Cobb, who questioned whether National Guard officers would also be presented. “Anything to intimidate minority voters, particularly immigrant voters, and also I think anything that allows them to try to seize voting machines, as Trump wanted to do in 2020, but [then-attorney general] Bill Barr explained to him there was just no basis for it.”
‘Noncitizen voting … is just not a widespread problem’
After Trump’s TV address, a White House “Government Transparency Task Force” – composed of members of the office of the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – began releasing declassified “election integrity” documents on the White House website.
The first tranche included declassified intelligence memos which described electronic voting machine vulnerabilities, foreign access to state voter registration data and foreign digital manipulation strategies. Much of the material was already known to the public and amounted to a US intelligence assessment that found no evidence Beijing altered the 2020 vote, which Trump lost.
A week later, Trump and his allies quickly seized on an announcement from Mikie Sherrill, the New Jersey governor, that 6,600 non-citizens had registered to vote because of a software error. While fewer than 400 of them voted, the disclosure was used to escalate false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on the voter rolls.
On 31 July, DHS released a public notice arguing that New Jersey’s administrative errors demonstrated a need for standardized federal oversight.
The taskforce also declassified documents in a Michigan case where the FBI investigated suspected fraudulent voter registrations by a get-out-the-vote organization, in which no criminal charges were filed, and investigative material related to a data scrape of voter information in Maricopa county, Arizona.
The pace of releases has been accelerating.
On Monday, the taskforce declassified and released investigative files related to an investigation into Chinese intelligence, which disclosed how disgraced former Democratic US representative Eric Swalwell had told FBI agents how he had “occasionally hooked up” with Christine Fang, a Chinese national allegedly engaged in a political influence campaign.
On Tuesday, the US Census Bureau released a brief claiming it had identified 24,000 noncitizens voting in the 2020 election in a preliminary match of 128m records. It did not reveal its methodology and was sharply criticized by democracy advocates.
“This alleged analysis based on census data fails the laugh test,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “The administration does not provide a sufficient explanation of how it arrived at these numbers – and for good reason.”
Branch, of Elias Law Group, suggested the Trump administration is “searching for” the legal basis for an executive order. “I think they believe there may be one. I think such a document just doesn’t exist, because the fact is our elections are secure,” she said. “Noncitizen voting in our elections is just not a widespread problem … All of the fear and narrative around that issue is just completely unfounded, and it’s really just to stoke fear and lay the groundwork for future action.”
In July, DHS also released an analysis arguing that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections. It did not reveal its methodology for identifying the noncitizens, either, or disclose how confident its officials were in their assessment. The tool it used to flag noncitizens on voter rolls is known to be inaccurate.
‘The founders recognized the risk of centralizing power’
Asked about the possibility of an executive order declaring a national emergency on elections, the White House did not rule it out, refusing to comment on hypotheticals.
“Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the Save America Act,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, referring to legislation that would enforce a crackdown on voting. “The American people overwhelmingly support this commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections. President Trump is absolutely right: we fix this now, or we lose our country.”
The Save America Act would require states to submit their voter rolls to federal inspection, effectively give DHS the power to de-register anyone it deemed ineligible to vote. The act would also sharply curtail mail-in voting – a practice Trump repeatedly criticized, but has reportedly done himself as recently as in this week’s Florida Republican primary – and require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and a narrow set of photo IDs to cast a ballot.
“I mean, we’ve been closely monitoring what the administration is saying,” said Branch, who sees the rhetoric itself as an act of intimidation.
“The constitution is extremely clear on this, and the founders recognized the risk of centralizing power over elections in the executive branch,” she added. “Very helpful, in terms of litigation to push back on these types of efforts.”

Rough drystone walls frame sunken home on Greek island by Alexandre Pavlidis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23

Is Russia preparing an offensive against the Kyiv region: Zelenskyy named the conditions and a possible direction

At the same time, there is currently no troop grouping near Ukraine's northern border necessary for such an operation, reports UNN.
Details
According to Zelenskyy, the Kremlin's further plans may depend on the situation in eastern Ukraine and the launch of a new wave of mobilization in the Russian Federation.
If he has the success there that he is counting on, then he may redistribute forces to another direction. For example, to create a "buffer zone." There could also be an operation in the Chernihiv–Kyiv regions

At the same time, Ukraine currently does not see the number of personnel necessary there to conduct a large-scale offensive operation, although it is detecting Russian military equipment near the border.

In the view of the Ukrainian leadership, most of this manpower could primarily be sent to eastern Ukraine, where Russia seeks to intensify its offensive actions.
Context

At the same time, in August, Ukrainian intelligence and the State Border Guard Service reported that they had not detected the formation of a Russian strike force near the northern border.

The State Border Guard Service also emphasized that it is not currently observing a buildup of Russian forces either near the border with Bryansk Oblast or on the territory of Belarus. At the same time, Ukraine continues to strengthen the defenses of its northern regions, fortifications, and border protection system.
Reminder

How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:20 UTC
19:00:20 KST

How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
The priorities are clear: reach every affected area, protect frontline workers, and turn commitments into action.
Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we first go to listen.
In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas. Their message is direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They are right.
Ebola spreads through communities and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it. They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help identify and trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through access to treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response always moves faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.
One hundred days ago, the government of the DRC declared the country’s 17th Ebola outbreak, following confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus. WHO subsequently declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, followed by Africa CDC’s declaration of a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security.
The scale of the emergency is immense. As of August 21, the DRC has reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths across 56 health zones. This is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded and it is moving faster than any previous one. It is being fuelled by insecurity caused by decades of armed conflict that have undermined law, order and social services, and displaced more than a million people.
At the centre of the response are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.
They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure and hard-to-reach areas. Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty.
Their service must be met with action: safety, protective equipment, training, sufficient medical supplies, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill. The safety of frontline workers is central to stopping transmission.
The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, Africa CDC and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.
Neighbouring Uganda has interrupted locally acquired transmission of the virus. Several health zones in northern Ituri and South Kivu provinces in the DRC have also interrupted transmission. These experiences prove that the outbreak can be stopped more quickly when rapid detection, decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities break the chains of transmission.
But the continued emergency in the rest of Ituri province and five other provinces demands urgently scaled-up action.
To turn the corner, surveillance teams are being expanded and equipped to detect cases early and rapidly identify contacts. Safe clinical care and infection prevention measures are being increased wherever people seek treatment.
More risk communication and community engagement teams are being deployed to reach out to communities to empower them to participate in the response and address barriers to care. More safe and dignified burial teams are working to prevent transmission associated with deaths. Special efforts are being made to reach vulnerable populations and communities in insecure and hard-to-reach areas.
But despite all these efforts, more is needed. We need to scale our response by two to three times current capacities, across all the response pillars.
Health facilities also require urgent protection from infection. As of August 20, 158 health workers have been infected and 45 have died. Every facility in an affected or high-risk area needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water, sanitation and functioning infection-prevention systems.
National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Local organisations need direct support to work consistently with communities. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.
Delayed financing costs lives. Fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both. On the ground, we at WHO and Africa CDC have established tight integration among health and relief organisations working with the government. Donors therefore need to support and enhance that integration, rather than back siloed and disconnected efforts.
Cross-border coordination also must remain strong. People move within and between countries to trade, work, study, seek care and support their families. Borders must serve as bridges for coordinated public health action. This does not require closing borders or imposing blanket travel and trade restrictions. Such measures can disrupt response operations and livelihoods without stopping transmission. The priority is coordinated surveillance, rapid information-sharing and prepared health services along movement routes.
The first 100 days have made the priorities clear.
Find every case. Follow every contact. Break every chain of transmission, protect every health and frontline worker, save lives and ensure that no community is left behind. Bring testing and treatment closer to every affected community. Bolster cross-border coordination. Scale up international support. Turn every pledge into action.
WHO and Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, neighbouring countries, communities and partners to deliver on these priorities. Our responsibility is to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally-led response.
Uganda and areas in DRC have shown how the course of the outbreak can be turned, through rapid detection, decisive action and close cooperation with communities. But these measures must be delivered at scale. Success depends on sustained national leadership, continental solidarity and international support. We must rise to this challenge, together.
The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Why Chinese media says US historians are giving ‘ammunition’ to separatists
As ethnic issues grow ever more sensitive, Beijing is alleging the New Qing History movement seeks to fracture the nation
China has stepped up its offensive against a US-born school of thought on China’s last imperial dynasty, accusing it of providing “theoretical ammunition” for attempts to divide the country.
An article published by the state-run China Ethnic News last Monday warned that New Qing History was “seriously eroding the historical foundations of the community for the Chinese nation in the real world” and should be “forcefully refuted”.
That marked the latest broadside in a two-year campaign by the outlet to attack the loosely defined scholarly movement, which began to take shape in the late 1980s.
Rather than being an organised movement with a unified doctrine, New Qing History refers to a broad revisionist approach to understanding how the Manchu-led Qing managed both China’s Han majority and the many other ethnic groups under their rule.
Scholars taking this approach have drawn on Manchu-language sources to question the long-held assumption that “Sinicisation” – the idea that conquerors of China and even neighbouring peoples were transformed by Chinese culture, often portrayed as a spontaneous and largely one-way process – was the only explanation.

Why More Medical Testing Doesn’t Always Make Us Healthier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Today, if you wish, you can go get a staggering amount of granular data about your health without your doctor’s involvement. All on your own, you can get an MRI of your entire body, a CT of your coronary calcium, an ultrasound of your blood vessels, and maybe someday an immersion ultrasound in a spa.
Direct-to-consumer medical imaging tests are a huge and growing business worth billions of dollars. Over 100,000 Americans are already customers. But do these test results actually make us healthier?
As a radiologist, a doctor specialized in the alchemy of turning information into health, I translate data hidden in images into words that motivate behavior to promote healthier, longer lives. Because it is central to what we do, radiologists have grappled for decades with the question of whether and how information improves health. It turns out to be surprisingly complicated.
In order to make a difference in someone’s health, the test must accurately predict or diagnose a condition, resulting in a change in mindset and behavior, and that change in mindset and behavior must produce a better outcome than not doing the test.
For example, whole-body MRI of the general public, a test not recommended by any medical guideline, medical society, or payer, creates information by taking a picture of your body. That information is accurate for some diseases but not others. It might change your mind by finding something you didn’t know about, like a small mass in your kidney or thyroid gland, which then might change what you or your doctor does. For example, your doctor might order another test to better understand if the mass is important or perform surgery to take it out.
This seems logical. But the reason whole-body MRI of the general public isn’t recommended while other screening tests are is because in the absence of evidence, it is believed to be unlikely to produce a better outcome than doing nothing at all.
Many people think, as I once did, that early diagnosis always improves health. That logic is especially intuitive for an early diagnosis of cancer. But in many cases, that intuition, however understandable, can be wrong. Finding something with a diagnostic test might not help, despite creating an illusion that it does.
For both examples I gave—small thyroid masses, small kidney masses—it has been well documented that aggressive efforts to treat them, despite many being cancer, does not help most people. Isn’t that strange? Yet despite ourselves, we keep finding and removing them.
That’s the tricky thing with diagnostic tests. It’s terrifically hard to unsee something. For those who receive no benefit from treatment, only secondary harm results: surgical pain and complications, the anxiety of a scary diagnosis, and financial burden.
There are numerous non-intuitive examples like this in which only in retrospect do we realize patients have been harmed because a diagnostic test and its downstream actions were promoted to millions before confirming things worked as intended. This is why scientists and medical professionals are so obsessive about evidence and statistics. It’s really hard to know if something is hurting or helping if we rely on common sense.
The likelihood of benefit and the likelihood of harm matter tremendously. For example, if whole-body MRI is performed on a high-risk patient with a cancer-causing genetic syndrome, it is much more likely to create health benefits than if it were to be performed in the general population. This is one of the paradoxical things about diagnostic tests. It’s not just about test accuracy. Equally important is the people being tested, because baseline risk strongly influences the benefits.
Harm is often caused not by the test itself, but from actions taken to manage the information of unknown significance it produces. It is in this way that a seemingly harmless test can hurt people. We do tests to find things, and when we find things, we commonly act, even when we shouldn’t, because we aren’t rational decision-makers.
Direct-to-consumer testing will change how medicine is practiced. It empowers us to make personal decisions about our health and generates novel, complex information that will unlock scientific breakthroughs.
When buying one of these tests, we should pay attention to what the company is claiming. Is their test a curiosity, an entertainment product, a research tool, or clinical care? The lines are often intentionally blurry.
The need for scientific support, informed disclosure, and regulatory compliance increases as the test moves from curiosity toward clinical care. If the test has only been shown to provide information or to make a diagnosis, or has only been shown to improve health in patients with specific risk factors different from our own, we should be skeptical. As they say, buyer beware.
Many companies encourage us to assume their test improves our health. In such cases, the information we are buying may help us, hurt us, or be a placebo and do nothing at all.

Extreme weather hits Europe as wildfires, floods and storms force thousands to evacuate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:59:53 UTC
18:59:53 KST

Extreme weather is hitting Europe, with wildfires in Serbia and Bosnia, floods and fires in Spain, and severe storms in Poland. Thousands have been evacuated as firefighters battle fires, floods and power cuts.
Europe continues to struggle with the consequences of extreme weather, with Serbia, Bosnia, Spain, and Poland all facing severe conditions.
In Serbia, the EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to support local crews battling a blaze that has engulfed more than 1,600 hectares of vegetation in the Deliblatska Pescara nature reserve, 60 kilometres east of Belgrade. The effort is also being assisted by a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 water bomber deployed since Thursday, alongside several Serbian army helicopters.
"The situation is extremely difficult," says Ivica Dacic, Serbia's Interior Minister, adding that "more than 400 people are deployed there on a daily basis."
The crisis extends further into the region, where a large fire broke out on Saturday in the border area between Bosnia and Croatia. Bosnian police closed the main highway connecting Trebinje in Bosnia to Dubrovnik in Croatia, forcing thousands of tourists to turn back and alter their holiday plans.
Several villages around the small town of Ivanica were evacuated as the flames approached homes, and local firefighters reported that some livestock was caught in the fire and burnt. Croatian firefighters from nearby Dubrovnik arrived to assist Bosnian crews in battling the forest fire, which is spreading over an area more than 16 kilometres in diameter across narrow, difficult-to-access terrain. Supported by helicopters, emergency teams continue to fight the blaze, but relentless heat and strong winds have pushed the fire further inland. The Trebinje area has not seen rain for months, leaving the parched landscape exceptionally vulnerable during one of the hottest and driest summers in recent history.
Wildfires and floods in Spain
Meanwhile, Spain has faced a weekend of contrasting weather extremes. Torrential rain and flooding in Tarragona left 11 people injured and disrupted road and rail services after more than 145 mm fell in some areas. Further strong thunderstorms are forecast across eastern and northeastern Spain, while an unusually powerful Atlantic low is bringing heavy rain to Galicia.
Elsewhere in the country, firefighters in Spain’s eastern Valencia region continued battling intense wildfires. A blaze broke out in the town of Segorbe late Thursday after a lightning strike and began spreading rapidly Friday afternoon as winds shifted, leading authorities to raise the wildfire emergency to Level 2.
Personnel from Spain’s Military Emergency Unit and local fire departments joined the response, while more than 1,000 residents from the nearby town of Gatova were forced to evacuate over fears for their homes. Supported by aerial resources, crews have since managed to stabilise the fire after it burned around 630 hectares. The events mark a sharp shift from extreme heat earlier in the week, when temperatures reached up to 44°C.
Poland struggled, but the situation is improving
Further north, severe weather has also struck Poland. Since Friday, storms have wreaked havoc across the country, with firefighters responding to more than 6,500 incidents.
The storms hit residents in many areas, forcing the precautionary evacuation of 12 scout camps amid floods and power cuts. Brigadier Karol Kroć from the State Fire Service told the Polish Press Agency that no injuries have been reported so far.
On Sunday, storms are still expected in northern Poland, as the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management has issued yellow weather warnings for two small regions, with a local forecast of heavy rainfall up to 30 litres per square metre and wind gusts of up to 70 kilometres per hour. Hail is also possible in some areas. Ho
However, the general weather in the country on Sunday has improved significantly. Therefore, the weather conditions across the rest of Poland are expected to be much calmer.

Step aside, Usain Bolt, there's a new speed king in town - TienKung the robot.
The Chinese humanoid, manufactured by the Beijing Centre for Humanoid Robotics, ran the 100 metres in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games on Saturday, beating the Jamaican great's 9.58 world record time - which he set at the Olympiastadion in Berlin in 2009.
"This is a hugely impressive feat," organisers of the Beijing robot games wrote in a post on X, noting that last year's winning time clocked in at 21.50 seconds.
"In 1 year alone the robots competing have become twice as fast. This highlights the pace of advancement both in the market, and specifically in Chinese robotics," they added.
The World Humanoid Robot Games, held in Beijing's "Ice Ribbon" stadium, is bringing together 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries as they compete across events including athletics, boxing, football, weightlifting, and gymnastics.
Video footage of the robots has been shared widely on social media over the last few days, particularly clips showing the humanoids slamming into large mats and slowly falling backwards at the end of races.
While the rather amusing clips have been entertaining viewers, organisers of the games say people should be impressed.
"It shows a pace of technological advancement that almost beggars belief," they said. "Only a year ago, at the last WHRG, robots were slow, ponderous machines that struggled to complete a track sprint. This year they are expected to obliterate world records. The pace that the Chinese robotics industry is advancing at, much like the robot in the video shows no sign of deceleration".
China has been leaning in hard to the humanoid robot industry, and investors appear to be on board.
Morgan Stanley Research has estimated that the humanoid market is likely to reach $5 trillion by 2050, with more than a billion of the robots potentially in use by then.
According to a report published by the bank last year, China is expected to have around 302.3 million humanoid robots in use by 2050.

Zelenskyy said that earlier this year the Defense Ministry had told him that SpaceX had agreed to allow Ukraine to use Starlink over Russian territory to carry out deep strike operations, subject to political approval.
Acting on that, Zelenskyy said, he raised the issue directly with U.S. President Donald Trump. He told Trump that Musk had confirmed the proposed use. Zelenskyy said the two sides subsequently sought Musk’s confirmation and discussed financing for the project.
But at a later meeting, Zelenskyy said Trump told him that Musk had rejected the proposal and accused him of having misled the U.S. president. Musk considered the move a dangerous escalation, according to Zelenskyy.
“He said that I had supposedly deceived him because Musk had denied Ukraine the use of Starlink on Russian territory. I went back to our Ministry of Defense and they said that maybe it was so,” he said.
Zelenskyy did not explicitly accuse Fedorov of lying. He said this episode was among the reasons behind “some of the steps.”
Zelenskyy also pushed back against protesters’ vilification of former army chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, whom he dismissed, and current Defense Minister Maj. Gen. Yevhen Khmara, saying they had gone too far.
“Maybe someone doesn’t like Syrskyi for one reason or another. But the slogans ‘Syrskyi is the devil, Khmara is the devil,’” he said. “Listen, this is too much. Do you understand? In principle, you can’t treat the military like this and tolerate it, especially when it was the military that made it possible for any peaceful protests to take place in the Ukrainian capital at all.”
Pressure on defense budget but military successes
The president also described severe financial pressure on Ukraine’s defense effort. He said the Defense Ministry faced a $27 billion budget shortfall after spending decisions earlier in the year brought forward funds originally intended for the second half of 2026.
Touching on a corruption probe that led Zelenskyy to fire one of his most senior officials this week, he said anti-corruption investigators do not believe the president was involved. The investigators had named a deputy head of the presidential office among the suspects in a money-laundering case.
“The heads of anti-corruption agencies have zero questions for me. They understand perfectly well that I am not involved in anything like that. And this is important to me,” he said.
On the battlefield, Zelenskyy was optimistic, saying Ukraine had almost completely regained control of the Dnipropetrovsk region, with only about 10 square kilometers and three small villages remaining outside Ukrainian control.
He said another operation was underway elsewhere and that its results were expected by the end of August.
He also predicted that by the end of 2026 Ukraine could reach parity between the territory occupied by Russia since the beginning of the year and the territory retaken by Ukrainian forces. Zelenskyy said Russia had occupied about 990 square kilometers since the start of the year, while Ukraine had restored control over roughly 820 square kilometers.
The president said Russia’s principal objective remained the Konstantynivka-Sloviansk-Kramatorsk axis and that Moscow was still demanding Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas region as a condition for a settlement.
Still struggling for access to Patriot missiles
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was receiving substantially fewer Patriot interceptor missiles even as Russian ballistic attacks are increasing.
He said Ukraine received 675 Patriot missiles in 2023, compared with 364 in 2025 and an expected 264 in 2026. Zelenskyy said he wanted to secure 300 additional Patriot missiles for the coming winter, while Ukraine’s Air Force had requested 360.
The shortfall is particularly serious because the United States and European partners are struggling to expand production. Zelenskyy said he hoped Ukraine could obtain even 5% or 10% of U.S. reserves and was able to pay for them.
Zelenskyy said Russia could eventually produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, compared with an estimated current capacity of 600.
He said Ukraine was also preparing alternatives to Starlink, including a European communications project, as Russia and China work on their own competing system.
In other developments
— Debris from a Ukrainian drone hit two industrial facilities including a warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon, local officials in Russia’s Orenburg region said Sunday.
As well as shifting the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across Russia, Ukraine has unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of online retailers, including the country’s biggest online retailer, Wildberries, and competitors such as Ozon.
— One person was killed and six wounded in Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia’s Belgorod border region, local authorities said Sunday.

NEW YORK, August 23. /TASS/. Neither Republicans nor Democrats will gain a significant advantage in the US House of Representatives following the midterm elections in November, Professor of Political Science from the California Institute of Technology Rod Kiewiet told TASS.
"The president’s party almost always loses seats in the Senate and the House in the midterms, so that is the baseline expectation," Kiewiet said in an interview with TASS.
"The Democratic candidates for Senate in Maine and in Michigan are problematic, however, so they may have squandered their chances there. If so, the Republicans retain control of the Senate," the expert continued.
"The House will be harder for the Republicans to hang on to. I’m pretty sure, though, that whichever party is in the majority after November will have a very slim majority," he noted.
"As a consequence, no meaningful legislation is likely to emerge from the House over the next two years," Kiewiet concluded.
The US midterm elections will be held on November 3. One-third of the Senate and the entire House of Representatives will be up for election. Both chambers of the US legislature are currently controlled by the Republican Party.

U.S. Army’s top general warns force over drones, training shortcuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:50:47 UTC
18:50:47 KST

- Acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve published "The Army Azimuth" on August 19, 2026, outlining homeland defense, warfighting, and power projection as his top priorities.
- The statement calls for a "warrior mindset," faster adoption of AI and autonomy, and forward positioning to maintain what LaNeve calls land dominance.
The U.S. Army’s top general has a message for the force: cut corners in training, and it will cost blood.
Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who has run the Army in an acting capacity since April, published a strategic vision statement on August 19, 2026, called “The Army Azimuth.” The blunt warning sits near the end of the document, but it captures the tone of the whole thing: less bureaucratic memo, more a demand that soldiers get back to basics while the Army rebuilds itself for a very different kind of war.
That different war, in LaNeve’s telling, is one shaped by drones and long-range weapons that let an enemy strike without ever coming close enough to be seen. He writes that the Army must counter enemies who use “stand-off weapons,” a term for systems fired from a safe distance, so the attacker never has to enter direct contact with U.S. forces. Defeating that kind of threat, he argues, means moving faster and hitting harder than the enemy from the first moment of a fight, not catching up after the shooting starts.
Homeland defense comes first on his list, which LaNeve calls “our most sacred duty”: securing U.S. borders, protecting Americans from attack, and responding to domestic crises. He argues a secure Western Hemisphere is what makes it possible for the Army to project power anywhere else in the world.
The Army has already reorganized around that idea. Units built for rapid, all-at-once coordination across land, air, space, cyber, and the electromagnetic spectrum, what the service calls multidomain operations, have replaced the old system of fixed brigades. New long-range weapons can now strike ships at sea. Air defenses have been rebuilt for skies crowded with drones. New units fold space, cyber, electronic warfare, and artificial intelligence directly into how commanders run a battle.
LaNeve wants that technology paired with something more old-fashioned: a “warrior mindset,” grit and discipline drilled into soldiers through training centers built to simulate real combat. He is explicit that neither piece works without the other. Advanced systems do not save an Army that has let its basic soldiering skills slide, and disciplined soldiers without modern tools cannot keep pace with adversaries building drone-heavy, AI-assisted forces of their own.
He also wants the Army positioned to move fast when a crisis hits, not scrambling to get there. That means keeping equipment forward-based, running exercises abroad, and stockpiling supplies in the regions where a fight is most likely to start.
LaNeve took charge of the Army after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Gen. Randy George in April, and his own nomination for the permanent chief of staff job has stalled in the Senate over concerns about his limited four-star command experience. None of that appears in the Azimuth. The document is signed with his Senate-confirmed title, 40th Vice Chief of Staff of the Army, the position he holds by law while performing the chief of staff’s duties in an acting capacity.
The statement sets no budget, no numbers, and no deadline. What it does set is a standard LaNeve says he will hold the force to: “The battlefield does not forgive weakness.”

Taiwan to begin clinical trials of new pancreatic cancer treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:46:05 UTC
18:46:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is set to begin clinical trials of an experimental targeted therapy for pancreatic cancer, with about five medical centers expected to participate and Taipei Veterans General Hospital planning to begin enrolling patients in early September.
The development comes as new research offers hope for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, which remains one of the most difficult cancers to treat. According to a National Health Insurance Administration cancer care survey, pancreatic cancer had the lowest five-year survival rate among the 11 cancers examined, at 9.8%, per UDN.
Taipei Veterans General Hospital held the 2026 International Symposium on Multimodal Treatment of Pancreatic Cancer on Saturday and Sunday, bringing together experts from Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea to discuss integrated approaches to treating the disease.
Hsu Shao-jung (許劭榮), an attending physician in the hospital’s Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, said more than half of pancreatic cancer patients are diagnosed after the disease has already reached an advanced stage.
Chemotherapy remains the internationally recognized standard treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer. Hsu said that among 100 patients receiving treatment, only about 50 are still able to continue treatment after 10 to 12 months.
However, he stressed that this does not mean patients survive for only 10 to 12 months, as some can live significantly longer with continued treatment. Hsu said a breakthrough in targeted therapy had emerged this year, describing the development as exciting news for patients and the medical community.
For patients with advanced disease receiving standard second-line treatment, survival has historically been about six months. Clinical trials of the new targeted treatment have reported survival of more than one year, representing a substantial improvement.
Hsu said the new targeted treatment uses a molecular mechanism to target an important cancer-causing gene and prevent it from functioning. Research targeting the gene had faced repeated setbacks for nearly three decades, but significant progress has been made over the past three years and quickly confirmed in human trials, per UDN. The treatment is now undergoing review by the US Food and Drug Administration.
About five medical centers in Taiwan are preparing to participate in clinical trials of the targeted treatment. Taipei Veterans General Hospital expects to begin enrolling newly diagnosed patients with stage 4 pancreatic cancer who have not received cancer-related treatment in early September. The number of participants has yet to be determined, per CNA.
Hsu also said pancreatic cancer vaccines had emerged as another promising area of research over the past three to four years. These vaccines are primarily being studied in patients who have undergone surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence.
The approaches include mRNA and personalized vaccines. However, Hsu emphasized that these treatments remain in the early stages of clinical development and that their effectiveness must be confirmed through larger clinical trials.
Shan Yan-shen (沈延盛), a member of the Healthy Taiwan Promotion Committee’s cancer prevention group and an attending physician in the Department of Surgery at National Cheng Kung University Hospital, said future pancreatic cancer treatments are likely to include cell therapy and vaccines.
As treatment options continue to expand, Shan urged patients not to give up on treatment and encouraged them to maintain a healthy lifestyle and exercise regularly.

Trump’s special envoy established contact with Lukashenko through jokes and vodka - NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:41:43 EEST
18:41:43 KST

Trump’s special envoy established contact with Lukashenko through jokes and vodka - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
John Coale uses informal communication to secure the release of political prisoners and ease sanctions against Belarus. With U.S. assistance, more than 500 people have been released.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus, John Coale, uses informal conversation, alcohol toasts and crude jokes to establish a personal rapport with Alexander Lukashenko. This approach has become part of Washington’s negotiations with Minsk over the release of political prisoners and the gradual easing of sanctions. This is reported in an article by The New York Times, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Coale has built a personal relationship with Lukashenko, which he uses to advance agreements between the United States and Belarus. During one of the first lengthy meetings, the sides repeatedly raised toasts. Coale said that he drank two shots of vodka and tried to discreetly pour out the rest in order to remain sober during the negotiations.
The American diplomat also deliberately used crude humor. According to him, this style helped ease tensions and establish a personal rapport with the Belarusian leader. Coale had previously described one such episode to the Associated Press. After Lukashenko made harsh remarks about European politicians, the American representative responded with an even cruder phrase.
Coale himself stated that he was prepared to use even "locker-room language" if it would help secure the release of people from Belarusian prisons. According to him, humor is one of the important tools in negotiations: if one manages to make the interlocutor laugh, it helps reduce the level of mistrust.
The informal conversations between Coale and Lukashenko even touched on weight loss. The American, who had lost about 18 kg, told the Belarusian leader about the drug Zepbound.
Context
Behind the unusual diplomatic style are quite specific political agreements. In June 2025, following negotiations involving an American delegation, Belarus released 14 prisoners, including Siarhei Tsikhanouski.
In September of the same year, Minsk released another 52 people. In response, the United States eased some sanctions against the state airline Belavia.
In December, the Belarusian authorities released 123 prisoners, including Nobel laureate Ales Bialiatski, Maria Kalesnikava and Viktar Babaryka. Washington subsequently eased restrictions on Belarus’s potash industry.
In March 2026, the largest simultaneous release took place: 250 people were freed. In response, the United States lifted some sanctions against Belarus’s financial sector and a number of potash-industry enterprises.
Coale stated that if Minsk releases the remaining political prisoners, this could create grounds for further lifting of U.S. sanctions.
According to estimates by the American side, as of August, more than 500 people had already been released from Belarusian prisons with U.S. assistance.
At the same time, human rights defenders emphasize that repression in the country has not ceased. According to the Viasna Human Rights Center, at the beginning of August, about 880 political prisoners remained in Belarus, while the authorities continued to detain new people alongside the releases.
Representatives of the Belarusian opposition also warn that this model could turn into a kind of "revolving door," in which Minsk releases some political prisoners in exchange for concessions from the West while simultaneously increasing their number with newly detained people.
Negotiations between the United States and Belarus are already going beyond the issue of prisoners. Coale has discussed the possibility of restoring the full operation of the U.S. embassy in Minsk, further normalizing relations and reaching economic agreements.
Washington is also considering Lukashenko as a possible informal channel of communication with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, given Minsk’s close relations with Moscow.
Recall
In May 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday mentioned Belarusian ruler Alexander Lukashenko, thanking him for his "cooperation and friendship," amid the release of five imprisoned citizens of Poland and Moldova from places of detention in Belarus and Russia.

Syria's FM says Israel security talks frozen since Iran war, expects them to resume soon

Negotiations between Syria and Israel over a security agreement have been frozen since the start of the Iran war, and contact between the two countries was cut entirely after Israel's strike on the Abu al-Duhur airbase last Tuesday, said Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said in a Reuters interview in Damascus. Despite the freeze, Shaibani said he expects negotiations to resume soon, urging Israel to seize a "historic opportunity" for diplomacy.

Shaibani said Syria's priority remains halting Israeli attacks, calling for confidence-building steps in that direction. No date has been set for talks to restart, though he said Washington "is trying continuously to put pressure on Israel to return to the dialogue table."
Shaibani said that around the beginning of the year, the two sides had "agreed on paper to almost everything" on a security deal that would require Israel to halt attacks on Syria and tie into its withdrawal from territory seized after Bashar al-Assad's fall. It concerns them far more than their own domestic issues and the problems of millions of Russians. That is why, in 2014 and in February 2022, Russia attacked to take this flag away from us – to take away our symbols, our freedom, and our independence. They came to take everything from us. Russia has not abandoned these ambitions. Massive – truly massive – strikes, terror, and killings are all driven by one man’s manic dream: that Ukraine should not exist. The Kremlin is obsessed with this, but it will ultimately lose precisely because of it,” Zelensky said.
The President stressed that blue and yellow are the colors of Ukraine, the colors of its people and their courage, while the Ukrainian flag is a symbol of strength, resilience, freedom, and the triumph of life.
Zelensky thanked Ukraine’s international partners who joined the celebrations in Kyiv, including the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia.
High-ranking foreign guests also addressed the ceremony.
As reported, Ukraine celebrates the National Flag Day on August 23.
The holiday was established to honor the centuries-old history of Ukrainian statehood and the national symbols of independent Ukraine, as well as to foster citizens’ respect for state symbols, in accordance with a presidential decree issued on August 23, 2004.
In 2009, the decree was amended to establish an annual official flag-raising ceremony on August 23 across Ukraine.

Zelenskyy: Fedorov suggested "honestly dismissing both" himself and Syrskyi

Zelenskyy: Fedorov suggested "honestly dismissing both" himself and Syrskyi
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that, amid the conflict between then defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov and commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, Fedorov suggested dismissing them both.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists, as reported by Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne
Details: According to Zelenskyy, a "very serious" conflict arose between Fedorov and Syrskyi over the division of responsibilities between the Ministry of Defence and military command.
Zelenskyy said the defence minister and commander-in-chief effectively stopped communicating directly and only discussed issues during meetings in his office.
Quote: "There can't be a conflict at this level between leaders. Whatever operation is taking place on the battlefield, that's primarily a matter for the military. Logistics and support fall under Ukraine's Ministry of Defence. If someone steps into another's area of responsibility, that will inevitably lead to conflict. And a conflict did happen – a very serious one."
Details: Zelenskyy said that during one meeting, Fedorov suggested "honestly dismissing both of them".
The president noted that he decided not to change both the defence minister and the commander-in-chief at the same time during the war, and planned to make personnel decisions sequentially.
Two weeks before the personnel changes, Zelenskyy claims, he suggested that Fedorov and Syrskyi meet separately to resolve their differences, but this did not happen.
After deciding to change the Defence Ministry's leadership, Zelenskyy offered Fedorov four different formats for continuing to work as part of the team, but he turned down all of the proposals.

Zelensky Warns Against Wartime Elections, Calls for Unity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:36:00 UTC
18:36:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized the idea of holding national elections during the ongoing full-scale war, warning that such a move poses a direct threat to Ukraine’s existence and internal stability, Ukrinform reported.
Speaking to journalists on Saturday, Aug. 22, Zelensky addressed the recent public debate sparked by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who had called for a mechanism to hold wartime elections.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” Zelensky said. “My strategy is to bring the country to the end of the war and preserve an independent and sovereign state. And I am fulfilling it.”
The president stated that while Ukraine has faced pressure to hold elections over the past year, no partners have provided concrete proposals on how to conduct them safely and legitimately amid active hostilities, ensuring the participation of frontline soldiers and millions of refugees.
He emphasized that holding a vote is impossible under the current security conditions, as Russian President Vladimir Putin shows no genuine interest in a ceasefire.
Zelensky also stressed the importance of maintaining internal unity, warning against the creation of “internal borders” or dividing the country into “camps.” While acknowledging that the right to protest is important and demonstrates that freedom exists even during wartime, he cautioned against societal fracturing.
Russian Attack Kills 2 in Donetsk Region
“We can be different, but we must understand and focus on the main thing. And the main thing is to preserve Ukraine,” Zelensky said, specifically noting that dividing civil society from the military is a dangerous risk that could lead to “dangerous events.”
Zelensky said that Mykhailo Fedorov presented him with the concept of a “ministry of war.” He turned it down, but the then-defense minister began taking steps in that direction
The president explained that he had an agreement with Fedorov regarding how the army operates and who is responsible for operations. Military operations are carried out primarily by military personnel.
“The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine is responsible for logistical support. If someone encroaches on another’s area of responsibility, it will inevitably lead to conflict. And a conflict did occur – a very serious one. The Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine cannot operate without the Ministry of Defense or the Minister of Defense, and the Minister of Defense cannot operate without the Commander-in-Chief. This is simply a disaster in a country at war,” he explained.
“I really did have – and still have – a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo. We’ve been through a lot together. But I believe that he is either choosing – or being pushed – into the wrong course of action,” the president added.
Frontline gains and potential offensives
During the briefing, Zelensky provided an update on the battlefield, noting that Ukrainian forces have almost entirely liberated the Dnipropetrovsk region.
Following a report from Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, Zelensky stated that only three small villages – amounting to 10 square kilometers – remain under occupation, and Russian forces are practically absent from those areas.
He also indicated that Ukraine aims to reach parity in lost and regained territory by the end of 2026. Currently, Russia has occupied 990 square kilometers this year, while Ukraine has regained 820 square kilometers. Another localized operation is expected to conclude by the end of August, he added.
However, Zelensky warned that the threat from Russia remains fluid. While Putin’s immediate deadline for his generals is to capture the remainder of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions – targeting Kostiantynivka and Sloviansk – by the end of the year, a success there could lead to a shift in forces.
Zelensky suggested that if Russia achieves its eastern objectives, Moscow could redirect its 300,000 mobilized troops toward other areas, including a theoretical offensive from Russia’s Bryansk region toward Ukraine’s Chernihiv and Kyiv regions.
While no Russian troops are currently amassed in Bryansk, Ukrainian intelligence is monitoring military equipment stationed along the border.
Negotiations and security guarantees
Zelensky also addressed potential future peace negotiations, specifically mentioning efforts by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, allies of former US President Donald Trump, to find a diplomatic off-ramp.
“In my opinion, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner very much want to bring victory to [US] President Trump. And they want to find a format for negotiations with the Russians,” Zelensky said.
However, he noted that finding a workable format is incredibly difficult because Moscow’s absolute demand is that Ukrainian forces withdraw from the east. He stated that Russia is indifferent to its own casualty numbers or the time required to achieve this goal.
In this context, Zelensky reiterated that Ukraine requires ironclad security guarantees to prevent future aggression, stating that NATO membership is the only viable option, as the alliance has never faced a full-scale attack.
Zelensky noted that these ideas are a joint effort and that all parties have reacted positively thus far, though further proposals from the US side are expected. He stated that a “corridor of opportunity” for diplomacy exists from the upcoming G20 summit until late summer 2027, just prior to the next US presidential election cycle.
Additionally, Zelensky stated that Ukraine is open to sector-specific agreements, specifically offering to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure if Russia agrees to stop attacking Ukrainian energy and agricultural facilities. He noted, however, that Russia has not yet demonstrated a willingness to agree to such terms.
Deep strikes and the defense budget
The president confirmed that Ukraine is facing a financial hurdle, with the Ministry of Defense currently operating with a $27 billion budget deficit. He explained that funds originally earmarked for the second half of the year were spent early to accelerate domestic drone production.
Kyiv is currently working with European partners, particularly France and Germany, to expedite the release of a planned €30 billion in European funds to cover the shortfall and secure the $8-10 billion necessary to begin procuring weapons for 2027.
Addressing Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign, Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) has been running an 18-month campaign known as Operation “Kylym” (Carpet), designed to force Russian military airports to halt operations.
He also denied rumors that Ukraine targets civilian aircraft, stating, “We are not terrorists.”
Zelensky addressed the recent strikes on Russian logistics infrastructure, including the e-commerce giant Wildberries, describing them as calculated retaliation for Russia’s years-long targeting of Ukrainian logistics companies like Ukrposhta and Nova Poshta.
Zelensky noted that the strike on Wildberries alone caused approximately 1 trillion rubles ($12.5 billion) in direct damages, with total associated economic losses for Russia potentially reaching 3 trillion rubles ($36.3 billion).
He argued that these strikes, combined with internal Russian polling showing 60% of the population wants the war to end, are deeply damaging to Putin. Zelensky claimed that Putin’s recent escalation is a desperate attempt to retain the support of his radical, pro-war base as his broader public approval ratings continue to decline.

Ukrainian defender Serhii Udut, who spent three and a half years in captivity, has died
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:35:00 EEST
18:35:00 KST

Ukrainian defender Serhii Udut, who spent three and a half years in captivity, has died
Marine and Mariupol defender Serhii Udut, who returned home in October 2025 after three and a half years in captivity, has died in Odesa Oblast.
Source: his mother Olena Udut; the Rozdilna hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories on Facebook
Quote from Olena: "He held out where it seemed impossible to hold out. He went through pain, fear and captivity, and came home… but sadly, his heart couldn't withstand the toll of that terrible war. It's hard to find the words when death takes someone who had already given so much for Ukraine. He leaves behind a memory that time will not erase, and gratitude for his courage, bravery and service."
Details: Olesia Bohdanova, daughter of another Mariupol defender and a member of the community of families of the 501st Separate Naval Infantry Brigade POWs, said Serhii died from a blood clot.
Serhii held the rank of junior sergeant and served with the 36th Separate Mykhailo Bilynskyi Marine Brigade. He was a defender of Mariupol, where he was later taken prisoner by Russian forces, Suspilne Odesa reported.
He was held in occupied Luhansk Oblast and in Russia's Kemerovo Oblast. His mother Olena sent more than 450 inquiries to find out her son's fate, but the Russians did not allow him to make a single phone call or write to his family.
Serhii returned home in October 2025 as part of a prisoner exchange. A month later, following rehabilitation, he was welcomed back to his hometown of Rozdilna, where his daughter, mother, friends and fellow soldiers were waiting for him.
"There were so many emotions. When I hugged him, there were tears, joy, sadness – I went through every emotion. It was so strange to greet him with a hug after four years. But I believed he would come back," his daughter Yevheniia said at the time.
After returning, Serhii took part in meetings with pupils at local schools and volunteers, telling them about his service and his experience in captivity.
Quote from the hromada: "Today it is especially hard to grasp that Serhii's life ended so soon. A man who went through the defence of Mariupol, captivity, and finally made it home, has passed away far too early [...]
Serhii Udut will forever remain in our community's memory as a defender of Ukraine who fulfilled his military duty, endured extraordinarily difficult trials, and returned home to Rozdilna."
Background: In late July, former police officer Oleh Kotov from Kharkiv Oblast, who was abducted in 2022 and unlawfully held by Russian forces, died in a hospital in Kyiv.

Israeli army arrests 13 Palestinians as occupiers escalate attacks in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:34:21 UTC
18:34:21 KST

Hosni Nedim and Serdar Dincel
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
The Israeli army on Sunday arrested 13 Palestinians, including a child, during raids in the occupied West Bank, amid attacks by occupiers that included the burning of property and the destruction of agricultural land.
Occupiers burned a residential room belonging to a Palestinian in the northern part of the town of Osarin, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, local sources told Anadolu.
They also set fire to a vehicle, partially burning it, and spray-painted racist slogans at the site, the sources added.
In Bethlehem, Israeli occupiers attacked the Khala'il al-Louz area east of the city, damaging irrigation pipes used for crops, cutting down trees, and damaging Palestinian property and agricultural land.
Occupiers also uprooted olive and grape trees from Palestinian-owned land in the village of al-Minya, east of Bethlehem, according to the official Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Meanwhile, Israeli forces detained two Palestinians, including a child, from the village of al-Rashaydeh in Bethlehem.
In Qalqilya, the army arrested six Palestinians after raiding the city and searching homes in the Kafr Saba and al-Naqqar neighborhoods, according to Wafa.
The army also rounded up five Palestinians from the city of Tulkarem in an incursion.
In Ramallah, Israeli forces closed the western entrance to al-Mughayyir village, northeast of the city, preventing Palestinians from entering or leaving. They also subjected some Palestinians to field interrogations and fired tear gas toward vehicles.
Local sources told Anadolu that the western entrance is currently the village’s only access point after the Israeli army closed its eastern entrance on Oct. 7, 2023.
According to the same sources, Israeli occupiers burned a tent, equipment and animal feed belonging to a Palestinian farmer on the outskirts of Burqa village, east of Ramallah.
The West Bank has witnessed a surge in occupier attacks and Israeli military raids since the outbreak of Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023, amid Palestinian and international warnings over the consequences of the continued escalation.

Norway to give over $9 billion to Ukraine in 2027
OSLO, Aug 23 - Norway plans to give another 85 billion Norwegian crowns ($9.2 billion) in financial support to Ukraine in the 2027 fiscal year, in line with the amount given in 2026, the Nordic country's government said in a statement on Sunday.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere and leaders from across the Nordic and Baltic region are visiting Kyiv on Sunday in a show of support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
Norway's donation will be for both military and humanitarian spending, Stoere was quoted as saying in the text of a speech released by the government in Oslo.
"Supporting and rebuilding Ukraine is not assistance alone. It is an investment in Europe's own security," Stoere said.
In comments published on Saturday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Kyiv had opened a "Pandora's box" with its strikes on Russian economic targets and that Moscow would hit back at Ukraine's "most sensitive economic sectors".
Russia and Ukraine are both ramping up drone campaigns aiming to cripple each other's economic infrastructure, often striking targets far beyond the frontlines of the war started by Moscow, as fighting on the battlefield grinds toward the 4-1/2-year mark. REUTERS

7 Basic iPhone Tricks I Built With iOS 27’s Revamped Shortcuts App
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

I’ve never used Apple's built-in Shortcuts app before, despite owning an iPhone for years. While automating tedious tasks sounded nice, the necessary scripting to trigger actions and thread them together felt overwhelming when I first opened the app. But my experience with the iOS 27 beta has completely changed my perspective on Shortcuts. What was previously clunky and forgotten now feels streamlined and essential.
When iOS 27 lands this fall, Siri AI might be the most tangible change for many users, with its improved capabilities and stand-alone app. Even so, Apple Intelligence integration into the Shortcuts app has me humming “Zero to Hero” from Disney’s Hercules.
Called “Describe a Short,” it lets you say what you want it to do conversationally, then the app generates an automation flow. You can also tweak it by sending a follow-up prompt in the app; the manual scripting option remains available for power users. Since I was testing this app through the iOS 27 beta, I experienced a couple of glitches where the automations didn’t generate perfectly. Even so, this new Shortcuts feature was incredibly fun to tinker with. After a few tries, I generated automations that actually feel useful as part of my daily smartphone habits.
Here are a few basic shortcut ideas worth trying once you download and install iOS 27. My examples only scratch the surface of what you can automate with the app, but hopefully it will spark ideas for your needs.
Habit Breaking
This might be the most basic automation I’ve set up, but it's already my favorite. I spend so much time mindlessly scrolling on my phone that when I close social media apps, like Instagram, to focus on something else, I sometimes reopen them almost immediately out of habit.
I asked the app to generate a shortcut that triggers whenever I open Instagram. Now I get a notification asking: “Do you really want to use this app?” If I choose yes, then the pop-up goes away. But if I pick no, the phone automatically closes out of Instagram and locks the screen. It’s not exactly transformational, and there are other options for reducing screen time, but this little nudge feels helpful for breaking my repetitive habits.
Quality Checking
Since I live in California, I often check the air quality in my neighborhood on my way out of the apartment to gauge whether I should pack a mask. Rather than manually checking the air quality index each day, I wanted to automate the process. So, I set up a shortcut that runs every morning at 6:40 am. It checks the current weather, looks at the air quality index, and then sends me a notification. If the air quality index is above a certain threshold, I get an alert; if it’s below, it sends me the all-clear.
Battery Saving
Shortcuts can also be triggered based on your location. Whenever I leave my apartment, no matter the time of day, I want my phone to be charged, or I have to grab a battery pack just to be safe. To help with this, I generated a shortcut that triggers when I leave home and checks my device’s current battery level. If it’s below 50 percent when it runs, I get a friendly notification that reminds me to bring that power bank. (A quick trip back inside to grab it is better than being miles from home with no way to communicate.)
Plant Watering
These next two automations are a good example of how you can build shortcuts on your home screen and tie shortcuts together. While plenty of apps log plant watering, I wanted to see if Shortcuts could do it for me. First, I created a shortcut that, whenever I run it, grabs the current date and time and adds that to a dedicated plant watering note to keep a consistent log. I then tapped on the drop-down menu at the top of the app and clicked Add to Home Screen. Now, each time I do the chore, I can tap that app icon to log it.
That alone could have been helpful, but I wanted to push the automation a little further. I created another shortcut that, every morning at 9:00 am, finds the plant watering log and sees if it was modified within the last week. If no changes have been added within the last week, it sends me a notification reminder to check on the plants.
Screenshot Extracting
Although this automation is a little more niche, I use it fairly often as someone who’s chronically online and often taking screenshots. Now, whenever I take a screenshot, my phone automatically extracts any text in the images and copies it to my clipboard. This simplifies my previous process of saving screenshots, manually opening the Photos app, then copying the text from the images.
Plane Landing
This one isn’t very complicated, but it makes my life just a little bit easier. I often travel without my partner and can be negligent in sending updates. So I asked the Shortcuts app to generate an automation that sends a “just landed” text to my partner every time I turn off airplane mode. Simple. During setup, the app asked me to select which iPhone contact was my partner. It's an easy automation that solves the issue of me being incredibly distracted when deplaning.
Sound Recognizing
While this shortcut requires you to adjust your accessibility settings, the extra hassle seems worth it for the payoff. I’m almost always wearing headphones when working from home, with the music turned up quite loud. I’m also anxious about not hearing someone knocking on my door or ringing the bell. There's a fix! Start by going into your Accessibility settings, then find Sound & Name Recognition. Here you can enable sound recognition for everything from glass breaking to babies crying; I picked Door Bell and Door Knock.
Since I don’t always have my phone on me while wearing headphones, the basic notification wouldn’t be that helpful. So I beefed it up by building a shortcut so that when my iPhone recognizes either sound, it pauses whatever is playing. Now I can blast my podcasts without worrying about missing a package delivery.
