Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Adding those groups would amount to an additional 100,000 arrivals, bringing the total to 230,000 — 5,000 more than the budget forecast of 225,000 in the coming four years.
"What we're doing is we're focusing on the NOM in its true form, and then we've got these programs that have been available now for over a decade that drive our economy," Farley told Insiders.
"The raw number is not too different, but the reality is, where do we need them?
"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."
One Nation 'effectively backing' Labor's plan
The comments come as public debate continues around the optimum level of migration to Australia.
Net overseas migration dropped to 306,000 in 2024-25, brought down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000 under Liberal-National government policy.
Cabinet minister Chris Bowen said net overseas migration could not just be redefined.
"My overwhelming conclusion was he's pretty comfortable with what the government's doing," Bowen told reporters.
"I'm not sure what campaign One Nation's going to run on migration if they're effectively backing in what the Albanese government is doing."
Opposition immigration spokesman Jonno Duniam said voters were owed a clear explanation of what the party's immigration policy actually is.
"These are not semantic distinctions. They have real consequences for housing, infrastructure, essential services, wages, jobs and the economy," he said.
"For a party that has spent years telling Australians it has all the answers on immigration, One Nation is having extraordinary difficulty answering the most basic question of all: how many migrants would actually come to Australia under its policy."
Opinion polls have shown that voters trust One Nation to manage migration better than the two major parties.
Hanson says One Nation's cuts will come from "fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs".
"Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration," she wrote.
Individuals must stay in Australia for 12 months in a 16-month period to be included in NOM figures, meaning short-term seasonal workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme are typically not counted.
Long-term workers on the same scheme are counted, as are backpakers and working holiday makers who typically stay in the country for more than a year.
Hanson will test racial discrimination laws in the High Court.
The confusion comes as Hanson declared she would take her racial discrimination challenge with Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to the High Court.
The senator lost a Federal Court appeal last month against a ruling which found her in breach of racial vilification laws after she told the Greens senator to "piss off back to Pakistan".
Asked if racial discrimination laws should be changed, Farley said he wasn't convinced they should be.
He said his leader's comments "can be taken as an insult" but weren't inciting racial discrimination.
"Hanson's got every right to challenge it," Farley said.
"I think if we went through the pub test, I know which way it would go. It'd go in Pauline's favour."
This is the second time Hanson has had to correct comments made by Farley after he said he would display both the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags alongside the Australian flag at his electorate office.
One Nation's policy is to only fly the Australian flag on public buildings. Hanson has described having multiple official flags as "extremely divisive".

North Carolina firm to supply parts for Marine Corps’ NMESIS launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:01:35 UTC
18:01:35 KST

- Corvid Technologies received a $33.86 million sole-source IDIQ contract to build a weapon sled assembly for the NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher.
- The Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps issued the award under FAR 6.302-1, with no funds obligated until individual task orders are placed through August 2034.
Corvid Technologies LLC has been awarded a $33.86 million contract to build a weapon sled assembly for the Navy/Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, the U.S. Marine Corps’ land-based anti-ship missile launcher.
The award is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract combining firm-fixed-price, cost-plus-fixed-fee, and cost reimbursement terms. Work will be performed at Corvid’s facilities in Mooresville, North Carolina, where the company is headquartered. The contract’s ordering period runs through August 2034, giving the Department of War nearly nine years to place orders against it.
No funds were obligated at the time of award, meaning the Department of War has not yet committed any money against the $33.86 million ceiling. The Department of War will issue individual task orders and delivery orders as the work is scheduled, and money will be committed against those orders rather than the base contract.
The Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps, based at Quantico, Virginia, is the contracting activity, and the award carries the contract number M67854-26-D-1008.
The contract was not competitively bid, meaning the Department of War did not solicit offers from other companies before making the award. It was issued under Federal Acquisition Regulation 6.302-1, which allows agencies to sole-source a requirement when only one company can reasonably meet it.
NMESIS pairs the Naval Strike Missile with the ROGUE Fires carrier, an unmanned launch vehicle that Oshkosh Defense builds on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle chassis. Raytheon, an RTX business, produces the Naval Strike Missile in partnership with Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace. The missile has a stated range of roughly 185 km (115 miles). It is designed to fly low over the sea to avoid radar detection before striking a ship near the waterline.
A weapon sled assembly is a structural component of a missile launcher. It supports and positions a missile canister on the launch platform before firing. The Department of War announcement does not specify further design details, integration requirements, or which portion of the NMESIS system the assembly will serve.
NMESIS entered low-rate initial production in 2024, after the Department of War awarded Raytheon a contract worth nearly $50 million to begin building launcher units, with deliveries due by August 2027. The U.S. Marine Corps fielded its first six NMESIS systems to the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment at Marine Corps Base Hawaii in November 2024. Marine Corps Systems Command has said the service ultimately plans to field 48 NMESIS launchers.
Marines took NMESIS to the Philippines for Exercise Balikatan in April and May 2025, staging a launcher on Batan Island in the Luzon Strait. In June 2026, the 12th Marine Littoral Regiment on Okinawa, Japan, received its own NMESIS launchers, giving the unit land-based anti-ship missiles along the first island chain.
NMESIS is organized under Medium-Range Missile batteries within Marine Littoral Regiments, formations built for Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations. Naval News reported, citing a Marine Corps release, that each battery is structured into six sections of three launchers, for a total of 18 anti-ship missile systems per battery. A separate system, the Marine Air Defense Integrated System, provides close-in protection for NMESIS batteries against drones and aircraft.
Corvid Technologies is a small, employee-owned defense contractor founded in 2004 and based in Mooresville. The company employs more than 200 engineers and scientists. It specializes in computational physics modeling and uses an in-house supercomputer to simulate high-rate physical events such as blast and ballistic impacts. Corvid holds an 8(a) small business designation and has previously worked with the Missile Defense Agency and the U.S. Navy.
The company’s existing Navy work includes a contract for short and medium range sub-orbital target vehicles used in missile defense testing, awarded in 2025 and valued at up to $268.4 million, and a potential 10-year, $385 million contract to support Missile Defense Agency test instrumentation. Corvid has also served as a subcontractor to Kratos Defense on Department of War hypersonic flight test work.

‘The line’s running half-empty’: Llanwern steelworks feels the heat from cheap steel imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:00:28 UTC
18:00:28 KST

At Tata Steel’s factory in Llanwern, south Wales, production lines that should be running full-time are now falling quiet for parts of the day, with workers being put on to maintenance and cleaning work while machines sit idle.
There aren’t enough orders to keep them running all the time, the company says, because of a surge of cheap steel coming from Asian countries that is threatening the viability of several UK sites that make similar products, and risk hundreds of jobs.
“The line has been left running half empty, and the result of that is it won’t last very long unless we can find a solution here,” said one insider.
New 50% import tariffs introduced by the government in July were designed to protect against cheap steel from countries including China and India from undercutting UK producers such as Tata.
But for some types of product, such as the galvanised steel made at Llanwern, near Newport, the situation has worsened, after the government increased the tariff-free quotas – the amount of steel that can be brought in without paying the levy – for some countries.
India’s allowance of galvanised steel rose from 98,000 to 125,000 tonnes, while Vietnam’s more than tripled, from 51,000 to 174,000 tonnes. South Korea was given an increased quota of 100,000 tonnes.
The larger quota for India is understood to have been a last-minute move to help get a trade deal with the country over the line, which was first reported by the Financial Times. World Trade Organization rules require comparable exporters are. reated equally, forcing the increase in quotas to Vietnam and South Korea.
Earlier this summer the Tata UK boss, Rajesh Nair, said he was “very concerned” about the new arrangement.
Now, nearly two months later, Llanwern is struggling to compete on price and running at about half capacity as a result. The factory produces about 600,000 tonnes of galvanised steel a year, nearly half the UK’s total demand.
Galvanised steel is a type of steel that has been dipped in molten zinc, giving it a protective layer that can last for decades and stop it corroding. It is widely used in items such as bridges, outdoor signs and car bodywork.
The company is understood to have met Blair McDougall, the minister for industry, two weeks ago, and laid out the scale of the problem facing Llanwern.
Russell Codling, the commercial director of Tata Steel, said: “Our world-class Zodiac galvanising line in Llanwern, south Wales, is already being significantly impacted by the new quotas, and that situation just isn’t sustainable.
“The quotas have the power to turn this around and make us a truly sustainable business.”
Tata is in the process of switching from its old blast furnaces in Port Talbot, south Wales, to a 3m tonne electric arc furnace. The move will reduce its carbon emissions but it cost 2,000 jobs in the region when the blast furnace was closed down in 2024.
The process involves £1.25bn in investment, about £500m of which has come from a government grant. But a steel industry source said prolonged tariff pressure could even endanger that switch.
The person said: “If there is a prolonged impact across a number of Tata Steel’s core sectors that affects the outputs of its downstream processing sites, that in itself could have a knock-on effect on the ability of its electric arc furnace and green steel making to transform the future of the business as they were hoping.”
Alasdair McDiarmid, the assistant general secretary at the Community union, said: “There is no doubt that the increase in duty-free steel imports from China and Vietnam poses a threat to our domestic steel industry, and at Llanwern our members are already feeling the impact.
“We will continue to call on the government to adopt a more robust approach to ensure that the long-term sustainability of Llanwern steelworks is not jeopardised.
“Llanwern is a crucial strategic site for the Welsh and UK steel sectors, supplying top-quality galvanised steel to the automotive and construction sectors. It is vital that the plant and its dedicated workforce have security for the future.”
The government has previously said it will review the quota system before it changes again in July 2027.
A government spokesperson said: “Our steel measure aims to strike the right balance between protecting domestic production and maintaining a secure supply, and final quotas were shaped by extensive engagement with industry.
“While category 4 imports are currently below the quota levels that have been set, we will continue to take industry feedback into account, monitor the impact closely and review the measure after 12 months.”

When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised | Sanghmitra Singh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:00:28 UTC
18:00:28 KST

Scottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.
As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.
In June, we saw disorder and racists assaults in Glasgow as hundreds of masked protesters marched through the streets. Asian business owners were harassed and people were attacked – according to the police – “because of the colour of their skin”. Later that month, a man was charged with attempted murder after allegedly attacking men leaving a mosque in Edinburgh. A video appeared to show him shouting that he was “protecting the country”. In July, a delivery driver was assaulted after anti-immigration protesters, many of them masked, some shouting racist abuse, once again “rampaged” through Glasgow. We have seen mosques defaced with “hate graffiti” – one is attacked in Britain every five days, according to new data. We’ve heard a speaker at a protest outside an asylum hotel in Falkirk calling for a crowd to “keep Britain white”. There have been activists outside the Scottish parliament staging fascist-style demonstrations. It goes to show top-down propaganda funnels to real-life incidents.
I feel this increasing hostility personally, too. Strangers point-blank question me about my nationality, accent, religion or clothes. A stranger once told me that my accent was weird. An acquaintance said immigrants were taking away jobs from locals, after I told them I was struggling to find work despite being qualified. People jump queues and are quickly confrontational. The “outsiders” that Glasgow loved and accepted have seemingly become the subject of derision and suspicion.
I find people staring at me, head to toe, for an uncomfortably long time. A customer in a Govan pub casually remarked aloud that immigrants are criminals and that we “need to go back”. An old lady on a bus interrupted me and my very white, very British husband to tell us to stop talking the way we were talking. Was it because we’re clearly an interracial couple? Is it because we categorically don’t sound like the locals? I’ll never know, but it’s gnawing now at the back of my mind when it never would have a few short years ago.
Colleagues who have been here since the 1980s and earlier tell me that racist violence has happened in Scotland before, but this time it feels different. We’re afraid to step out now. There’s a clear, marked shift in our levels of nervousness. It is certainly more imminent, more immediate – closer to home.
I blame a combination of factors for this unsettling change: the high cost of living, the worsening climate crisis and the rightwing agenda of some of the mainstream media have all increased resentment and suspicion of one’s neighbours. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many people felt that they had been left alone. That the state wasn’t taking care of them as a democracy is supposed to do.
Even a global health emergency, it seemed, couldn’t make for a better world. Instead of a fairer, more equal or accessible society, we have extreme wealth inequality that is persistent and increasing. And it doesn’t help that inflammatory posts are favoured by social-media algorithms. All of this creates a tinderbox in which people of colour understandably feel afraid.
Many places, including Leith and Glasgow, held anti-racist, pro-immigrant, pro-humanity rallies days after the racist incidents occurred. People carried signs reading: “Racism is weird, have you tried hobbies?”; “Migrants make the NHS”; “Hate has no home”. They made passionate speeches about standing up to bigotry. But is that enough? While it was heartwarming to see thousands of people come out, uniting for diversity, inclusion and multiculturalism, it won’t stop a growing hatred and fear of people like me. And so every time I’m out in public now, my stress levels go up. Am I safe alone? What is my exit strategy? Can I even afford to be angry? Others feel it, too.
I understand why many British people feel overlooked and badly done by – it’s true that Britain is unequal and unfair. But I wish that the media would not validate people’s inherent biases and misconceptions, nor politicians legitimise their worst sentiments by calling for reactions like “pure, cold rage”. It is easy to whip up hatred between neighbours, but systematic hatred and divisiveness can take decades to undo. The only individuals who benefit from scapegoating are the powerful.
We have to say “no” to this normalisation of bigotry, violence and othering. We have to focus on the living conditions and inequality we all share. We need to remember we have more in common with each other than with any billionaire. We must remember that the real blame lies with the system that wants us divided. Talk to real people who look and sound different from you. You’ll realise we’re all humans. We can do better than this.
- 
  Sanghmitra Singh is a human rights lawyer and a writer

Is Expensive Bottled Water Actually Better for You?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Water is supposed to be the simplest thing we consume. The premium bottled water industry has transformed it into something that requires a backstory.
Supermarket shelves now distinguish between glacial, iceberg, volcanic, spring, mineral, and alkaline water. Restaurants are introducing water menus, while trained water sommeliers assess bottles by their mineral composition, mouthfeel and provenance. At the extreme end of the category, Svalbarði Polar Iceberg Water sells Arctic water for as much as €100 (around $116) a bottle.
The category’s growth rests on a mixture of verifiable differences and carefully constructed associations. Water can contain different minerals. Those minerals can change how it tastes. But claims about purity, alkaline pH, and remote natural sources can also create the impression that expensive water must be healthier.
According to Michael Mascha, who founded the platform FineWaters in 2002 to train water sommeliers and drag premium bottled products out of the commodity aisle, prices often reflect remote sourcing and difficult transport rather than superior health benefits. Luxury water, he argues, is better understood as a dining experience than as a more effective source of hydration.
Does Expensive Water Hydrate You Better?
There is no established evidence that luxury water hydrates an otherwise healthy person better simply because it is more expensive or comes from a celebrated source.
“Fundamentally, true hydration is about consuming enough water throughout the day to replace daily losses rather than brand status or origin,” says Lucy Semerjian, associate professor of environmental science and technology at the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates.
What matters most is drinking enough safe water to replace the fluid the body loses. Its chemical and microbial composition must also remain within safe limits.
Are the Minerals in Bottled Water Better for You?
Minerals are responsible for some of the genuine differences between waters. As water travels through soil and rock, it can absorb calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, sodium, and other dissolved substances. Their type and concentration depend partly on the geology surrounding the source.
These minerals are already dissolved into ionized forms, meaning the gastrointestinal tract can absorb them. Mineral water can therefore contribute to a person’s calcium or magnesium intake, although its nutritional significance depends on the concentration, the quantity consumed, and the rest of that person’s diet.
The word “mineral,” however, does not tell consumers how much of any particular nutrient is present.
“People see terms like rich in minerals, high TDS numbers, or alkaline pH on a premium label and assume those are automatically markers of superior quality,” says Maria Abi Hanna, cofounder and CEO of nutrition intelligence software Food Label Maker, “when in reality none of those numbers tell you anything on their own.”
Total dissolved solids, or TDS, measures the combined concentration of dissolved substances in water. A higher number does not function as a score for safety, purity, or health. It mainly describes the water’s mineral load.
The same problem applies to alkaline water. Its higher pH is frequently positioned as a wellness advantage, but pH alone does not establish that a bottle is healthier. The stomach is already highly acidic, and the body tightly regulates the pH of the blood.
Consumers should instead look at which minerals appear on the label and in what concentrations. People limiting their sodium intake, for example, may have different priorities from someone specifically looking for a water containing calcium or magnesium.
Does Mineral Content Change How Water Tastes?
Minerals may not transform hydration, but they can transform taste.
“Some waters taste very light because they have very low mineral content,” Mascha says.
Rainwater that has had little contact with the ground may contain very few dissolved minerals. Iceberg and some glacial waters can also fall towards the low end of the TDS scale, producing a relatively light or neutral taste.
At the other end, water containing upwards of 2,000mg of mineral content can have a noticeably heavier mouthfeel and a stronger flavor. Individual minerals can introduce salty, bitter, chalky, or slightly sweet characteristics.
The differences are real. The leap from “tastes different” to “is healthier,” however, is usually where the marketing begins to outrun the evidence. Luxury water makes the most sense when treated as a taste category: something selected for a particular mineral profile, dining experience, or personal preference. The price is not a reliable shorthand for its nutritional value.
Is Glass-Bottled Water Safer Than Plastic?
The most consequential thing about a bottle of water, though, may not be the water itself.
Premium brands often use glass packaging, reinforcing the perception that the water is both luxurious and protected from the concerns surrounding plastic.
“Plastic bottles are sensitive to thermal stress, UV radiation, or extended storage times,” says Nidia Rodriguez-Sanchez, senior lecturer in physiology and nutrition at Scotland’s University of Stirling.
This is particularly relevant in hot climates. Leaving bottled water inside a vehicle or storing it for prolonged periods at high temperatures can increase the migration of substances from PET into the water. Studies have found that heat can increase the release of antimony, a substance used during PET manufacturing, although the concentrations vary by bottle, temperature, and storage time.
Glass is not an entirely plastic-free solution. A 2025 study led by France’s Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety, or ANSES, found microplastics in beverages packaged in glass.
The glass itself was not identified as the main source. Researchers traced many of the particles to the painted coating on metal bottle caps, which could become scratched as the caps rubbed together during storage.
The results also varied by beverage. Soft drinks and beer in glass bottles contained considerably more particles than the same drinks in other packaging. Water contained far fewer particles overall, although glass-bottled water averaged slightly more than water packaged in plastic or cartons.
The study does not prove that glass packaging is more dangerous than plastic. It demonstrates that changing the bottle material does not eliminate every other potential source of plastic exposure.
Mascha’s response to all this is that the anxiety is selectively applied. “Everyone talks about microplastics in water. There’s also microplastics in wine, in beer, and in Coke,” he says.

New travel guide traces Ian Fleming's footsteps in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:59:15 UTC
17:59:15 KST

New travel guide traces Ian Fleming’s footsteps in Switzerland
Even before James Bond was created, Ian Fleming had a passionate romance in Switzerland with a young woman from the canton of Vaud. A new travel guide now traces the writer’s connections to French-speaking Switzerland and Lake Geneva.
In the Footsteps of Ian Fleming in Switzerland, published in English and French by Editions romandes 180°, invites readers to follow in the footsteps of the man who would later become the creator of James Bond during his time in the 1930s. The itinerary includes Geneva, where Fleming undertook an internship at what was then the League of Nations, as well as Coppet and Vich, where his love story with Monique Panchaud de Bottens unfolded.
A relationship as the central theme
This relationship forms the central theme of the book. It led the two young people to become engaged before they went their separate ways. “When he met her, she was very avant-garde for her time,” travel guide author Cornelius Schregle told Keystone-SDA news agency. He highlighted her love of skiing, the high mountains and driving – activities that were still unusual for a young woman from her social circle at the time.
More
James Bond: half-Swiss, totally profitable
According to the author, this story may also have left its mark on the James Bond universe. “The women who populate the Bond universe have something of Monique about them: free-spirited women who take their fate into their own hands,” said Schregle.
At the Beau-Rivage Palace in Lausanne
Fleming discovered Switzerland at a very early age. Among other places, his family stayed at the Beau-Rivage Palace in Lausanne. Later, the landscapes and locations of French-speaking Switzerland reappeared in his work, while certain scenes from the James Bond films, in turn, turned Switzerland into a mythical backdrop.
The travel guide brings together historical and contemporary photographs, maps, archive documents and extracts from the novels. The majority of the places mentioned in the guide can therefore still be visited today, allowing the reader to turn reading into a journey.
With this journey through Switzerland, Cornelius Schregle sought not so much to write a new biography of Fleming as to shed light on a little-known phase of his life. “I wanted something lighter, something more entertaining,” with the aim of enabling everyone to discover these places “at their own leisure”.
Nevertheless, the work is the result of several years of research and encounters, in particular with members of the Fleming and Monique Panchaud families, as well as with the British biographers Nicolas Shakespeare and Andrew Lycett.
It builds on Cornelius Schregle’s work on the links between Switzerland and the cinema, which began with the book Backdrop Switzerland, published in 2016. The latter focuses on films that were shot in Switzerland or used Switzerland as a backdrop.

Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections citing "huge risk" and "split" for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected the idea of holding elections during the war with Russia, four days after the former defense minister publicly called for them.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in remarks made public Sunday.
Ukraine's former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who was fired last month, posted a video Tuesday where he called for the country to be given a chance to go to the polls.
In the video, Fedorov said "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia," and called for a "legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amidst a prolonged war."
"We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state," he added.
The move was widely seen as the largest challenge to Zelenskyy's power since the start of the conflict, but the ousted minister did not reveal whether he had any political ambitions for himself. The president imposed martial law, which prohibits elections from being held, when Russian forces invaded the country in February 2022.
In an interviewed aired Sunday by the BBC, which is CBS News' international partner, Fedorov said the Ukrainian president had "questions to answer" about alleged corruption in his government, citing a money laundering investigation announced last week. He also told the BBC Ukrainians should not be afraid of discussing the idea of holding elections during the war.
"If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for," Fedorov told the BBC.
Zelenskyy fired Fedorov in mid-July, citing an unsolvable feud between him and Zelenskyy's top general, Oleksandr Syrskyi. The move sparked weeks of protests from thousands of people across the country, criticizing the removal of the widely respected minister.
Fedorov was credited with turning the tide of the war in Ukraine's favor, increasing Ukraine's strikes deep into Russia tenfold and bolstering its domestic arsenal.

Hungary Paks nuclear plant could operate at full capacity by Wednesday, PM Magyar says
BUDAPEST, Aug 23 - Hungary's Paks nuclear plant restarted its reactor 3 late on Saturday and the facility could be operating at full capacity by Wednesday, a day or two sooner than expected, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday.
The 2-gigawatt plant, which produces nearly half of Hungary's electricity, was forced to cut output to just over 10% earlier this month, barely escaping a full shutdown due to a historic drought and record-low water levels on the Danube.
• The nuclear plant currently produces about 800 megawatts of electricity, based on data from its operator.
• "Four turbines out of eight are producing electricity already at Paks. Full restart is underway, the nuclear plant could be producing 2,000 megawatts again by Wednesday," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Facebook on Sunday.
• Rising water levels on the Danube, the facility's main coolant source, as well as engineering work done at the river near the plant helped avoid a full shutdown.
• Hungary last week began to construct a riverbed sill, a crosswise dam-like structure at the river bottom, to regulate water flow.
• As a short-term solution, the government sank two barges near Paks to raise the water levels enough so that the plant's two turbines could be kept working while the riverbed sill was under construction. REUTERS

Taiwan’s National Security Council expands role in countering Chinese pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:55:46 UTC
17:55:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s National Security Council (NSC) has taken on a broader role in countering Chinese coercion, according to Nikkei Asia.
Nikkei Asia cited multiple sources as saying the council is driving military and civil defense reforms aimed at bolstering asymmetric warfare capabilities and whole-of-society resilience. The sources said the council is also coordinating with other government ministries and conducting diplomatic outreach to garner international support for Taiwan.
Referring to the military’s focus on drones, Tristan Tang, a nonresident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, said, “The NSC is important because it helps the president develop and coordinate that policy, track how the defense ministry is implementing it, and identify problems that may require intervention,” per Nikkei Asia.
“Militaries are naturally conservative institutions, so political authority from NSC can be important in pushing major defense reforms forward,” Tang said.
Over the past 10 years, the NSC has taken on a broader role because the boundaries among security, foreign policy, and domestic policy have become less clear, a former senior NSC official told Nikkei Asia.
Issues such as international trade policy and technology restrictions are now more closely linked to Taiwan’s foreign affairs and national security decisions rather than being treated separately.
“The NSC has emerged as the core executive power of security and intelligence and policymaking,” the former official said.
An official from a G7 government, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the NSC has played an important role in improving Taiwan’s maritime security, Nikkei Asia reported. The official also praised NSC Deputy Secretary-General Lin Fei-fan (林飛帆) for “truly impressive” work on urban resilience.
“I’m not sure other countries could pull together such an ambitious agenda, at all levels of government, this fast,” the official added.
However, a Western official warned that the NSC and the government must accelerate reforms in asymmetric warfare and civil defense, according to Nikkei Asia.
“The urgency is implementing the changes in the armed forces, not think-tank style discussions,” the official said.
British lawmaker Tom Tugendhat said Taiwan is already facing online and offline attacks, as well as maritime intimidation. Without better coordination, he warned, Taiwan could be “divided and overwhelmed by Beijing before it can mount any meaningful response.”
Britain and Japan have recently moved to establish new intelligence bodies. Philip Shetler-Jones, an Indo-Pacific security expert at the UK’s Royal United Services Institute, said there was room for cooperation between the NSC and these agencies.
Given Japan’s acknowledgment that a Taiwan emergency is also a Japanese one, “it is natural that the new intelligence services would benefit from a link with Taiwan’s NSC as a source of information to complete assessments on a potential crisis,” Shetler-Jones said.
Earlier this month, NSC Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) told Nikkei Asia that the council had not changed its mission but had expanded its priorities.
“In the old days, defense of Taiwan was a responsibility of the (Ministry of National Defense),” Wu said. “But nowadays, thinking about the resilience of Taiwan’s government or Taiwan society as a whole, we need to coordinate among government agencies so that when a crisis comes, whether it’s a natural or man-made disaster, society can understand how they can survive, how they can help themselves, and how they can help others.”

Kazakhstan parliamentary vote to cement president's power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

Kazakhstan parliamentary vote to cement president's power
August 23, 2026
Kazakhstan's 12.3 million eligible voters will elect the Central Asian country's parliament on Sunday.
The polls come after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past.
Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019.
The pro-presidential Adilet party is expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, with a number of smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also pegged to enter parliament.
Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned.
The election is taking place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead.
Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election
Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote is also taking place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom, with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers.
Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, has touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world.
"Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday.
"Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added.
Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union.
Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind.

Russian attacks kill 5, injure 44 across Ukraine over past day, as jet-powered drone hits passenger train in Odesa Oblast
Russian attacks killed at least 5 people and injured at least 44 across Ukraine over the past day, as its forces attacked a passenger train in Odesa Oblast, local authorities said on Aug. 22-23.
In Odesa Oblast, a Russian jet-powered attack drone hit a passenger train that was traveling from Zhytomyr to Odesa, Ukrainian Railways CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said in a post on Facebook on Aug. 23.
There were 593 passengers on board, including 15 children, but no casualties were reported as an evacuation was ordered in time and the train was brought to an emergency halt on the track, Pertsovskyi said.
Alongside the attack on Odesa Oblast, Russian forces launched 127 drones across Ukraine overnight on Aug. 23, the Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defense downed 97 drones over the north, south, and east of the country. Twenty-seven drones made it through and struck 22 locations, and the debris of downed drones was found at three locations, the report read.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, three people were killed, and 20 were injured by Russian attacks, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said on Aug. 23. Russian forces carried out 559 attacks on 40 settlements in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day, Fedorov said.
He later added at around 10 a.m. local time that Russia attacked the area around a shopping center in the city of Zaporizhzhia. A 49-year-old man was injured as a result of the attack.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed and five injured in Russian strikes in the region over the past day, governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region injured 11 people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, three people were injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported on Aug. 23 that overnight Russia launched a drone attack on a post office in the town of Lozova, Kharkiv Oblast, and a fire broke out covering an area of 350 square meters.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured two people over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported, according to the reports published on Aug. 22 and Aug. 23.
July of 2026 saw the most civilians killed or injured in Ukraine since March 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU).
At least 437 civilians in Ukraine were killed and 2,610 injured in July alone, the monitoring group said on Aug. 13. This represents a 30% increase from June, which previously held the record for the deadliest month since April 2022.
Ukrainian civilian casualties in July 2026 were 70% higher than July the previous year, while casualties among children also rose to their highest level since April 2022, with 17 children killed and 166 injured.

Michal is in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday and will co-chair a summit of Nordic-Baltic (NB8) and Ukrainian leaders with Zelenskyy, and will take part in events marking Ukraine's National Flag Day.
Estonia holds the NB8 presidency this year, and Michal's visit comes at a time of intensified attacks by Russia on Kyiv and Ukraine and stalled diplomatic efforts.
The visit also closely follows the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Estonian independence. "This year marks 35 years since Estonia restored its independence and Ukraine declared its independence. Both our countries secured the right to decide their own future. Today, Ukraine is defending that right on the battlefield while standing up for the freedom and security of all Europe," Michal said.
The Nordic and Baltic countries have stood with Ukraine since the first day of Russia's full-scale war of aggression, now in its fifth year. "Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself and resist Russian aggression," the prime minister went on, via a press release.
He noted that "everything Ukraine needs" primarily means more air defense, more ammunition and greater investment in Ukraine's defense industry. "At the same time, we must increase pressure on Russia, strengthen sanctions and close the loopholes Russia uses to evade them," Michal added.
"We are helping Ukraine prepare for winter and protect and restore critical energy infrastructure, which remains under threat because of Russia's brutality," the head of government went on.
While in Kyiv, Michal will meet his Ukrainian counterpart, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, to discuss bilateral relations and preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in January next year.
Michal's visit also coincides with Ukraine's National Flag Day, which is marked annually on August 23.
The NB8 format brings together the Nordic countries — Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden — and the Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — for regular dialogue on security and regional issues. Following the summit, a joint press conference is expected to outline outcomes and new commitments, as Estonia's NB8 presidency has placed regional security and support for Ukraine at the top of the agenda.
Estonia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, providing military aid, humanitarian assistance and political backing, while consistently calling for increased international pressure on Russia. The Reconstruction Conference in Tallinn next January will bring together international partners to coordinate Ukraine's long-term recovery, and Michal's visit continues a pattern of high-level engagement between the two countries.
Michal's visit is scheduled to last one day, with the prime minister returning to Estonia later Sunday.
The summit comes as diplomatic efforts to end the war remain stalled, with Russia insisting any deal must reflect "realities on the ground" — a reference to its control of around one-fifth of Ukrainian territory. On the battlefield, fighting has intensified, while Russia continues its long-range strikes on Ukrainian cities . Ukraine has expanded its own deep strikes inside Russia.

Former spy Jonathan Pollard announced Sunday that he is joining Israel First, a political platform established by former deputy minister Sharren Haskel ahead of Israel’s October election.
Speaking alongside Haskel near the Western Wall in Jerusalem, Pollard said the failures surrounding the October 7 attack had convinced him that Israel needed a new government and new political leadership.

Pollard, 72, is an American-born Jew who spied for Israel while working as a civilian intelligence analyst for the U.S. Navy in Washington. He was arrested by the FBI in 1985 and pleaded guilty to providing classified information to Israel. He was sentenced to life in prison in 1987.
He was released on parole in 2015, and after restrictions on his movement expired, he moved to Israel in 2020.
Pollard has previously weighed into Israeli election campaigns. In 2022, ahead of the previous election, he announced his support for former interior minister Ayelet Shaked, only to withdraw the endorsement later the same day following pressure from figures on the Israeli right.
Haskel welcomed Pollard’s support, describing it as a significant boost for her party.
“Israel First is receiving meaningful support from an Israeli hero who paid an extremely heavy personal price for his commitment to Israel and the Jewish people,” she said. “To hear from him that he places his trust in me is a great privilege and a great responsibility.”

Reaffirming the Unbroken Canon in Ukraine’s 35 Years of Modern Independent Statehood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:42:00 UTC
17:42:00 KST

As Ukraine marks the 35th anniversary of its restored independence, its foundational documents affirm that modern Ukrainian statehood is not a Soviet residue or a post-Cold War accident, but the fulfillment of a long constitutional and political trajectory.
Nowhere is this continuity clearer than in a side-by-side reading of Ukraine’s two modern declarations of independence: the Fourth Universal of the Ukrainian Central Rada (Ukraine’s de facto parliament at the time) proclaimed on Jan. 22, 1918, and the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, adopted on Aug. 24, 1991, by the republic’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Separated by 73 years of Soviet suppression, forced famine, and totalitarian violence, these two texts read like sequential chapters of a single constitutional manifesto: crises engineered from Moscow, an unbroken lineage of Ukrainian state-building, a rejection of imperial rule in favor of uncompromised sovereignty, legitimacy grounded in the democratic will of the people.
But between them is silence that tells us as much about the fragility of independence as the declarations themselves do about its legitimacy.
                                                                                                                                                                         
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul Arrives in Kyiv
Ukraine’s modern declarations of independence compared
Recall the atmosphere in Kyiv during the winter of 1917-18. The Russian Empire had collapsed into revolution, and the Ukrainian Central Rada led by the historian Mykhailo Hrushevsky, had initially sought autonomy within a reformed, democratic Russian federation. But as Vladimir Lenin’s Bolshevik regime launched a military invasion against the fledgling Ukrainian state, federalist illusions evaporated.
The Fourth Universal opens not with abstract theory but with the plain language of emergency, describing four years of war, economic collapse, and encroaching famine, before naming the immediate catalyst: Russian troops advancing on Kyiv to crush Ukraine’s young democracy.
Then comes the constitutional turn: “From this day forth, the Ukrainian People’s Republic becomes an independent, subjection-to-no-one, free, sovereign state of the Ukrainian people.”
Seventy-three years later, history repeated its cadence. On Aug. 24, 1991, in the immediate aftermath of the failed hardline coup in Moscow, Ukraine’s parliament convened in Kyiv.
Drafted by the democratic minority that included former political prisoners, the Act of Declaration of Independence was short, urgent, and historically decisive. Like its 1918 predecessor, it opens by invoking crisis: “In view of the mortal danger that hung over Ukraine in connection with the coup d’état in the USSR...”
It places the decision on three pillars – a thousand-year tradition of Ukrainian state development, the right to self-determination under the UN Charter, and the execution of the 1990 Declaration of State Sovereignty. With those words, the Soviet empire was legally dissolved on Ukrainian soil.
Ukraine’s Act of Declaration of Independence
Set beside each other, the two documents reveal the enduring mechanics of Ukrainian statehood. Independence in both cases was a matter of self-defense, not aggressive nationalism – a bulwark against instability and imperial manipulation, not a quest for territory or glory.
Each marks the exact moment Ukrainian leaders recognized that coexistence within a Russian-dominated federation was impossible – in 1917 the Rada sought autonomy and got war; in 1991 Ukraine was being pressured into settling for a reformed union treaty but got a coup aiming to preserve Moscow-rule over the crumbling Soviet empire.
Sovereignty, in each text, belongs to the people themselves rather than to a monarch or a party elite: the 1918 Universal vests power exclusively in the people of Ukraine, the 1991 Act invokes universal democratic principles and international law.
The aspiration behind these declarations reaches further back than either 1918 or 1991. The 1991 Act’s reference to a “thousand-year tradition” gestures toward the medieval statehood of Kyivan Rus, the democratic customs of the Cossack Hetmanate, and Pylyp Orlyk’s 1710 Constitution – one of Europe’s earliest attempts to limit executive power by written law.
Early modern maps labeled the region Ukraine, terra Cossacorum – “Ukraine, land of the Cossack” – while Orlyk’s own defiant phrase, Ucraina, quae libera semper fuit, “Ukraine, which was always free,” captured a belief that self-governance was inherent, not granted by a tsar. The great Voltaire conveyed this sentiment when he wrote in 1731 “Ukraine has always aspired to be free.”
In the 19th century, the poet Taras Shevchenko carried that conviction through generations of imperial suppression, turning the memory of Cossack freedom into a modern political awakening. Long before 1918, in other words, Ukrainians had already insisted – in law, in cartography, in verse – that they governed, or sought to govern, themselves.
How and why Ukraine’s first modern declaration of independence has been ignored
And yet, for all it shares with its 1918 predecessor, the 1991 Act withheld something crucial: any mention of 1918 itself. It does not name the Fourth Universal, does not acknowledge that Ukraine had proclaimed – and briefly held and fought for – modern independence once before.
That silence is not a minor omission. It reveals how deeply Soviet historical consciousness had penetrated even the moment of its own undoing.
The parliament that voted for independence in 1991 still held a Communist majority, inherited from the very system it was leaving. To acknowledge 1918 openly meant admitting that Ukrainian independence had a pre-Soviet history – that the Ukrainian SSR was not Ukraine’s original or natural form but the product of conquest and forced incorporation.
It meant recasting 1991 as restoration rather than creation: a renewal of sovereignty violently interrupted, not a first arrival at it. Whatever calculus individual deputies made, the effect was to let Ukraine’s newest independence appear unprecedented, experimental, uncertain – Soviet in origin even as it broke from Soviet rule.
The consequences were not merely symbolic. By declining to fasten itself to 1918, Ukraine’s new state missed a chance to root itself in a deeper constitutional memory – to insist that it was not a novice learning self-rule for the first time, but a nation reclaiming a sovereignty it had already, however briefly, exercised and lost.
Instead, the country inherited a subtler version of the narrative it was trying to escape: that Ukrainian statehood began with Soviet power and that anything before it was prelude, irrelevant, or illegitimate.
The perpetuation of a damaging myth
The importance of what had occurred on Jan. 22, 1918, was further obscured under President Leonid Kuchma in early 2001 by his focusing on what had happened exactly a year after the Fourth Universal.
On Jan. 22, 1919, the union of central and western Ukraine was proclaimed by the representatives of their respective independent republics even as they were fighting the Russians in the east and the Poles in the west. Of course, this too is an important historic date. But the seemingly calculated celebration on Jan. 22 only of the “Day of Unity” had the effect of removing the Ukraine’s first modern declaration of independence from national memory.
It is worth recalling that this occurred when the “patriotic” Viktor Yushchenko was already Kuchma’s prime minister. The same president went on to publish a book named “Ukraine is not Russia,” and when Yushchenko was himself elected president he did not set the record straight about the significance of Jan. 22, 1918.
This half-completed reckoning helps explain why decommunization proceeded so haltingly through the 1990s, why Soviet-era elites slid so easily into post-Soviet institutions, and why Ukraine struggled for years to articulate a national identity distinct from both Soviet and Russian frameworks.
Even in 2018, on the centenary of Ukraine’s declaration of independence, the then also “patriotic” president, Petro Poroshenko, observed Jan. 22 in the presence of foreign diplomats as simply the Day of Unity. President Zelensky also seems to be neglecting to emphasize that independence was declared in early 1918 and the attempt to unite western and central Ukraine in one sovereign state followed logically a year later.
Lessons for today
In 1991 the formal empire had fallen; the revolution in consciousness took much longer – and in some respects is still underway.
That unfinished work of memory is not an academic footnote to the present war – it is one of its stakes. Russia’s invasion is not a contemporary border dispute; it is the latest iteration of a centuries-old imperial campaign to deny that Ukraine has ever governed itself or ever had the right to.
Just as Lenin’s forces invaded Ukraine in 1918 under the language of “brotherly assistance,” Putin’s forces invaded in 2022 claiming to rescue a country from an identity it does not, in Moscow’s telling, own. The argument has not changed in a century. Only the weapons have.
The failure to hold the state won in 1918 offers a sober lesson that Ukrainians have not forgotten: internal fragmentation and insufficient outside support allowed the Bolsheviks to conquer a fledgling republic, and the price was seven decades of totalitarian rule, the engineered starvation of millions in the Holodomor, and the attempted erasure of a people’s memory of itself and their very identity.
Ukraine’s 1991 declaration should have said, plainly, that it had happened before, had been crushed, and was now being restored. It did not say so.
But 35 years on, during a protracted war fought explicitly over the question of whether Ukraine has the right to exist as a sovereign state, Ukrainians are saying yes and still reclaiming a thousand years that no empire’s manipulation or internal foes can undo.
Ukraine was not created by bureaucratic fiat, and it was not created by the collapse of an empire it happened to be trapped inside of. It was built on an ancient inheritance of self-rule, reasserted at moments of mortal danger, and is now being defended by a generation that understands, with total clarity, what earlier generations sometimes could not yet say aloud: without a sovereign state, there is no liberty, no democracy, and no peace worth the name.
As Ukraine celebrates its 35th anniversary of modern independent statehood, it is time Ukraine’s current government set the record straight and finally acknowledge unambivalently that Aug. 24, 1991 was an affirmation of what had already occurred on Jan. 22, 1918, and what the patriots of the day were also fighting for.
There are no more excuses for forgetting or pretending that it was otherwise.
The author is completing a book examining Ukraine’s first 35 years of modern independent statehood, provisionally titled “Indomitable Ukraine 1991-2026: The Reemergence of a European Nation.”

Israeli wounded in occupied West Bank stabbing

Israeli wounded in occupied West Bank stabbing
Israeli forces launch wide search in Jordan Valley after stabbing incident in the occupied West Bank village of al-Auja.
Israeli forces have launched search operations in the Jordan Valley after an Israeli man was wounded in a stabbing attack in a village in the eastern occupied West Bank.
Israeli public broadcaster Kan reported on Sunday, citing a security source, that the man was stabbed at a commercial complex on the main road near the village of al-Auja.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Palestinian victims of Israeli settler attacks face battle for justice
- list 2 of 3Palestinian teen shot and killed in West Bank attack, UN responds
- list 3 of 3Over 100 ex-diplomats urge France, UK to sanction Israel over Palestine
The victim, a man aged in his 20s, was moderately wounded, Israeli police said.
The suspect escaped from the scene after carrying out the attack, according to the Israeli army, which launched a large-scale search operation in the area, supported by a substantial police presence.
The army said it had set up roadblocks in the village and the surrounding areas. The military is “in constant contact with the residents and security forces in the area”, it said in a post on Telegram.
Al-Auja village council head Hani Najoum said Israeli forces carried out a major operation in the village, Wafa news agency reported. The military presence also led to the closure of local shops, Wafa cited Najoum as saying.
Israeli soldiers searched a number of homes and collected surveillance footage from private residences and businesses, he added.
The Palestinian group Hamas said the attack was a response to what it called Israeli violations and military operations in the occupied West Bank and Palestinian territories, as well as an escalation of violations at the Al-Aqsa Mosque complex in occupied East Jerusalem.
“This operation demonstrates that our people are determined to resist the occupation in every part of Palestine, despite all the campaigns of oppression, persecution, and escalating terrorism against our people,” it said in a statement.
The incident comes amid a rise in state-backed Israeli settler violence against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Data from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) shows that between January 1, 2025, and June 31, 2026, there were 3,033 Israeli settler attacks.
Some 1,291 settler attacks were recorded in 2023, rising to 1,449 in 2024, 1,835 in 2025, and 761 in the first four months of 2026. That equates to an average of 190 attacks per month in 2026, up from 153 per month in 2025 – a 24 percent increase in the monthly rate.
Teenager critically wounded
In a separate incident on Sunday, a 14-year-old Palestinian was critically wounded by Israeli gunfire during a military raid on Askar refugee camp, east of Nablus in the northern West Bank, Wafa reported.
The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its crews treated a child who sustained a live-bullet wound to the chest, Wafa reported.
Meanwhile, Israeli forces used gas bombs and closed the western entrance of al-Mughayyir village, north of Ramallah, according to video footage and Palestinian officials.
Video clips documented Israeli forces firing gas canisters while blocking the western entrance to the village. The Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that Israeli troops prevented residents from entering or leaving al-Mughayyir, subjected a number of them to field interrogations, mistreated young men, and fired gas bombs towards vehicles.
The agency added that the western entrance is currently the only outlet for the village after Israeli forces closed its eastern entrance in October 2023.

“Today we have another success. We cannot provide many details because of the sensitivity of the operation, but the fact remains. We struck an Iskander launcher near our border. I am grateful to our soldiers who carried this out. This is our operation to hunt down their systems deployed nearby,” he said.

As previously reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine and its European partners have agreed to jointly develop the Freya anti-ballistic missile defense system, which is intended to combine Ukrainian missile technologies with European radars, sensors, and control systems.
The project already involves Eurosam, the manufacturer of the SAMP/T system, as well as Leonardo, Thales, and Saab.
The project’s lead industrial partner is Ukrainian company Fire Point, which developed the Flamingo cruise missile. Last month, the company announced an agreement with the German defense manufacturer HENSOLDT to supply a radar for the system.

'Words being put in my mouth': Deepender Hooda denies calling Sajjan Kumar a 'role model'
Edited by: Karan Manral / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 23, 2026, 14:12 IST
Comments

Congress MP Deepender Hooda (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Deepender Hooda on Sunday denied calling Sajjan Kumar a “role model” following the ex-Congress leader’s death on August 20.Kumar was serving two life sentences in connection with the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and died at the age of 80.When reporters asked Hooda if he had called Kumar a "role model," he replied, “I did not use the words, nor did I harbour any such sentiment. These words are being put in my mouth by those who wish to play politics by undermining the spirit of brotherhood.”“As for the Sikh community, people know that we have always stood by them and supported them in every way. We share a centuries-old bond of brotherhood with Sikhs; our family has been connected with them through both joys and sorrows, and we have stood by them in every struggle," he added.Hooda, son of former Haryana chief minister Bhupinder Singh Hooda, described the anti-Sikh riots as a “grave injustice” and demanded strict punishment for the guilty.“A grave injustice took place; the guilty must face strict punishment; the Sikh community deserves justice — this has been our consistent stance. We stand fully with the Sikh community,” he said.Condoling Kumar's demise, Hooda had termed it a “loss to the country’s political landscape”, and praised the former Lok Sabha MP for his “connect with people and contribution to Delhi’s development”.
The comments drew sharp reactions, particularly in poll-bound Punjab, where the SAD, BJP and AAP hit out at the Congress over its “anti-Sikh mindset”. Leaders from his own party also condemned the remarks.Congress leader and former Punjab chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi described Kumar as a “murderer of Sikhs” and a “traitor”.“He conspired to have Sikhs killed... Far from being a role model, even uttering his name is a sin. If such people become role models, the country will be destroyed,” Channi said.Punjab Congress president Amrinder Singh Raja Warring also sought to distance the state unit from Hooda's statement, saying it may have reflected the Rohtak MP's “personal view”.
AAP MLA from Punjab Kuldeep Singh Dhaliwal stated that the wounds of the 1984 anti-Sikh massacre were still alive in the hearts of Sikhs, calling Kumar’s remarks deeply hurtful to the community.“If a senior Congress leader calls Sajjan Kumar his role model, it raises serious questions about the mindset and politics of the party,” Dhaliwal remarked.Punjab BJP president Kewal Singh Dhillon also said the wounds of the victim families remained unhealed.“At such a sensitive time, describing a key convict in the 1984 anti-Sikh riots as a role model was a condemnable attempt to rub salt on the wounds of the victim families and reopen their painful memories,” Dhillon said.(With PTI inputs)

Pakistan army chief to visit Tehran in continuation of mediation role between US, Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:32:46 UTC
17:32:46 KST

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir will visit Tehran on Monday to continue efforts to bring peace and security to the region, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday, according to a statement by the ministry.
Pakistan has taken on a mediator role in negotiations between Iran and the US aimed at ending the war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Two Pakistani government sources confirmed Munir's visit to Reuters. The first source said that Iran and Pakistan were in direct contact.
A second source said the talks would also address recent developments in the conflict, including US President Donald Trump's threat of tougher sanctions on Iran.
"He (Munir) will discuss peace under Islamabad's MoU, Trump’s warning and the situation after the Pakistan-Turkey-Saudi Arab Agreement and Houthi issues with Iranian leaders," the source said.
Iran threatens military response against US sanctions plans
The visit comes amid heightened tensions as Iran threatens a military response to US plans for sanctions that could further put a strain on the Islamic Republic's ailing economy.
It will coincide with a Monday announcement on details related to the planned sanctions, which US officials have said would be "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran.
Trump had warned of economic consequences against any country that provided "any type of lifeline to Iran" as he seeks to isolate the Islamic Republic.
Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorized oil tankers that try to transit the vital waterway, and Iran's economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions.

Syria expects to resume negotiations with Israel, aiming for IDF withdrawal, foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
08:32:34 UTC
17:32:34 KST

Syria expects negotiations to resume soon with Israel over a security deal it hopes will lead to Israel's withdrawal from Syrian land, a top Syrian minister said, urging Israel to seize a "historic opportunity" as the door for diplomacy is open.
In a Reuters interview in Damascus on Saturday, days after Israel bombed a Syrian airbase, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also stressed that Damascus' priority is to halt Israeli attacks, saying confidence-building steps were needed in this direction.
Washington has been seeking to forge a security deal between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a new US ally in the Middle East, for over a year. But it has proven elusive as Israel has sent troops into Syrian territory and attacked government assets, citing threats to its security.
Shaibani said negotiations over the security agreement had been frozen since the start of the Iran war, but he expected them to restart. Contact between Syria and Israel was cut after the airbase strike, he said.
"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn’t bring results, then we don’t need it," Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently."
The Israeli prime minister's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Sharaa has said Syria poses no threat to other countries, with Damascus focused on rebuilding from 14 years of war.
Israeli officials have talked about a range of potential dangers in Syria since Bashar al-Assad was toppled, with some describing the new rulers as barely disguised jihadists last year, even as Sharaa forged close US ties.
In the days after Assad fell in 2024, Israel seized territory in southwest Syria, citing the need to safeguard its citizens against attack, and bombed scores of Syrian military sites.
US pressuring Israel to return to dialogue with Syria, Shaibani claims
"Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force, and it hasn’t succeeded" anywhere, Shaibani said. "I believe negotiations will resume soon."
No date has been set.
"The US is trying continuously to put pressure on Israel to return to the dialogue table," he added.
Asked how optimistic he was, Shaibani said: "It’s very hard to bet on Israel." But Syria had "very great hope" of building stable relationships with its neighbors.
"Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy" and regional stability.
Tensions over Syria were brought into focus on Tuesday when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase, saying Damascus was about to allow Turkish forces to deploy there. Syria and Turkey denied the claim.
Shaibani said Syria respected Israel's security concerns but that Israel must respect those of Syria, including Israel's use of its airspace, Israeli raids, and arrests in the south.
He said that around the beginning of the year, the sides had "agreed on paper to almost everything" regarding a security deal that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and was tied to its withdrawal from territory seized after Assad fell.
The deal would include several security zones in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, including a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present, and others where Syrian forces would deploy in varying degrees of force.
But he said Israel had sought to evade implementation, adding: "We did not see they had the real will to reach an agreement."
Syria and Israel have technically been in a state of war since 1948. Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria in a 1967 war.
The priority now is to "stop Israeli aggression even before reaching a security agreement", Shaibani said. "Then perhaps we can open the topics of peace and the Golan."
Washington working on conflict-prevention mechanism for Israel, Turkey, Syria
US special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said on Tuesday that Washington was working to establish a mechanism to prevent conflict among Israel, Turkey, and Syria.
Shaibani said there was no agreement yet on the mechanism, which he said must stop attacks and pave the way for the security deal rather than "entrenching... Israeli occupation."
The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Shaibani said Israel had bombed Abu al-Duhur even after Syria conveyed a message that it would not be a Turkish base.
Syria draws on Turkish support in military training and cooperation, he said, noting that this was also the case with Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and others.
Damascus was thankful for Turkey’s support in rebuilding its military “and we won’t forgo support," he said.

Tributes are being paid to two police officers who died on Teesside when a car travelling the wrong way along the A66 crashed head-on into their vehicle, also killing five young men.
PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed when the marked armed response vehicle they were in was struck by a Volkswagen Passat in the early hours of Saturday morning.
On Sunday, Anna Turley, the Home Office minister and local Redcar MP, said it was “devastating” to think about the grief of the families of everyone who lost their lives on Saturday morning. The whole community was “reeling”, she said.
“All of us in the community here are sending our heartfelt thoughts and sympathies to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically,” she told BBC Breakfast.
Turley said it was important to avoid speculation about what might have happened and allow families the privacy to grieve. “I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”
She also said it was important to thank the emergency services who attended at the scene during “a really horrific incident”.
Security camera footage from local houses appeared to show the police pursuit moments before the fatal crash on the A66.
Andy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear two police officers had lost their lives on duty, as well as five members of the public. The prime minister said: “My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”
The Cleveland police chief constable, Victoria Fuller, said she and her deputy had on Saturday visited the families of the two officers to offer condolences and support.
“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” she said. “This loss is being felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies. These were brave officers, protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”
Lauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said the grief among officers was “all-consuming, overwhelming”. She said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling.”
The Tees Valley mayor, Ben Houchen, said in a statement on Facebook: “A horrible and tragic incident in South Bank this morning and my thoughts are with those affected, their families and the emergency services who attended the scene.
“Our police officers are heroes who put everything on the line to protect us, and I know all of Teesside will want to pay tribute to the officers and other emergency service workers involved for the bravery they have shown in responding to this incident.”
The five young men in the VW Passat have not been named by authorities, although they have been named on social media. The Independent Office for Police Conduct has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash at 3.39am in South Bank after a mandatory referral from Cleveland police.
Police vehicles had been pursuing the car before it joined the A66 although it is understood the pursuit had ended before the fatal crash. Ring doorbell footage published by several websites minutes before the crash shows a car being driven at speed down a residential road and being followed by police cars.
Ellie Westerman, who lives locally, told the Sun: “The noise woke me and I shot out of bed. You could feel the vibration in the house as the car went past and the police vehicles followed with their lights and sirens going. It was frightening that cars were being driven at that speed through a residential area.”

Asia is reaching for the open road that Chinese AI offers

Asia is reaching for the open road that Chinese AI offers
Countries seeking sovereign AI want to control their own AI capabilities rather than rent them from a foreign platform
At a recent Apec digital technology and AI forum in Chengdu, ministers across the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum issued a statement in support of open-source artificial intelligence models – a rare point of agreement in a debate often framed as a zero-sum US-China contest.
Across the region, countries are entering that order along three distinct roads: the flagship national model built directly on a Chinese base, the government pilot that puts Chinese systems into public services, and the private start-up that ships on whatever is most open. China’s rising influence flows from aligning with those goals rather than from any strategy that has outpaced Washington’s.
The economics leave little room for hesitation. Building a frontier model costs billions of dollars and demands rare talent, leaving just China and the United States still training at the frontier. For everyone else, an open Chinese model removes the barrier: the weights are free, they run on local servers without sending data abroad, and they cost 60 to 90 per cent less to operate than the leading American systems while trailing by only months.
