“Chandrayaan-3 achieved a soft landing near the south pole of the Moon. Today, it is not only about the soft landing; we have also obtained a wealth of scientific data,” Narayanan said.He described the mission's ability to inspire Indians as another major achievement, saying, “One of the major achievements of Chandrayaan-3 was that it inspired 140 crore Indians across the globe.”National Space Day celebrations are aimed at highlighting India's achievements in space exploration and encouraging greater interest in science, technology, research and innovation.

New museum exhibition in Lovech draws strong interest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:27:02 UTC
15:27:02 KST

Sunday 23 August 2026 08:10
Sunday, 23 August 2026, 08:10
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Lovech’s rich history is attracting an increasing number of young visitors thanks to the new permanent exhibition at the city’s Regional History Museum. Opened at the beginning of July, it has already become the museum’s second most visited attraction, with particularly strong interest among students, families, and local residents, said Silvia Vuteva, curator and ethnographer at the Regional History Museum-Lovech, during a special press conference.
Silvia Vuteva
PHOTO BTA
Located along the Osam River in northern Bulgaria, the city holds an important place in Bulgarian history. During the 19th century, Lovech was a major center of trade and craftsmanship and was associated with the activities of Vasil Levski, who established one of the most important centers of the Internal Revolutionary Organization here in the period before Bulgaria’s Liberation in 1878.
PHOTO BTA
The Regional History Museum’s newest exhibition is spread across seven themed halls and traces the development of Lovech and the surrounding region from antiquity to the present day. Among the nearly 5,000 exhibits on display are archaeological finds, everyday objects, documents and materials related to the city’s cultural, spiritual and economic life.
PHOTO BTA
The history is presented through digital technologies, multimedia and educational materials. Some of the halls also feature reconstructions, including a Neolithic dwelling, a military trench, and the interior of a home from Bulgaria’s socialist period.
Visitors spend an average of between one and one and a half hours exploring the exhibition. Since the beginning of August, it has welcomed 17 groups, including 43 university students.
PHOTO BTA
One of the exhibition’s main objectives is to present local history in the context of the nation’s broader history and to show how the past has shaped the identity of Lovech and its residents.

Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:23:00 UTC
15:23:00 KST

Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
The Level 2 storm which hit Estonia on Saturday has started to subside, though strong winds and rain are still forecast for Sunday.
Heavy rain — with some locations receiving the average monthly rainfall in the space of 24 hours — and strong winds swept across Estonia over the weekend, bringing down trees, causing power outages and disrupting ferry services.
The weather warning has been downgraded to Level 1 (yellow) in western and southern Estonia as of Sunday morning. Eastern Estonia – Ida-Viru, Lääne-Viru, Järva, Jõgeva and Tartu counties – are now not subject to the warning and the weather map is showing green as of the time of writing.
Heavy rain is to continue over Estonia on Sunday morning, with 24-hour totals of 50–70 millimeters and up to 90 millimeters in some areas. These higher figures are roughly the same as the overall average rainfall for August, usually the wettest month, in Estonia.
Wind gusts reached as high as 30 meters per second on Saturday and the Rescue Board (Päästeamet) has been notified of fallen trees on roads and power lines.
The storm also left households without power: On Saturday evening, 3,410 households were without power according to Elektrilevi. As of 9 a.m. Sunday, that figure had fallen to around 2,600, though around half the outages were in southeastern Estonia.
Heavy rainfall of 50–100 millimeters overnight threatened Tallinn's sewage and drainage system, and Tallinna Vesi issued flood prevention advice, including clearing gutters, avoiding parking in flood-prone areas, and reducing water use during the rain.
Urmas Kütt, head of pipeline operations at Tallinna Vesi, noted that during and immediately after heavy rain, the public should avoid using large amounts of water to avoid placing additional strain on the wastewater system. Stormwater should not be directed into the sewer network to avoid overloading the system, and Kütt stressed people should avoid flooded basements and manholes due to electrocution and other hazards.
Rescue Board gets 250 callouts
Rescuers were called out 250 times across Estonia as a result of the storm and its effects, with western Estonia and on the western Estonian islands accounting for nearly half these: Rescuers were needed on 121 occasions in this region. Rescuers responded to 65 storm-related incidents in northern Estonia, 49 in southern Estonia and 15 in eastern Estonia. Most callouts involved removing fallen trees and branches from roads and there have been no known serious incidents nor injuries.
Ferry services were subject to cancellation during the storm but are back online as of Sunday morning. The 8.30 a.m. sailing from Rohuküla to Heltermaa (Hiiumaa) went ahead, and the 10 a.m. service in the other direction is also on schedule. No changes to the Virtsu to Kuivastu (Muhu/Saaremaa) route timetable are currently expected.
The storm also hit Latvia and Lithuania. Latvia's weather service issued a storm warning, outdoor events were canceled and roads were flooded in several places. In Riga, water accumulated beneath viaducts, disrupting traffic. According to Lithuanian media, at least one person was killed after being struck by a falling tree and over 150,000 households were left without power.
Trains coming from Latvia, Lithuania disrupted
The conditions in Latvia and Lithuania disrupted cross-border train schedules, with delays affecting services to both Tallinn and Tartu. "The train which departed Vilnius early this morning will arrive in Riga nearly an hour and a half behind schedule, which will also cause delays all the way to Tartu and Tallinn," Elron spokesperson Kristo Mäe said Sunday.
Mäe added that storm‑downed trees on tracks between Riga and Valga were causing further delays. Elron advises passengers to check its website for real‑time updates. In the opposite direction, trains departing Estonia for Latvia and Lithuania are currently running on schedule.
 
Editor's note: This piece was updated to include statistics on rescue callouts and information on train travel disruption.

blue portals and brick vaults shape DKA’s apartment renovation in rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:14:46 UTC
15:14:46 KST

In Rome, DKA – Diele Kerciku Architetture renovates A12 Apartment, a 100-square-meter home where the existing architecture becomes the basis for a more open domestic layout. Brick vaults, generous ceiling heights and a sequence of enclosed rooms defined the original apartment, and instead of concealing these features, the studio used them as a framework for the intervention.
The clients asked for a larger and more convivial living area capable of connecting the kitchen, living room and everyday spaces. DKA responded through a process of subtraction, opening portions of the load-bearing walls to create new visual and spatial connections while preserving the rhythm of the original openings. The brick vaults remain clearly legible throughout, allowing the historic structure to run continuously through the updated plan.
the bespoke bookcase acts as an architectural element | images courtesy of DKA
BLUE JOINERY TURNS THRESHOLDS INTO ARCHITECTURE
The entrance works as a central distributive axis between the apartment’s two wings. Along it, a long pale-blue bespoke joinery element integrates wardrobes, storage and access to service spaces into one continuous volume. Deeper blue portals mark the transitions between rooms, framing views and giving the thresholds a stronger architectural presence.
In the living area, a large custom-designed bookcase extends beyond the role of furniture and begins to operate almost as part of the room itself. The kitchen, designed by Poliform, introduces a more technical palette of etched glass and steel, set against light oak parquet and the apartment’s existing finishes. These reflective surfaces sharpen the contrast between the new intervention and the heavier material character of the historic shell.
deep-blue portals frame views between rooms and emphasize the transition between domestic spaces
COLOR ORGANIZES THE HOME
The same strategy continues into the private spaces. In the children’s bedroom, a suspended net creates an additional level for play, rest and movement, turning the room into a more flexible domestic landscape. Elsewhere, shades of blue, pale blue and red identify volumes, emphasize passages and connect architecture with bespoke furniture, rather than operating simply as decorative accents.
Lighting by Flos and Artemide further reinforces these relationships, adding depth to the contrast between old and new materials. Through selective structural changes, custom-made elements and a tightly controlled chromatic palette, DKA preserves the legibility of A12 Apartment’s historic fabric while making its spaces work for contemporary life. The result does not attempt to smooth away the difference between periods; it lets the brick vaults and the blue joinery share the room, each very much aware of the other.

Quick hits: A Shoriful stunner amid more left-arm carnage in the 29th two-day Test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:08:39 UTC
15:08:39 KST

Australia vs Bangladesh quick hits: Shoriful Islam's ball of the series, more Mitchell Starc carnage in the 29th two-day Test
Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match.
Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.
1. Shoriful's ball of the series
It wouldn't have taken a rocket scientist to determine that Cam Green held the key for Australia at the start of day two.
The towering all-rounder, buoyed by his drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again looking precisely the player he had for so long promised to be.
With Green well set on 67 and clattering boundaries to either side of the wicket, it was going to take something special to remove the big man.
And Shoriful Islam, having already ripped through Australia's middle order late on day two, delivered something very, very special.
The left-armer's pinpoint yorker swung in late and dramatically, with Green falling over himself in a futile attempt to keep it out.
The ball thudded into the Australian's big toe on its way past the stumps and, after a brief consultation with DRS, was given out LBW to what was surely the ball of the series.
And that wasn't the end of the story for left-arm seamers on day two …
2. Starc continues the left-arm carnage
Shoriful, who was almost inconceivably yanked from the bowling attack after that stunner against Green, ended the innings with figures of 7-48, the best-ever return for a Bangladeshi bowler while playing away from home.
Combine that with the 6-12 Mitchell Starc plundered early on day one, and left-arm seam had returned overall figures of 13-60, while accounting for 13 of the 20 wickets to fall in the match.
And it wasn't long before those numbers were improved even further.
He couldn't manage a wicket in his first set, but Starc struck with his eighth delivery of the innings, extracting some extra bounce to have Shadman Islam caught off a leading edge at point.
And the very next ball, Starc had his eighth of the match, having kissed the top of Mominul Haque's off stump with the Bangladeshi attempting an ill-advised leave.
An almost-customary double strike from Australia's supreme new-ball destroyer.
Starc eventually finished with figures of 4-39 for the innings and, with 10-51, the second-best match figures of his career.
3. Smith takes a screamer after tea
Tailender Taskin Ahmed had set himself well in the lead-up to the tea break, but he fell at the very first hurdle in the evening session.
Lyon's first delivery was a beauty, pitching and turning away from the leftie, who swung hard and found a healthy outside edge.
And Steve Smith, in place at his familiar position at slip, had to have his wits about him to complete a very good one-handed grab.
He's Test cricket's most prolific catcher for a reason, after all.
Taskin, who had provided perhaps Bangladesh's brightest spot in an otherwise pitch-black innings in swatting a massive six over long on in the shadows of tea, was out for 7.
4. The shortest session ever?
With Shoriful in at No. 11, the end was very clearly nigh in Mackay.
However, Shoriful showed in the first innings that he had at least some ability with the bat, top scoring with a rather frenetic 14 from 19 deliveries.
He survived the first ball of his second dig, defending Lyon out into the off side.
But it was all over with the very next ball.
Shoriful had a big swing at one, caught a thick outside edge and ballooned a dolly out to Starc at point, with Australia's superlative spearhead fittingly bringing the match to an end.
With two wickets falling in just three balls, it had to be close to the shortest non-weather-affected session in Test history.
5. The 29th two-day Test
There have been 2,632 Test matches played in cricket's lengthy red-ball history, with 457 of them held in Australia.
As of today, there have been just 29 finish inside two days.
Only five of those have happened in Australia.
And yet, in the last 20 Tests that have been played on these shores, it has happened four times.
Australia thumped South Africa on a Gabba green top in 2022, and then there were two, two-day Tests during last summer's Ashes, one in Perth and the other at the MCG.
The only Australia-hosted Test to finish inside two days before that game in Brisbane four years ago took place in Melbourne against the West Indies, in February 1931.
Eleven of the two-day Tests in history took place before World War I (between 1882 and 1912), a further three either side of World War II (1931-1946) but then none between 1946 and 1999.
Then, since 2000, there have been 13 two-day Tests. The cost of a fast-paced world, perhaps.

'A little more unique': Wrong design accidentally added to Sydney Marathon medal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:05:04 UTC
15:05:04 KST

in brief
- The race medal depicts Allianz Arena in Munich rather than Sydney's Allianz Stadium.
- Marathon organisers have acknowledged the "unfortunate error".
Organisers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon have been left red-faced after unveiling a finishers’ medal featuring a stadium in Germany — thousands of kilometres from the race finish line.
The two-sided medal features Sydney landmarks, including the Opera House and Sydney Harbour Bridge, but also depicts the distinctive Allianz Arena in Munich.
Marathon organisers have acknowledged the "unfortunate error", with the medal showing the German stadium’s distinctive diamond-patterned exterior rather than the flatter design of Sydney’s Allianz Stadium.
"A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers' medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.
"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error, though it's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The medal's reception on social media was light-hearted.
"Oh, dear. Oh, this is bad," said Instagram account @morningcoffeerun, speculating that someone may have mixed up the stadiums in an online search for Allianz.
Munich's Allianz Arena treated the medal muddle with good humour.
"Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!" it posted on Instagram.
"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena — Sydney Opera — Unique Architecture — Both are worth a visit!"
The reverse side of the Sydney Marathon medal features a widely praised blue-and-gold design by Indigenous artist Ambrose Killian, who told the Agence-France Presse news agency that he was not involved in creating the Sydney skyline design.
"My artwork and creative contribution to this year's medal was specifically for the lanyard and the front side of the medal only," he said.
"I had no involvement in the design or production of the reverse side of the medal, including the incorrect inclusion of Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney.
"I take my work very seriously and would like to reiterate that my artwork story, importance and originality remains."
Marathon organisers say they expect a record number of more than 40,000 participants this year, each of whom will earn the medal as a "badge of honour" for completing the 42.2-kilometre course.
"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive," the Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.
"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.
"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

South Koreans ‘intoxicated by stocks’ swarmed market frenzy – and lost everything
‘I don’t think I will ever invest in the Kospi again,’ says an emotionally drained retiree who, like others, is reeling from the rout
It has also raised questions about how South Korea, a tech powerhouse, can progress to developed market status when it hosts such extreme behaviour by retail investors, known locally as “ants” for their tendency to swarm into trades.
“Ultimately many who entered the market may have suffered severe losses and a majority of them could become so traumatised that they lose interest in investing altogether,” said Jeon Suk-jae, a YouTuber whose investment channel has 3.7 million subscribers.
In the two months since the market’s peak, Jeon has seen the comments on his channel, which hosts videos like the one titled “the entire nation is intoxicated by stocks”, flip from euphoria to gloom, broadly tracking the national mood.
Beyond the losses – some realised, some still on paper – there is a psychological reckoning that the nation’s leaders are dealing with.
Demand for psychiatric help is rising and other signs of stress are rattling the public. Police in Busan said they had arrested a man in his 20s who is suspected of attempted murder over the stabbing of a YouTuber he allegedly blamed for his stock losses.

Nine out of 10 unsolved murders in London linked to minority ethnic victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

Killers who take the lives of black people have a greater chance of getting away with their crimes than those who target white people, new research shows.
Analysis of unsolved homicides in London between 2019 to 2023 reveals a stark disparity: minority ethnic British people represented 61.7% of reported homicide victims, but 92.9% of all unsolved murder victims.
Also between 2019 and 2023, black people were victims in 40% of all homicides and represented 73% of all unsolved murder cases during that period. Black victims made up 83.7%, 36 victims, of unsolved shootings and 73.5%, 39 victims, of unsolved stabbings.
The Metropolitan police say the racial disparity is due in part to black people having lower trust in the police, which they say they are trying to improve.
The Met’s head of homicide, commander Paul Brogden, told the Guardian: “We know serious violence disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly young black men, who have the lowest trust in policing. This means sadly victims or witnesses are less likely to come forward and trust us.”
The study, conducted by Action on Armed Violence, also found that deaths by shooting were more likely to be unsolved than those by stabbing. Between 2019 and 2023, London averaged 124.6 homicides a year, with stabbings accounting for 65.3% of all killings and shootings 8.7%.
Yet among the 41 murders from this period that remain unsolved, shootings made up 38%, more than four times their share of overall homicide total.
Brogden said: “As this report outlines, that is an added complexity following shootings or stabbings on the streets, where identifying suspects requires more detailed investigative work, particularly when compared to domestic murders.
“While we use every tool at our disposal such as CCTV and forensics, often it’s witness evidence which can prove vital in securing convictions.”
DCI Alex Gammampila, a senior Scotland Yard homicide detective, said: “There tends to be more planning and thought to it [a shooting], rather than a spontaneous pick up of a knife and stabbing thrust.
“All this makes firearms offences more challenging to solve.”
The average age of homicide victims in London is about 36. However, for unsolved cases, the average victim’s age drops significantly to 28, indicating a notable skew toward younger victims.
Iain Overton, of Action on Armed Violence, said of the findings: “Our data suggest that London’s unsolved murders are not evenly distributed. Instead, they are concentrated among young Black men and in cases involving firearm violence.
“While there are many reasons for why such murder investigations are especially difficult, the result must seem often clear to the victims’ families: those communities most affected by deadly violence are often the least likely to see those responsible brought to justice. This in itself risks deepening existing mistrust and creating the perception of unequal protection under the law. And that can’t be a good thing.”
The Met has a high clear-up rate for homicides, running at nine out of 10 killings resulting in justice. Last year the Met recorded 97 homicides in London, down from 153 in 2019, and the lowest in a decade.
The study says between 2015 and 2024 there were 110 unsolved homicides, 9%, of 1,222 killings in that period.

New licensing for game shoots could stop poisoning of birds of prey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

From the end of August, Land Rovers load up with tweed-clad shooters, who go off to large estates and compete to fill the biggest “bag” of game birds, often shooting dozens at a time – a practice which has long appalled bird conservationists.
Soon, the years-long campaign to stop the poisoning of birds of prey, as well as the release of tens of millions of pheasants into the countryside, could be victorious as a result of government plans for a new licensing scheme for shoots.
The scheme could end the centuries-long tradition, or at least severely curtail it. Currently, about 30 million pheasants are set loose each year by shooting estates for people to pay to shoot.
This number could be reduced if shoots are given licences to release only a certain number of birds. The introduction of licences would also mean estates that are linked to the poisoning or shooting of birds of prey could lose their ability to host shoots.
Beccy Speight, the chief executive of the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), has been campaigning on this issue for many years and is preparing documents to send in an “evidence sprint” to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has committed to consider only allowing estates to shoot under licence.
“We think this is a totally reasonable step to take. It is not to ban shooting in any sense; it is about saying we need shooting to be in a sustainable form, and it needs to be licensed so this wildlife crime can’t continue,” Speight says.
There is currently a licensing scheme for grouse in Scotland. Estates are given five-year licences to host shoots as long as they follow a code of practice, including protecting habitat for other birds such as waders. Shoots that are linked to the poisoning of birds of prey can lose their licence. Speight thinks a similar scheme could work in England.
Deaths of raptors such as buzzards, eagles and hen harriers are often linked to shooting estates because of fears from gamekeepers that they will prey on birds including grouse, partridge and pheasant.
Magnificent white-tailed eagles can now be found swooping in the skies of south-west England thanks to a reintroduction programme. But raptors have faced persecution. Natural England recently found five white eagles in Dorset that had died from the same brand of rat poison. The Health and Safety Executive is investigating whether the poison was used in accordance with legal requirements designed to protect wildlife.
“It makes me feel sick,” Speight says. “All that work, these eagles are amazing birds. It is why we need licensing.”
Seven satellite-tagged hen harriers were found poisoned or shot on or near grouse moors last year. Speight adds: “We find the satellite-tagged bodies and that is probably just the tip of the iceberg- buzzards, for example, aren’t satellite tagged so we can never find or test their bodies. It’s a serious problem that is going on in our natural world.”
Many people shoot sustainably, killing what they can eat or give to friends and family, and keep estates in a wilder condition, promoting biodiversity beyond just the birds which are kept to shoot.
Under a licensing system, this would be preserved. Speight explains: “Shooting is a continuum, from small walk-up shoots up to very intensive bag-driven shoots, and it would probably result in more shooting at the start and middle rather than at that extreme end.”
The shooting industry has been furious at Speight’s campaigning. Roger Seddon, of the Countryside Alliance, recently described her as a “pied piper” and a “puppeteer controlling the environment secretary like a marionette”.
Asked about this, Speight was exasperated: “It’s absolutely not true. It’s the job of the RSPB to drive its cause, which is a world where people and nature thrive side by side.”
Speight is exhausted after dealing with the fallout from three devastating wildfires on RSPB reserves this summer. “They still have people putting hotspots of fire out,” she says.
This is relevant to the shooting debate, too. For example, large intensive grouse moors are made up of dry heather habitat, which involves draining wet peatland and creating a monoculture of one plant. “Heather is incredibly flammable. Dried out peat is releasing carbon into the atmosphere but also becomes very susceptible to fire,” Speight says.
Speight says recent claims that wildfires are caused by rewilding are “nonsense”. “There is no evidence to back that up,” she said. “With rewilding, you get these more broken, natural mosaics with water in the landscape, which creates breaks and holds water in the landscape more. That has to be good from a wildfire perspective.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “Sustainable shooting has an important place in our rural communities, and we want to make sure high environmental and animal welfare standards are in place so that the practice succeeds and we’re protecting our ecosystems.
“We will work with key groups to explore other moves, such as licensing or other conditions for recreational game bird shooting and release. This will begin with evidence gathering and any changes will be subject to public consultation.”

Onshore windfarm applications hit 10-year high in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

Plans for new onshore windfarms in England have reached their highest annual level in a decade, after the government overturned the Conservatives’ de facto ban in 2015.
About 45 applications for new onshore windfarms were submitted in the year to March,according to a Guardian analysis of government data.
Onshore wind power capacity entering the planning system has more than tripled since Labour dropped the blocks on onshore developments within days of coming to power just over two years ago, the analysis revealed.
Before the party’s election victory, applications for about 9 megawatts of onshore wind were submitted in England each month on a 12-month rolling average basis. But by the beginning of this year that rate reached about 36MW a month, according to the data, as renewable energy developers began to return to England.
The onshore wind resurgence is even greater when compared with the nadir of onshore wind in England in the months before September 2023, when Conservative ministers first began to loosen the regulatory red tape on onshore wind developments.
Then, onshore wind applications averaged about 1MW a month. At the time, the Guardian revealed that Ukraine was completing more onshore windfarms than England, even as it was occupied by Russian soldiers.
A government spokesperson said: “For too long, a de facto ban held back onshore wind in England, despite its potential to strengthen our energy security, grow the economy and get bills down for good.
“That is why we lifted the ban, backed the largest onshore windfarm in England in a decade through our flagship renewables auction, and made it easier for farms and factories to install a single small turbine – no bigger than an oak tree – without needing planning permission.”
The Imerys project, near St Austell, Cornwall, became the largest onshore windfarm in England to secure a government subsidy since the ban was lifted earlier this year. The 20MW project is dwarfed by many Scottish onshore windfarms, and underlines the trend for smaller windfarms in England since the ban was lifted.
The Guardian’s analysis shows that since the onshore ban was lifted, the average onshore windfarm proposed in England had just two turbines, delivering 8MW of renewable power capacity. In Scotland, the average onshore windfarm proposed over the same period had nine turbines, with 59MW of capacity.
Only one windfarm with a capacity above 100MW has been proposed in England since the onshore ban was lifted. Meanwhile, there have been 18 onshore windfarms with a capacity greater than 100MW proposed in Scotland over the same period.
In total, England’s onshore wind proposals since the ban was lifted have climbed to 438MW, compared with applications totalling 490MW in Wales and 5,280MW in Scotland over the same period.
Tara Singh, CEO of RenewableUK, welcomed the return of onshore wind to England.
“Onshore wind is one of the UK’s cheapest sources of new electricity, generating power at around half the cost of new gas-fired generation,” she said. “What’s more, new projects can be built quickly, strengthening our energy security and reducing our exposure to volatile global gas prices at a critical time for the country.
“With the new prime minister focusing on driving growth across every part of the UK, onshore wind can make an immediate contribution by delivering investment, skilled jobs and lower energy bills for households and businesses.
“The benefits are being felt locally too. Community benefit funds worth £5,000 a year for every megawatt of onshore wind capacity installed across England are helping local people invest in the priorities that matter most to them – and we have nearly 3,000MW fully operational in England so far. For every £1 in post-tax profit a developer makes, around 37p is typically invested back into the local community.”
The UK’s onshore wind supply chain could add up to £56bn to the economy by 2050 by increasing the manufacturing of high-value components such as blades, towers and cables, according to data from Renewable UK. About 70% of developers’ life cycle spending takes place in the UK, the trade group added.

‘Friday afternoon fraud’: warning for UK homebuyers on bank scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

You are poised to move house and are awaiting the solicitor’s instructions that things are ready to go and it is time to hand over your deposit. When the email arrives giving you their bank details, you set up the transfer and move the cash. And then the solicitor calls to ask where the money is.
Conveyancing fraud involves criminals getting access to an email chain between homebuyers and their solicitors or estate agents and requesting payment to a bank account they control. Sometimes the solicitor has been hacked, but often the homebuyer has been the victim of a phishing exercise.
The scam is sometimes known as “Friday afternoon fraud” as it tends to take place at the end of a sale, which is often timed before a weekend.
The sums of money involved in a property sale mean the fraudster only has to land a few victims to make a lot of cash.
Report Fraud (formerly known as Action Fraud) says there were 3,657 scams involving persuading people to pay into the wrong bank account in the 2025-26 financial year, and these cost victims a total of £101m.
Conveyancing fraud is a subset of this. Between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025 Report Fraud recorded 140 property cases with an average loss of £78,393. In the worst case the Guardian has covered, a homebuyer transferred the entire £300,000 purchase price to the wrong account.
City of London police has warned that this type of fraud isn’t limited to purchases – it’s also been reported by renters who have lost money they thought they’d paid to their letting agent, and in probate transactions.
What it looks like
The message looks just like an email from your solicitor or estate agent. It asks for you to make a payment you are expecting to make but may come earlier than you were expecting.
It may say that the solicitors’ firm has new bank details and the payment needs to be made quickly.
If your solicitor’s email has been hacked the message could come from its genuine address, but usually the fraudsters will be using a spoofed email address so if you look carefully you may spot something slightly different from the genuine company’s one. There may be a missing letter or extra punctuation mark, for example.
What to do (and not do)
Don’t post about your impending move on social media as fraudsters could spot this and realise that you are a good person to target.
Make sure your side of the email chain is secure by setting a strong password for your account and using any extra protection that’s offered, such as two-factor authentication.
Avoid logging into public wifi and using it to check your emails as this gives fraudsters a potential access point.
If you are expecting to exchange on a property soon, make sure you have asked for the solicitor’s bank details either in person or over the phone in a call that you have made to it.
Any message suggesting your solicitor has changed its bank details should be checked out – again ask them in person or by phone.
Take heed of any warnings from your bank as you try to transfer the money. It should tell you if the name of the account does not match what you expect, and when this happens you should stop and check everything is as it should be.
Contact your bank straight away if you have made a transfer that was not legitimate.

Kazakhstan parliamentary elections begin: What’s at stake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
05:55:10 UTC
14:55:10 KST

Kazakhstan parliamentary elections begin: What’s at stake?
People are voting to elect 145 members to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral legislature.
Voting is under way in Kazakhstan for a snap parliamentary election that is expected to strengthen President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s rule over the country. The last parliamentary elections were in 2023.
The election comes just weeks after Kazakhstan, a nation of 21 million that borders Russia and China, revamped its legislative system by introducing constitutional changes and shifting from a dual-chamber parliament to a single-chamber one as it seeks to assert itself as a major democratic power in Central Asia.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Kazakhstan’s train hospital brings healthcare to remote regions
- list 2 of 3Germany arrests Kazakhstan citizen accused of spying for Russia
- list 3 of 3Kazakhstan releases first tiger to restore extinct species
How does the election process work and what’s at stake?
Here’s what we know:
When is the election happening?
Elections for the 145 seats of the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral legislature, is taking place on Sunday.
To enter government, parties must receive at least 5 percent of the overall vote.
Before July 1, when Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system came into effect, the parliament was bicameral, with the Mazhilis (lower house) and Senate (upper house). On the day the new system came into effect, President Tokayev signed a decree calling the snap election.
According to national media outlet Astana Times, under the previous system, “legislation passed through the Mazhilis before moving to the Senate. Under the new model, the Kurultai concentrates legislative consideration, and adopted laws are then sent to the President.”
Under the new constitutional system, presidents will only be permitted to serve a single, seven-year term. However, when his current, second term as president is up, Tokayev will be able to run for a third seven-year term of office, since the introduction of the new legislature resets his time in office.
He won the last presidential election, in 2022, with more than 80 percent of the vote, having run largely unchallenged, as all five of his competitors were unknowns.
International observers will attend the parliamentary election on Sunday.
The OSCE Parliamentary Assembly announced last week that nearly 80 parliamentarians and staff from about 30 countries would be deployed to observe the election.
Who is contesting in this year’s election?
Seven political parties are fielding candidates in this year’s elections.
These include the newly formed Adilet party, Auyl, Aq Jol, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, Baytaq, and Respublica.
Amanat, the party that has dominated Kazakh politics under various names since the 1990s, officially voted to dissolve itself into Adilet – which means “Justice” – a new party led by top aides to Tokayev, in June this year, largely to distance itself from Amanat’s former leader, the previous President Nursultan Nazarbayev.
Nazarbayev, who was once close to Tokayev and considered his mentor, was the country’s president from 1991 to 2019. While he led economic modernisation of the country, his rule was defined by corruption, civil unrest and authoritarianism. He was elected president five times in widely criticised votes.
In the run-up to the election on Sunday, Adilet has been running on the campaign message of “Just Kazakhstan”, pledging to raise household incomes, strengthen the country’s economy and improve public services, infrastructure and digitalisation.
Around Almaty, Kazakhstan’s largest city, election posters – mostly in support of Adilet – have been ubiquitous for weeks, the Reuters news agency reported.
Opinion polls suggest the new party is likely to win a large majority of the vote, with a number of smaller opposition parties, which analysts also consider broadly loyal to Tokayev, also likely to enter parliament.
The Aq Jol Democratic Party is running on a campaign pledging support for entrepreneurship, while the Auyl party is advocating for stronger rural communities and the Baytaq Green Party is campaigning on the environment.
Kazakh political analyst Rustam Burnashev told Reuters that while this snap election offers Tokayev a chance to remove figures associated with his predecessor, Nazarbayev, from the political stage, major reform of the political system is unlikely.
Despite the new Adilet party having been formed to distance itself from Nazarbayev’s legacy, analysts say little is likely to change materially.
“All the parliamentary candidates are known,” Burnashev said. “Nor can one say that the parliament itself will be a transformative one.”
Although Kazakhstan has enjoyed rapid economic growth in recent years, tax rises and inflation have hit living standards.
Atapsha, a fruit seller who declined to give his full name, told Reuters that he would cast a vote, but without any particular expectations.
“I am 73 years old. I’ve been waiting for things to get better for 73 years, but so far, nothing has really worked out. Still, I hope that this year things will finally improve.”
What’s at stake?
In 2022, Tokayev launched the “New Kazakhstan” package of reforms for the political system. A referendum was held on the legislative changes, which came in in July.
Analysts say the upcoming elections will determine if the country’s new leaders can adhere to the renewed unicameral legislature and uphold its foreign policy.
Besides these changes in the country’s legislative makeup, the elections come at a time when Astana is trying to showcase itself as a democracy and key power in Central Asia.
To this end, Tokayev has focused on revamping the country’s infrastructure and economy and expanding ties with both China and the European Union.
The country has also been beefing up relations with the United States in recent years. Last November, Kazakhstan signed a $4.2bn agreement with the US locomotive parts maker Wabtec. According to the US Department of Commerce, the deal will provide Kazakhstan with 300 kits to build locomotives for the Kazakh national rail company, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy.
US President Donald Trump took to Truth Social to trumpet the deal, referring to it as “the largest Railroad Equipment Purchase in History”.
Traditionally close to Russia, the country has preferred to play a neutral role in Moscow’s war on Ukraine and has called for peace. It has also offered itself as a venue for peace talks in the US-Iran war.
In an article published in April by the Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs at Harvard Kennedy School, Nargis Kassenova wrote: “Kazakhstan has begun positioning itself as a middle power.”
According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 6.5 percent to about US$335bn in 2025 compared with last year, using the consumption method of calculations.
“While a ‘lightweight’ by conventional standards, it has assets that make it significant for the rest of the world. Its geostrategic location at the heart of Eurasia makes it both an important connector and buffer between Europe, Russia, the Middle East, South Asia, and East Asia. It is also a regional leader in Central Asia,” she wrote.
Oil-rich Kazakhstan accounts for about 2 percent of the daily world oil supply, with the bulk of its exports shipped to European countries via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium to Russia’s port of Novorossiysk. The pipeline and tankers serving it have periodically come under attack by Ukrainian drones, causing disruptions in exports.

Ukraine: Could ex-defense minister challenge Zelenskyy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
05:46:00 UTC
14:46:00 KST

Ukraine: Could ex-defense minister challenge Zelenskyy?
August 23, 2026
This week, Ukraine was rocked by a series of political scandals. A month after stepping down as defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov addressed the Ukrainian people in a nine-minute speech posted on his YouTube channel.
In his video message, he declares that Ukraine "cannot remain without a fully appointed minister of defense." But, he continues, "the main problem goes much deeper than one position or one ministry."
He says Ukraine's greatest challenge is a "systemic crisis of governance," of which corruption is only a symptom. Fedorov also criticized the fact that no national elections have been held in Ukraine since 2019.
A few hours earlier, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had proposed Yevhenii Khmara to parliament as the new defense minister. Khmara had been made acting minister of defense on July 20, and parliament confirmed him in the position on August 19.
Corruption scandal involving public authorities
When Fedorov spoke of corruption in government authorities, he may not have known about the scandal that would break the very day after he published his speech. On August 19, Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators searched the premises of several high-ranking officials, including a presidential deputy chief of staff, Iryna Mudra, and a member of parliament, Vadym Stolar.
Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) stated that it was "conducting a special operation to expose a criminal organization" in conjunction with the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office.
According to the investigating authorities, this organization was led by a current and a former Ukrainian lawmaker, and involved senior officials from the president's office. Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Mudra from her post as presidential deputy chief of staff the same day.
In his video, Mykhailo Fedorov warns that "it is especially dangerous when society feels that the main criterion for appointing a person is not their professionalism, results, or ability […] but their personal loyalty to the system." He says that a "legal, safe, and realistic mechanism" needs to be found to make it possible to hold elections, even if Russia's war against Ukraine continues for a long time.
Ukraine's constitution forbids elections in time of war
The president dismissed Fedorov from his post as defense minister on July 15. Protests calling for his reinstatement began the following day in Kyiv, Lviv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and other cities. According to polls conducted by the Rating opinion research institute on July 20 and 21, trust in the ex-minister rose from 35% to 65% in the first week of the protests. Of the respondents, 72% thought Fedorov should not have been sacked.
A poll conducted on August 5 and 6 showed Fedorov in third place in the presidential ratings, on 12.5%. Volodymyr Zelenskyy led with 25.2%, followed by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian army, on 16.7%.
Ihor Chalenko, a political scientist from the Center for Analysis and Strategies in Kyiv, says Fedorov's address was an attempt to consolidate the political capital he won during the protests. Even though Fedorov does not present a full election program in his video, Chalenko thinks he is calculating on positioning himself as an independent political player who could stand against Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"For 35 days, people were out on the street. The demonstrations started with the demand that Fedorov be reinstated as minister of defense. But the fear is that the spotlight has moved on from Fedorov, because the protest campaign became increasingly focussed on the fight against corruption and protecting the anti-corruption authorities. So the former minister has decided to position himself politically and secure the status he attained," Chalenko said in an interview with DW.
No opposition to the president?
However, Chalenko doesn't believe that Fedorov has shifted to "irreconcilable opposition" to Zelenskyy. While there is clearly a conflict between Fedorov and the president's inner circle, Chalenko doesn't see this as a permanent rift with the government, and he doesn't rule out a return for Fedorov were he to be offered a position.
Oleksiy Haran, a professor of political science at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy, thinks Fedorov's remarks about elections and a renewal of the power of state send an important signal. However, he too says he sees no decisive change in opposition to the president. "We haven't heard any criticism at all of Zelenskyy," he told DW.
Demand for elections and change
Haran says Fedorov's speech expresses what the people want. Polls show that Ukrainians do indeed want a change of government. However, the political scientist emphasizes that there is a problem: "We agree that Russia cannot dictate to us when and how we should hold elections. But the question is: how should we hold elections if Russia continues the war?"
He believes that in order to hold full elections a stable ceasefire is needed, at the very least, and this is precisely what Fedorov does not mention in his remarks.
Vadym Denysenko, a political analyst at the Ukrainian thinktank Business Capital, believes Fedorov's speech is not an election campaign by one former minister but the start of a bigger political game. In a Facebook post, Denysenko describes two developments he is observing one month after Fedorov's dismissal. First, the social milieu he refers to as "Self-Help 3.0", which includes the anti-corruption movement, has found a political leader in Fedorov. Secondly, some of Zelenskyy's former followers have switched allegiance to Fedorov, and these, the analyst says, are now his strongest supporters.
Denysenko appreciates Fedorov's comments as a contribution to the discussion about renewing the power of state. He points out that these are the same ideas Zelenskyy campaigned on in 2019. Even though Fedorov doesn't directly say in his video that he would stand in an election, the analyst is sure this is what Fedorov's inner circle is working toward.
And, in his view, they have nothing to lose. "If elections were to be held soon, Fedorov stands a good chance of doing well," Denysenko says. "If there are no elections, they can strengthen his grassroots support, and further weaken Zelenskyy."
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

TEHRAN, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Iran's weaponry and defense equipment production has doubled over the past 12 months, a senior official said.
In an interview with state-run IRIB TV on Friday evening, Iranian Defense Ministry spokesman Reza Talaei-Nik said that since the beginning of the war in late February, the country's production of certain strategic military products and equipment had increased more than threefold.
The increase was achieved despite the fact that limited parts of Iran's defense industry sections were targeted during the 12-day war with Israel in June last year, said the official.
Becoming stronger is the only way to counter foreign powers seeking to attack Iran's independence, he said.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities, killing the country's then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, military commanders and civilians. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel as well as U.S. bases and assets in the region.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement. However, the two sides failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal as tensions continued to escalate. ■

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Record-warm overnight temperatures were reported in parts of the U.S. Southwest on Friday as an extreme heat warning remained in effect across parts of California, Nevada and Arizona, according to the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS).
The temperature at Death Valley, California, was no lower than 38.3 degrees Celsius on Friday, breaking the previous Aug. 21 record of 37.8 degrees Celsius set in 1919, according to the NWS Las Vegas office.
At Desert Rock-Mercury, Nevada, the low temperature held at 28.9 degrees Celsius, tying the Aug. 21 record set in 2018, the office said.
The weather service refers to such measurements as record high minimum temperatures, which measure the warmest daily low rather than the highest afternoon temperature.
The office said the warning covered Death Valley National Park, the Las Vegas Valley, Lake Mead, Lake Mohave and the Lower Colorado River Valley. The warning was in effect through Sunday evening.
The NWS San Diego office said above-average high and low temperatures would continue through next week. It said unusually warm nights would limit relief from the heat in some areas. ■

Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100-meter sprint world record in humanoid bot games
A humanoid robot has beaten Usain Bolt's 100-meter sprint record at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, China on Saturday.
The robot, made by Beijing-based X-Humanoid, was able to run the 109 yards in 9.39 seconds, beating the 2009 record of 9.58 seconds set by the Jamaican athlete.
At the end of the 100-meter dash, the robots slammed into a cushion and fell to the ground in order to stop, footage from the event showed, before being carried out in stretchers.
A separate robot made by the same company was able to beat the human record in the standing high jump. The humanoid reached 2.88 meters, surpassing the 2.45 meters set by Cuba's Javier Sotomayor in 1993.
Other robots were not so successful, with some tripping, falling and smashing into pieces during competitions or even catching fire.
Both records were set on the opening day of the Olympics-like event which sees more than 2,000 humanoid robots participating, according to the organizers. The event is in its second year and aims to demonstrate China's rapid progress in the development of advanced robotics, with competitions in sports such as running, table tennis and soccer.
At Saturday's opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination.
Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China's leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations.
China currently leads in the production of humanoid robots, with some manufacturers there saying they have thousands of orders from both government and private businesses. However, some experts say this technology is still mostly used for demonstrations and performances and will take some time to achieve mass real-world deployment.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Torrential rain hit southern Taiwan on Saturday, causing flooding in low-lying areas of Kaohsiung, Tainan, and Pingtung and prompting authorities to step up flood-control measures.
Rain in Tainan continued almost nonstop from late Saturday through Sunday morning, with occasional heavy downpours causing flooding in several low-lying areas. The northbound entrance to the Rende Interchange on National Freeway 1 was temporarily closed after floodwaters accumulated, per CNA.
Water in the worst-hit locations rose above an adult’s knees. Some vehicles became stranded after entering flooded sections, while residents in affected areas prepared sandbags and monitored water levels.
Tainan authorities imposed traffic controls on several heavily flooded roads and operated pumping stations and mobile pumps to reduce the impact. The city government had also announced the suspension of work and classes on Sunday because of the forecast rainfall.
Kaohsiung also experienced torrential rain under the influence of strong southwest winds and a low-pressure system. Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) inspected flood-control facilities in Renwu District and surveyed areas affected by slope erosion, urging officials to accelerate flood-control projects, per Newtalk.
Chen first visited the Bakong Bridge reconstruction project to review drainage in the surrounding area. The Water Resources Bureau said improvements to a nearby canal had increased its flood-discharge capacity. He later inspected ditch dredging on Bade North Road and surveyed slope erosion on Renyong Road.
Heavy rain also increased water pressure in a drainage culvert at a construction site on Niaosong Shennong Road, causing a manhole cover to rise above the road surface. The city immediately placed warning signs and dispatched personnel to direct traffic.
Some parts of Kaohsiung recorded hourly rainfall of 81 millimeters, while 24-hour rainfall exceeded 200 mm. City authorities said they would continue monitoring rainfall, water levels, and flood-control facilities as they urged motorists to drive carefully in wet conditions.
The Central Weather Administration said Taiwan would remain under the influence of a low-pressure belt and strong southwest winds Sunday, bringing abundant moisture to southern Taiwan. CWA forecaster Yeh Chih-chun (葉致均) said Taiwan was situated within a broad low-pressure belt containing several developing low-pressure systems, per CNA.
Rain was expected throughout the day in areas south of Chiayi, while northern Taiwan could see afternoon thunderstorms. Rainfall was expected to increase in mountainous areas of eastern Taiwan from Sunday night, with heavy or torrential rain possible. Yeh said rainfall over the previous 24 hours in southern Taiwan, particularly Kaohsiung and Pingtung, generally reached 250–300 mm.
Northern Taiwan also experienced localized heavy thunderstorms Saturday afternoon, with Fugui Cape in New Taipei City recording the day’s highest hourly rainfall at 101.5 mm. Meanwhile, Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of the year, was located over open waters east of Taiwan, according to the CWA.
The weather agency said the tropical depression previously located north of Taiwan had moved ashore in China’s Zhejiang province and weakened into a low-pressure system.

Licence to savour: Hong Kong craft brewers push for on-site beer permits

Unknown Publisher

14:26:52 KST

Untapped market: Hong Kong’s craft breweries push for permits to serve guests
Brewers in industrial buildings say licensing rules prevent them from hosting tours and walk-in customers, missing out on tourist revenue
When a 100-member tour group from South Korea approached a Hong Kong craft beer manufacturer about a visit and tasting session, the operator declined their request.
The refusal was not due to a lack of confidence in the product or a staff shortage. The brewery simply lacked a licence to serve beer on the premises.
“It is not easy doing manufacturing in Hong Kong,” said Luke Yardley, founder of local craft beer brewery Yardley Brothers.
“It is just a missed opportunity when in every other country – if you are in London, New York, Dublin – customers can go for a day out and visit the brewery. They get to have a nice experience where they can consume alcohol on site. And the key thing is they can buy alcohol on site.”
Yardley is not alone. Many of Hong Kong’s craft beer manufacturers operate in industrial buildings under food factory licences to house their giant equipment and save costs, which makes applying for liquor licences difficult.
The situation has prompted calls for a review of the licensing regime governed by the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department to allow breweries to offer samples for walk-in customers, which industry leaders and a lawmaker have said could help support tourism.

Buc-ee’s chain draws outcry in Ohio for launching fight over a mini mart’s beaver logo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
05:23:02 UTC
14:23:02 KST

Buc-ee’s chain draws outcry in Ohio for launching fight over a mini mart’s beaver logo
BEAVERCREEK, Ohio (AP) — A lip-licking alligator, a smiling moose and a hat-wearing bear are among the many cartoon animals to have found themselves in the crosshairs of Buc-ee’s, the popular Texas convenience store chain that has a penchant for protecting its buck-toothed beaver.
But now Buc-ee’s has set off a Buckeye backlash across Ohio and beyond after taking on a beaver in the city of Beavercreek.
It’s yet another Buc-ee’s Ltd. trademark infringement lawsuit. Supporters of Beaver’s Mini Mart have attacked Buc-ee’s online and boycotted the stores, and the mini mart’s home city passed a resolution making the beaver an official part of its history. British comedian John Oliver has even weighed in on the kerfuffle.
On an episode of “Last Week Tonight with John Oliver,” the comedian detailed Buc-ee’s aggressive history of trademark lawsuits targeting various woodland creatures and launched a website hawking merchandise bearing a knockoff “Buc-off” logo and a squirrel mascot named Mr. Nutterbutter. On X, #boycottbucees trended.
Buc-ee’s sued Beaver’s Mini Mart in late July, four months after the chain known for its extensive food offerings and massive restrooms opened its first Ohio store less than a half-hour’s drive away.
Buc-ee’s argues the shop’s beaver logo too closely resembles the convenience store giant’s branded Buc-ee (“Bucky”) beaver. The Texas-based company asked for a jury trial in federal court in Ohio.
Buc-ee’s claims a right to protect its valuable logo
Beaver’s Mini Mart occupies a long, low building with a shingle roof at a suburban intersection. In contrast, the new 74,000-square-foot (6,875-square-meter) Buc-ee’s off Interstate 70 near Dayton has more than 100 gas pumps, 24 electric vehicle chargers and 700 parking spaces. A second Ohio store has been approved to open in 2028.
While preparing to enter the state in February, Buc-ee’s sued the northern Ohio holding company for Mickey Mart gas stations, arguing its Mickey the Moose logo could be confused with Buc-ee. (The company’s response: “A moose is not a beaver.”)
The Buc-ee’s beaver logo features the face of a beaver with prominent buck teeth wearing a red ball cap against a yellow backdrop. The Beaver’s Mini Mart mascot is a full beaver, unclothed, waving and smiling against a white background.
Customers have been critical of Buc-ee’s decision to target the much smaller store.
“I love Buc-ee’s, but I don’t plan on going back until they start making better business decisions,” Austin Collins, 32, a project manager from Fairborn, said outside Beaver’s, where he was making his first visit to protest the lawsuit.
He called targeting a beaver-named business in Beavercreek “a little spiteful.” License plates from three states were visible in the parking lot.
Buc-ee’s has defended the lawsuit as protective of its valuable trademark. In a statement on its website, the company said it first learned of Beaver’s Mini Mart when its owner, Vic Boparai, filed a trade name registration on Oct. 23.
The small business, incorporated in 2017, changed its name from Hanes Road Carryout to Beaver’s Mini Mart in January 2025, according to the paperwork. That was about four months after Buc-ee’s broke ground near Dayton. Recognizing a conflict, the company said it repeatedly attempted to reach Boparai without success, so it was forced to sue.
Boparai has since issued a statement of his own, though without addressing the company’s concerns nor the merits of the lawsuit.
“We want to say thank you to the community and the entire country for supporting us and our business,” he said. “We are overwhelmed by your support for our business and other small businesses everywhere.”
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Boparai at Beaver’s Mini Mart or by calling the store.
Beavercreek adopts the beaver as part of city history
Beavercreek City Council responded to the dust-up by passing a resolution Aug. 10 making the beaver a permanent and official part of its 200-plus-year history. Bucky the Beaver, mascot of the Beavercreek Local Schools, visited the meeting ahead of the unanimous vote.
On social media, images lampooning the fight are rampant. One showed the Ohio State University football mascot, Brutus Buckeye, tackling Buc-ee the beaver.
Support has taken other forms, too. One was a GoFundMe campaign aimed at assuring that costs associated with the lawsuit don’t put Beaver’s Mini Mart out of business, as has happened to other establishments Buc-ee’s sued. It had raised at least $69,000.
The mini mart gave permission to The Original Goodie Shop bakery in Upper Arlington to use its logo on a signature cookie, with $1 from each one sold going to support Beaver’s legal fees. Cake, Hope & Love, a Beavercreek bakery, also is offering cookies adorned with buck-toothed beavers that urge shopping local.
Other Dayton-area businesses — including a Lego store and a root beer shop — temporarily altered their logos to include beavers in a show of solidarity. Dozens of businesses in Beavercreek already incorporate the city name or word beaver in their names.
Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who attended and praised the grand opening of the Dayton-area Buc-ee’s store in April, described the lawsuit as “absurd.”
“It is Beavercreek, for heaven’s sake,” the governor told reporters.

Alibaba to issue US$10 billion in new shares for huge AI push amid strong investor demand
The Chinese tech giant is going ‘full stack’, expanding beyond retail into chips, cloud and large language models as surging spending weighs on quarterly profits
Alibaba Group Holding will issue HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) worth of new shares and use all of the proceeds to invest in AI, the Chinese tech giant said on Sunday.
The move aims to “extend the company’s global AI leadership”, it said, adding that Alibaba would use the funds raised to “invest in its full-stack AI capabilities”, including expanding and enhancing its AI infrastructure.
The decision underscores Alibaba’s efforts over the past few years to transform from an e-commerce giant into a full-stack AI player with businesses spanning chips, computing infrastructure, large language models and AI applications.
Banks have received pre-launch indications of interest in excess of the deal size “on the back of strong interest received from sovereign wealth funds and global long-only investors”, according to a person familiar with the matter. Alibaba increased the size of the offering to HK$80 billion because of strong investor demand, the source added.
Last week, Alibaba announced a 45 per cent year-over-year jump in its April-to-June quarterly revenue in cloud and AI businesses, with capital expenditure expanding 75 per cent from a year earlier to 67.7 billion yuan (US$10 billion).
Alibaba was expecting its investments in AI computing to break even within three years, with the payback period potentially shortened to about two years as gross margins continued to rise, Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu Yongming said during an earnings call on Thursday.

Hong Kong may issue typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as Narra approaches
Observatory says storm expected to head towards southwestern tip of Guangdong province early next week
The Hong Kong Observatory may issue a typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as a tropical storm edges closer to the region.
“Tropical Cyclone Narra is expected to linger over the vicinity of Beibu Wan today and tomorrow, and then turn northeastwards gradually later on Monday to Tuesday, edging closer to the vicinity of Leizhou Peninsula,” the forecaster said on Sunday.
Leizhou Peninsula sits at the far southwestern tip of Guangdong province, some 400km (248.5 miles) west-southwest of Hong Kong.
“The Observatory will closely monitor its movement and the change in local wind conditions, and assess the need for issuing tropical cyclone warning signals on Tuesday or Wednesday,” it added, urging the public to pay attention to the latest weather information.
Narra is named after a tree species in the Philippines.
According to the forecast, there will be showers and squally thunderstorms early next week. The city’s temperatures will rise from 27 degrees Celsius (80.6 Fahrenheit) to 33 degrees on Friday.

Café Clement, London WC2: ‘Turns out it’s really rather good’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

Café Clement, the all-day restaurant inside Nick Jones’ new St Clement Hotel at 180 The Thames in central London, opened with a bang in June and immediately rocketed to the top of every “sell your grandmother for a terrace table” list in London. Which isn’t that much of a surprise, seeing as Jones, founder of Soho House, is the master of restaurant rumpus.
Within days, Stanley Tucci, Nick Grimshaw and full-length-trouser-phobic heart-throb Paul Mescal were all there, tucking into oeufs mayonnaise and lobster omelettes while politely ignoring the fact that the place was still, in many ways, a building site. The hotel itself isn’t due to open fully until early autumn, when a rooftop restaurant, Lunette, will also arrive with some of London’s most wondrous views and Florence Knight at the helm. Still, Café Clement opened to frothy praise, and I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany and, frankly, lunch is not free.
Café Clement is elegant but not overdone: white linen, vintage Cassina chairs. The staff, of whom there appear to be about 345, are a joy: everyone seems to have been hired for their personality and for having the chops to nail a busy service. There’s an open kitchen behind ornate glass screens, a south-facing terrace that gives itself to debauchery and a garden out the back. The menu, which is that of a broadly European, fancy, all-day bistro, offers the likes of spatchcocked chicken with speck and green bean vinaigrette, Dorset crab with marinated tomatoes and aïoli, and hearty meat and fish casseroles. There are pastas and grills, plus chocolatey, tarty things on the pudding menu.
As with most central London celebrity brasseries, the food offering here is designed to mollify and comfort: steak haché with crinkle-cut chips, roast duck with dripping potatoes, with cosmos on the cocktail menu and a hulking sharing chocolate mousse that will soothe any recent knock-back for a starring role. And if anyone can keep all of this classy, it’s chef Danny Bohan, who spent 20-odd years at the River Cafe, most recently as head chef, working alongside Rose Gray and Ruth Rogers, both of them names that make foodies genuflect. A reader told me recently that his life’s ambition was to eat at the River Cafe, where starters run to £51, pastas to £46 and mains to £69. Unfortunately, his partner misunderstood the assignment entirely and booked the now defunct and unmissed Rainforest Café in Piccadilly instead. Here’s hoping said errant partner finds out about Café Clement and tries to make amends by booking a table, because it turns out that it’s really rather good.
Café Clement’s food offering could be merely passable and many would turn a blind eye, but it’s pleasing and careful in equal measure. A plate of eggs mayonnaise arrives jammy and generously stuffed, the mayo earthy and mustardy without ever tipping into sickly. The eggs are served starkly – there’s no trout roe, no caviar – and they are all the better for it. You get the sense that this is a kitchen that wants to spend money on exceptional produce, rather than on garnishes that may well end up in the bin. The cheese soufflé is stunning: upright, luscious, deeply cheesy. A sharply pickly, well-seasoned steak tartare comes free-form on the plate, and is served with carta di musica Sardinian flatbread. Sea bass carpaccio is simply and beautifully arranged, all sweet and sharp in exactly the right proportions. A side of summer beetroots at £7 is, quite frankly, gorgeous: sweet, plump, properly baked, buttery, and made me wonder why baked beets aren’t on every side menu going.
Not everything lands, however. The fish casserole is thin and pale, a bouillabaisse in search of a meaning: some mussels, a piece of fish, not a lot else. Definitely good for those on a diet, though. A side of crinkles, or retro potato wedges, meanwhile, isn’t really worth the carbs. The £18 chocolate mousse for two, on the other hand, turns up with the energy of an unstructured brownie and the ability to put you on your back with a sugar high. Neither of those things is a quibble. A fresh, wobbly slice of custard tart is delightful, and comes with a mush of sweet strawberries and more custard.
Café Clement quietly surpasses expectations, and I’d go back any day. It is fun, joyous and well thought out. As this stretch of the Thames around 180 The Strand finally starts to flourish, it will become even more useful and ridiculously difficult to get into. Come for the celeb rumpus, and, if none of them is there, stay for the oeufs mayonnaise.
- 
  Café Clement St Clement, 180 The Thames, 12 Temple Place, London WC2, 020-4632 6660. Open all week, 7am-11pm (9pm Sun). From about £60 a head for three courses, plus drinks and service
