Erdogan, Netanyahu trade jabs after Turkey seeks arrest warrant for Israel PM
Turkey and Israel traded barbs on Friday after Ankara announced it had sought an international arrest warrant for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accusing him of "genocide" linked to the interception of a Gaza-bound aid flotilla.
Turkey has become a virulent critic of Israel's war in Gaza, following Palestinian movement Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has frequently accused Netanyahu of "genocide".
Israel's interception of the flotilla carrying some 430 activists in May sparked an international outcry. France, Italy and Australia have also launched judicial proceedings.
Turkey's Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X that his ministry had asked the interior ministry to issue an Interpol red notice for Netanyahu and another Israeli, named as Afek Moskovitch, "as part of the judicial proceedings concerning the attack in international waters on the Flotilla activists".
Netanyahu and Moskovitch are being prosecuted for "crimes against humanity, genocide, aggravated deprivation of liberty, 'intentional assault and battery,' torture, destruction of property, aggravated looting, and hijacking of transport vehicles," the ministry said.
In a statement, Netanyahu's office said Israel was "unimpressed by Turkey's hypocrisy".
"Erdogan is an antisemitic dictator who massacred Kurds, supports the massacre of the Hamas terrorist organisation, and oppresses his own people," it added.
'Outrageous ravings'
It added that Israel would "continue to act forcefully against Turkey's attempts to destabilise the region" -- an apparent reference to a previous accusation that Ankara was seeking to establish a military presence in Syria, where authorities said Israel bombed an air base near the Turkish border this week.
Turkey quickly fired back, with Erdogan's office calling the remarks "outrageous ravings" and accusing Netanyahu's government of "seeking to evade accountability".
Pointing to upcoming polls in which Netanyahu's job is on the line, it added: "This kind of cheap politics by Netanyahu and his associates, which is also intended to give him an electoral advantage, carries no weight whatsoever."
According to Turkey's IHA news agency, Netanyahu's co-accused, Afek Moskovitch, is an Israeli soldier, who is also accused over actions in Gaza.
IHA, citing the indictment, said Moskovitch had posted footage on Instagram showing tanks and a bulldozer destroying buildings at the Islamic University of Gaza, including a hospital and medical faculty.
About 50 vessels were in the Global Sumud Flotilla that left Turkey in May heading for the besieged Palestinian territory. The activists were detained in the Mediterranean by the Israeli military and then taken to an Israeli prison before being expelled.
Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir also sparked outrage by releasing a video showing himself taunting flotilla activists who were on their knees with their hands tied behind their backs.

South Korea sending first container ship through Arctic route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:46:22 UTC
01:46:22 KST

South Korea sending first container ship through Arctic route
The PanStar Acro, bound for Europe via the Arctic, is testing whether a route opened by melting sea ice can be commercially viable.
A South Korean container ship is sailing to Europe via the Arctic, in the nation’s first commercial voyage on the route to test its viability as the war in the Middle East rattles global shipping.
The PanStar Acro set sail from Busan New Port on Saturday. “We would like to inform you that the vessel for the Arctic route trial voyage departed” at 9:30pm (12:30 GMT), Seoul’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said in a statement to the AFP news agency.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4South Korea footballers urge safety after extreme heat statistics
- list 2 of 4Putin warns of tit-for-tat seizures of European vessels
- list 3 of 4Activists’ bid to sue Russia over climate change gets off to shaky start
- list 4 of 4Can China’s new Arctic sea route to Europe replace Middle East chokepoints?
The PanStar Acro will sail north, the Reuters news agency reported, hugging eastern Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, then cross the Bering Sea, and take the Northern Sea Route, stopping in Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and Poland’s Gdansk before returning.
The 2,758 TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit) container ship operated by South Korea’s PanStar has secured 837 TEU of cargo, including car parts, chemical products and about 100 empty containers on the government-backed voyage.
The journey is expected to take 40 to 45 days, according to the Oceans Ministry.
President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping a priority for South Korea, with the hope of turning the southeastern port of Busan into a global maritime hub and position the Arctic as a regular trade route by 2030.
But this new route has been criticised for several different reasons. Environmental groups have warned the route could accelerate polar ice melt, meaning the increase in shipping could worsen global warming.
The project also risks increasing friction with Western allies hoping to keep Russia isolated in its war with Ukraine. Seoul has consulted with Moscow about the journey, Reuters reported, including whether the ship needed help to tackle any problems, such as getting stuck in ice.
Last year, 103 transits through the route were made by 88 vessels, up from 97 in 2024 and 43 in 2022, chiefly from nations such as Russia and China, according to Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics.
But with the Iran war affecting global shipping, governments and shipping firms are scrambling to seek different routes, with the Arctic route increasingly viewed as a viable alternative due to technological advances and environmental degradation.
South Korea’s Vice Oceans Minister Nam Jae-hon said the Arctic route was “bound to become an alternative” to Middle Eastern shipping lanes.
The usual maritime route between Asia and Europe runs through the Suez Canal, but travelling through the Arctic can cut the journey by approximately 7,000 kilometres (4,300 miles) and about 10 days, according to the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.
However, major carriers including CMA CGM, MSC and Hapag-Lloyd have pledged to avoid Arctic shipping routes due to pressure from environmental groups. The Arctic sea route is believed to be accessible only during the time of year when the ice is melted enough to allow transits without icebreakers.
“The Northern Sea Route has become increasingly viable as the Arctic warms about four times faster than the global average, leading to a sharp decline in sea ice,” South Korean environmental group Paran Ocean Citizen Science Center said in a statement last year. “But making the route commercially viable would require further warming, putting the policy at odds with efforts to combat climate change.”

A Taiwanese passenger last week posted on social media their experience of taking an Etihad Airways flight from Abu Dhabi to Taipei earlier this month.
They said that upon arrival at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, the inflight announcement said “Welcome to Taiwan” in English, but “Welcome to Taiwan, China,” in Chinese, and also warned that bringing meat products from abroad could result in a penalty from the “Chinese government.”
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
The passenger said that they immediately asked a flight attendant whether referring to Taiwan as “Taiwan, China” reflects the airline’s policy. The cabin manager said that the announcement was read from a script and that the passengers could raise the issue with the company.

“The Republic of China, Taiwan, is an independent sovereign nation, and is not subordinate to the People’s Republic of China, which is an objective fact and the internationally recognized ‘status quo,’” the ministry said.

Trump tariffs hit as Canada tries to curb US reliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:58 UTC
01:45:58 KST

US President Donald Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on certain Canadian goods, which took effect yesterday, delivered another blow to bilateral trade, renewing focus on Ottawa’s efforts to reduce dependence on its southern neighbor.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s strategy involves a search for new markets, a focus on domestic trade and the launch of major projects.
The two economies are heavily inter-connected, with about 70 percent of all Canadian exports heading to the US.
Photo: Reuters
Previous Trump levies on autos, steel, aluminum and lumber have hit Canada hard, forcing job losses and stunting growth.
Canada has even entered a technical recession this year after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction.
The latest tariffs came into force after days of negotiations failed to produce an agreement.
They impact about US$20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the US, targeting products ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
Carney said Canada would match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”
The exports affected by the US tariffs include products that were previously protected under the North American trade pact, the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).
At first glance, “that’s frightening,” Laval University international economic law professor Richard Ouellet said.
“Until now, the USMCA acted as kind of a shield. The Americans are opening a breach,” he said.
Trump declined to renew the USMCA on July 1, making it subject to annual reviews.
While Trump ditching USMCA exemptions could forecast more extreme measures to come, Canada’s largest bank, RBC, predicted that the first package of 50 percent tariffs would not “significantly change broader Canadian growth.”
“That’s because the new tariffs, while significant, will still impact a small segment of total trade,” RBC said, adding that about 80 percent of Canadian goods would still enter the US tariff-free.
Since taking office in March last year, Carney has focused on diversifying economic partnerships to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US market.
“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said in a statement following the breakdown of negotiations with Washington. “We will not allow any nation to determine our future.”
Carney has headed to China, India and Saudi Arabia, and made several stops in Europe seeking deals to expand Ottawa’s economic relationships overseas.
In January, he signed a preliminary agreement with China, providing for the import of electric vehicles to Canada.
Relations with Europe have also been bolstered. Canada last month selected the German firm TKMS to build its new fleet of submarines.
Canada’s central bank last month said the economy was “showing signs of improving,” adding that some businesses were adjusting to US protectionism, including by finding new customers abroad.
A report from the Canadian minister of international trade said that last year, the value of exports to non-US markets jumped by 11 percent, hitting 33 percent at one point — the highest level in more than four decades.

Kaohsiung family falls ill from eating wild mushrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

The Kaohsiung Department of Health yesterday urged people not to eat wild mushrooms, as it reported that a family had sought hospital treatment after reportedly eating unidentified mushrooms picked in a grassland.
High temperatures and rainfall in the south made it easier for poisonous mushrooms to grow in grasslands, the department said.
A hospital on Friday reported that a family of three had sought emergency treatment for symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea and headaches after reportedly eating wild white mushrooms.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
The family on Thursday evening cooked unidentified mushrooms that a friend had picked in a grassland and given to them. Later that night, they began experiencing symptoms of food poisoning and sought treatment. One family member was hospitalized due to severe symptoms, the department said.
The department said some poisonous mushrooms look similar to edible mushrooms, making it difficult for members of the public to identify them safely based only on appearance, color or comparisons with online images.
The “green-spored parasol” is commonly found in Taiwan and is one of the poisonous mushrooms frequently eaten by mistake, it said, adding that it is medium to large in size and often found in open outdoor spaces at low elevations and on Taiwan’s plains.
Its gills are initially white, turning greenish-yellow or grayish-green as it matures, and it can easily be confused with edible species such as the parasol mushroom (Macrolepiota procera) or the termite mushroom (Termitomyces eurrhizus), it added.
Accidental ingestion can cause intense gastrointestinal distress within one to three hours, with common symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloody stool and dehydration, the department said.
The severity of symptoms can vary depending on a person’s condition and the amount consumed, but anyone who accidentally ingests a wild mushroom or feels unwell after eating one should seek medical attention as soon as possible, it said.
People should remember never to pick, cook or eat unknown wild mushrooms to prevent food poisoning, it added.
Separately, the Penghu County Health Bureau last month urged the public to avoid picking or eating wild plants and mushrooms or giving or receiving them as gifts, and to be mindful of the sources of food ingredients and their storage conditions.
It also promoted its “five do’s and two don’ts” principle for preventing food poisoning: people should wash their hands before handling food, choose fresh food ingredients, keep raw and cooked food separate, cook food thoroughly, store food in appropriate temperatures, and should not drink unpurified mountain spring water or pick and eat wild plants and animals.

As Europe rearms, Italy’s  space sector faces a scale test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

Italy’s fragmented space industry is facing growing pressure to consolidate as defense and government customers increasingly favor larger suppliers capable of handling complex programs.
The shift reflects a broader push across Europe to build strategic autonomy in defense and critical technologies, as governments respond to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, tensions with China and uncertainty over future US security commitments.
For Italy, whose space sector is known for niche engineering expertise, but remains dominated by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the challenge is whether firms can build the scale and financial strength needed to compete for large contracts without losing their flexibility.
Photo: Bloomberg
Limited access to capital remains a major obstacle, industry executives say.
“In Italy, we used to say: ‘Small is beautiful,’ but that’s not true,” said Alessandro Franzoni, CEO of optical instrumentation specialist Officina Stellare.
Leonardo, Italy’s largest aerospace and defense company, said new projects require integrated technological capabilities, industrial reliability and the capacity to manage growing complexity.
“When selecting and developing its supply chain, the group favors suppliers capable of offering solid expertise, production capacity, resilience and operational continuity,” a spokesperson said.
Satellite navigation and cybersecurity specialist Qascom said customers now expect suppliers to provide products, hardware and industrial capabilities, not just engineering know-how.
“You need to grow, because remaining small doesn’t work,” cofounder and CEO Alessandro Pozzobon said.
The pressure has intensified as Europe’s space sector becomes more closely tied to defense and security priorities.
Europe’s defense build-up and growing demand for dual-use technologies, which can serve civilian and military purposes, have increased the importance of resilient industrial capacity.
The rise of Elon Musk’s SpaceX has also highlighted the advantages of scale, vertical integration and access to capital enjoyed by larger industry players.
“I see a trend towards aggregation, driven by the market,” said Giuseppe Acierno, president of the DTA aerospace hub in Apulia, southern Italy. “It is a trend that should be supported.”
Renato Panesi, chief commercial officer at Italian space logistics company D-Orbit, said Europe remains disadvantaged by fragmented programs and weaker access to private funding than the US.
Yet consolidation brings risks. Qascom said much of Italy’s fragmentation reflects deep technological specialization, with smaller firms occupying globally competitive niches in navigation, cybersecurity and advanced communications.
The challenge is finding ways to build scale without sacrificing innovation, executives said.
Building larger companies would require funding.
Last month, Intesa Sanpaolo, the European Investment Bank and the European Space Agency (ESA) launched a program expected to provide up to 300 million euros (US$350.3 million) in financing for aerospace SMEs.
“For too many of our space SMEs, the barrier to growth is not technology, but access to capital,” ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said.
The Italian Interministerial Committee for Space and Aerospace Research Policies estimated the country’s aerospace sector would receive 7.8 billion euros in investment and program funding by 2028, including 3.5 billion euros linked to Italy’s contribution to ESA programs.
For some companies, acquisitions have become the quickest route to achieving the scale customers demand.
Officina Stellare merged with Global Aerospace Technologies Group in June, creating an aerospace and defense platform with a pro-forma order backlog of 192 million euros.
Franzoni said the deal was designed to combine complementary technologies, strengthen vertical integration and broaden the group’s offering.
“I see now an opportunity, mostly in Italy, for further aggregation. We are looking for synergies for technologies and for production synergies,” he said.
Officina Stellare reinforced that strategy last month through the acquisition of electric motor specialist Mavel.
D-Orbit has also expanded through acquisitions, buying Earth observation specialist Planetek before raising fresh capital to fund further deals.
“The driver of our M&A [mergers and acquisitions] strategy is the acquisition of additional capabilities and services to offer to government, defense and commercial satellite operators,” Panesi said.
Recent contracts appear to reflect the shift. Officina Stellare this month secured a 6.5 million euro contract from Leonardo for optical communications terminals and another worth more than 7 million euros from the Italian Space Agency for an Earth observation program.
The company said the awards showed its ability to move beyond technology development and deliver integrated systems at industrial scale.
For industry executives, the question is no longer whether Italy’s space companies need to grow.
It is whether a sector built on specialized SMEs can secure the capital and scale needed to compete in a changing European market before competitors, or foreign acquirers, do it for them.

The idea is simple: while people move through yoga poses, the presence of playful puppies is meant to create a joyful and relaxing atmosphere. Supporters claim the classes provide stress relief for humans. At the same time, they also help the dogs socialize with people.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片: AdobeStock
However, animal welfare experts have raised serious concerns about this trend. Some investigations have reported that puppies as young as six weeks old are used in these classes. Puppies should normally remain with their mothers for at least eight weeks to develop properly. Instead, they may spend hours in busy rooms filled with unfamiliar people.
Such environments can be overwhelming for young puppies. At this age, they need a sense of safety and the presence of a familiar caregiver when they are introduced to new experiences. Without this support, stressful situations may negatively affect their emotional and behavioral development.
For this reason, puppy yoga raises an important question about the healing economy. Although many wellness trends promise comfort and happiness for people, they may also create ethical concerns about how animals are treated.
有些療癒經濟趨勢著重在療癒人心的商品，其他則是體驗的形式。近期的一個例子是小狗瑜伽，在這樣的課程裡，參加者會在幼犬自由漫步於教室內的情況下練瑜伽。這個想法很簡單：當人們在做不同的瑜伽動作時，有愛玩的幼犬在場是為了打造歡樂又放鬆的氣氛。支持者宣稱這些課程能為人們提供壓力的紓解。同時，也有助於狗狗與人類互動。
然而，動物福利專家對這股趨勢提出高度疑慮。一些調查指出，這些課程中使用的幼犬年齡甚至只有六週大。幼犬通常應該與犬媽媽待到至少八週才能正常發育。牠們卻可能在充滿陌生人的忙碌教室裡待上好幾個小時。
這樣的環境對幼犬來說可能難以負荷。在這個年齡段，當牠們接觸新事物時，需要安全感以及熟悉照顧者的陪伴。若缺乏這樣的支持，充滿壓力的情況可能會對牠們的情緒與行為發展造成負面影響。
因此，狗狗瑜伽帶出了一個與療癒經濟相關的重要問題。儘管許多健康療癒的趨勢承諾能為人們帶來慰藉與快樂，但同時也可能引發如何對待動物的倫理疑慮。

1-2. 請從第二天文章中找出最適當的單詞填入下列句子空格中，並視句型結構需要做適當的字形變化，使句子語意完整、語法正確，並符合全文文意。每格限填一個單詞（word）。（填充題）
Puppy yoga supposedly provides human relaxation and opportunities for dog __1__ with humans. However, experts warn that early introduction to busy environments without a safe caregiver hinders the puppies’ proper development and raises questions about the __2__ of using animals.
答案:1. socialization 2. ethics
3. From (A) to (F) below, choose the ONES that are true for both JellyCat and puppy yoga.（多選題）
(A) They both involve direct interactions with animals.
(B) They are promoted through videos on social media platforms.
(C) They show how businesses respond to people’s emotional needs.
(D) They both have sparked discussions about their possible negative effects.
(E) They are mainly intended to improve animals’ well-being and development.
(F) They reflect a growing interest in products or activities that support mental well-being.
答案:C、F
Words in Use
1. participant n. 參與者
Each participant in the marathon will receive a medal after they complete the race.
馬拉松賽事的每位參與者在完賽後都會收到一枚獎牌。
2. wander vi. 漫遊，閒晃
Holly wandered through the narrow streets of the old town.
荷莉在舊城區的狹窄街道上漫步。
3. presence n. 在場，存在
The judge requested the presence of a translator for the foreign witness.
法官要求為外籍證人安排一名翻譯員在場。
4. atmosphere n. 氣氛，氛圍
The live music added a festive atmosphere to the outdoor market.
現場音樂為戶外市集增添了節慶的氣氛。
5. socialize vi. 社交，交際
socialize with... 與……社交
Ken is socializing with the other hikers while they rest by the lake.
在湖邊休息時，阿肯與其他登山客交流互動。
Practical Phrases
1. be meant to V 意在（做）……
These exercises are meant to strengthen the lower back muscles.
這些運動意在強化下背肌肉。
2. be introduced to. . . 初次接觸……
Those students were introduced to basic chemistry during the summer camp.
那些學生在夏令營期間初次接觸了基礎化學。
3. for this reason 因此
The hotel is close to the airport. For this reason, Alice booked a room there.
這間飯店離機場很近。因此，艾莉絲在那裡訂了房。

Taiwanese badminton veteran Chou Tien-chen on Friday advanced to the men’s singles semi-finals at the BWF World Championships in India, securing the second world championships medal of his career.
He was to play against Japan’s Kodai Naraoka after press time last night.
The 36-year-old world No. 6 defeated Indonesian rising star Alwi Farhan 21-15, 21-15 in 50 minutes to guarantee himself at least a bronze medal.
Photo: Reuters
Chou, who entered the match with a 2-1 career record against the world No. 12, used his defense and experience to neutralize Farhan’s attacks and claim his third win in their four meetings.
Chou after the match said that he took care of many of the details well during the match and was able to respond to many of the opponent’s tactics.
“His attacks were actually very sharp, but I went all out. I was able to defend successfully a lot of the time and maintained my advantage,” he said.
The opening game was closely contested from the start, with Chou winning a 60-shot rally to take his seventh point.
After Farhan scored three consecutive points, Chou capitalized on a series of unforced errors by the Indonesian to produce a 7-1 run and lead 14-11.
Leading 16-15, Chou was awarded a point when Farhan was called for serving above the permitted height. Farhan then lost four more points in a row as Chou closed out the game 21-15.
The second game remained tight until 11-11, when Chou began to take the upper hand as he switched up between the pace, drops and timely smashes.
Farhan was called for another service fault with Chou leading 14-12. The Taiwanese player later earned six match points with a body smash before securing victory when Farhan sent a net shot into the tape.
Chou said winning several long rallies shifted the momentum in his favor and boosted his confidence as the match progressed.
A regular BWF world championships quarter-finalist since making his tournament debut in 2013, Chou won his first medal at the event with a semifinal appearance in 2022.
“I won’t think about a particular goal,” Chou said. “I will just fight as hard as I can without any burden and leave everything to Jesus. I believe God will make the best arrangements.”
Meanwhile, Taiwan on Friday also secured a medal in men’s doubles as Lee Jhe-huei and Yang Po-hsuan upset world No. 2 Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri of Indonesia 21-19, 21-16.
The victory made Lee and Yang only the second Taiwanese pair to reach the men’s doubles semi-finals at the world championships, following Chen Hung-ling and Wang Chi-lin, who won bronze in 2018.
Lee and Yang were to face China’s Olympic silver medalists and world No. 3 pair Wang Chang and Liang Weikeng in the semi-finals last night after press time.

Vietnam’s rise could stumble on growth push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:49 UTC
01:45:49 KST

Vietnam’s economy is on a roll. Hanoi, basking in the kind of praise that Southeast Asian peers won prior to the region’s financial crisis in the 1990s, wants still more rapid growth. However, leaders should be careful — such enthusiasm might well hasten the boom’s undoing.
Recent advances recall the glory days. In the second quarter, GDP climbed by more than 8 percent, easily exceeding forecasts. The closest to that, Malaysia, managed 6 percent. China, which for decades appeared largely insulated from business cycles, slackened to 4.3 percent. Vietnam’s government has its sights on a pace of at least 10 percent for the year.
Like the former Tiger economies that inspired it, Vietnam’s progress has been driven by breakneck industrialization and securing a lucrative niche in supply chains. Factories have churned apparel, furniture and electronics bound for shelves in the West, racking up enormous trade surpluses in the process. Tariffs on imports to the US were widely expected to slow things down. That has not happened, yet.
The performance has translated into meaningful gains in living standards. In July, the World Bank promoted Vietnam to the ranks of upper-middle income economies, joining Malaysia and Thailand. The Philippines also scored an upgrade. However, the pace at which Vietnam scaled the ladder is revealing. The bank had only elevated it to a lower-middle income economy in 2009.
It is reasonable to question how long a performance like this can be sustained. The more prosperous a country becomes, the harder it is to keep clocking up torrid rates of expansion, while a notable overheating would jeopardize financial stability and prod authorities to take firm steps to rein in activity.
Policy is increasingly geared to meet Vietnamese President To Lam’s objective of achieving high-income status by 2045, a century after the country declared its independence in the aftermath of World War II. Credit growth is running high: The central bank has set a target of 15 percent and has signaled it could indulge a greater amount. State spending is also being harnessed, with the budget deficit projected to widen. Managing this will be tricky. Officials want muscular growth, but do not want inflation to accelerate much beyond their target of 4.5 percent. Consumer prices jumped 5.6 percent from a year earlier in May, but have since increased at a more moderate pace. And they need to limit swings in the currency, which is allowed to fluctuate in a narrow band against the US dollar.
In an echo of how its neighbors ran into trouble during the Asian financial crisis, Lam also has his eyes on mega projects, including a US$2.5 trillion “master plan” to reconfigure large swathes of Hanoi. Ho Chi Minh City launched its own blueprint for a makeover. The risk is that such grand initiatives become an end to themselves. Waste and over-development are seldom far behind. While the ventures seem doable when times are good, they can sour when the economic and financial cycle turns. Recall the Vision 2020 program of former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, who in 1991 beseeched citizens to reach for a Swiss-style standard of living by the second decade of this century. Years of strong growth did follow, but so did ostentatious projects like the Petronas Towers and a cavernous airport that is too far from Kuala Lumpur and too thinly staffed. (Mahathir eventually acknowledged the 2020 goal would not be reached.)
Another danger lurks in the dependence of Vietnam’s export machine on the world’s biggest economy.
Last year, the trade surplus with the US ballooned to a record US$134 billion, an increase of more than one-fifth. the US’ shortfall with the country is the third largest after China and Mexico. The levies that US President Donald Trump announced in April last year were regarded as a steep challenge for Vietnam.
At that time, the White House also made clear it wanted to crack down on transshipments from China, a hard-to-pin-down practice where parts of a product are routed through Vietnam to the US with Vietnamese duties paid rather than the steeper charges applied to its northern neighbor. The Trump administration is now renewing its focus on constraining such traffic.
Hanoi cannot control Trump, but it can take care to avoid a hard landing. Relaxing credit guidelines would be risky, and the central bank should watch that activity does not become too hot. It is important policymakers realize that outperformance cannot last forever. Pushing growth above 8 percent for a considerable period might see the country gallop further up the development ladder, but it could also easily lead to an unacceptable build up of bad debts and an economy increasingly vulnerable to shocks. China offers a sobering lesson: After growth tore along in excess of 10 percent a year in the early 2000s, the nation’s model hit a wall.
“If Vietnam does achieve sustained 10 percent growth, it’s more likely to be a warning sign than a reason for celebration,” Capital Economics senior Asia economist Gareth Leather wrote last week.
Vietnam has done very well. It could do even better if it learns the lessons of its neighbors and shoots for something less than perfection.
Daniel Moss is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian economies. Previously, he was executive editor for economics at Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Thousands of doses of Ebola vaccine arrive in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

More than 16,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine arrived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) late on Friday, as the country faces the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history.
The DR Congo’s 17th Ebola outbreak, which has killed thousands of people, was declared on May 15, but is thought to have been spreading for several weeks prior. It has hit regions in the north and east where the presence of the state is weak, health infrastructure is largely lacking and myriad armed groups have roamed for decades.
The WHO on Thursday announced that DR Congo would receive a total of 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, produced in Germany.
Photo: AFP
The vaccine, developed by the pharmaceutical company Merck, is approved against the Zaire strain of the virus, but not against the Bundibugyo strain circulating in the country.
WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.
The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak,” Congolese Minister of Public Health Samuel Roger Kamba said.
He was speaking on the tarmac of Kinshasa airport, where a batch of 16,250 doses was delivered by plane.
Of the 70,000 doses made available to the DR Congo, 20,000 are intended for a clinical trial, and 50,000 for “frontline and health workers,” the WHO said.
The Ebola outbreak in the country has already caused 2,516 deaths among 5,290 confirmed cases, the latest data published by the Congolese authorities showed.
“[It] is growing exponentially,” UN Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis said.
This month, WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of Ervebo, the only existing approved Ebola vaccine, to see if it offered cross-protection against the Bundibugyo strain.
Two vaccines specifically targeting the Bundibugyo strain are in clinical trial phases: one is being developed by the US-based group Moderna, which uses mRNA technology, and the other by the UK’s University of Oxford.
An “rVSV Bundibugyo” vaccine, described by the WHO as “the most promising,” is to be developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories.

Ex-Chinese priest gets naturalized after decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

A Catholic priest who was born in China and is now a US citizen has become a Taiwanese citizen after overcoming bureaucratic hurdles tied to his birthplace.
Xu Jingshan (徐景山), 67, who has been preaching in Taiwan for the past 20 years, said on Thursday that he first went to the US from China 33 years ago and later obtained US citizenship. He wrote off his household registration in China at the time.
He was assigned by the Catholic Church to Taiwan about two decades ago.
Photo: Hung Jui-chin, Taipei Times
Xu said that living in Taiwan without a national ID card had long caused practical inconveniences, such as difficulties in applying for a cellphone and obtaining a senior citizen card.
Upon learning about the government’s “Mackay Project” last year, he applied to become a naturalized Republic of China citizen for “making special contributions.”
His application was eventually approved by the Ministry of the Interior.
Because he was born in China, the National Immigration Agency (NIA) required that he provide documentation proving the cancelation of his Chinese household registration.
Xu said he had his relatives in China obtain the required documents from the local police station in his birthplace, but the NIA required the paperwork to be authenticated by Taiwan’s Straits Exchange Foundation.
However, the foundation only accepts notarized expulsion documents authenticated by Chinese notary offices, not expulsion documents directly issued by local police stations, Xu added.
A suspension in a Chinese notary office’s authentication service caused his application to stall, Xu said. In July, the office resumed the service, and his Taiwan ID card was ultimately issued.
During the process, he sought assistance from Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Yunlin County Councilor Tsai Yueh-ju (蔡岳儒), who in turn enlisted the help of DPP Legislator Liu Chien-kuo (劉建國). His case was also submitted to the Executive Yuan and the Presidential Office.
Tsai said Xu had previously served in churches in Yunlin County, where he devoted himself to grassroots education and helped establish a day center for seniors at Lunbei Catholic Church.
Xu was transferred to the Church of the Good Shepherd six years ago and has made significant contributions to rural communities and disadvantaged residents, Tsai said.

TikTok to pay US$400m in privacy lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:45 UTC
01:45:45 KST

TikTok has agreed to pay US$400 million to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice over claims that the video-sharing platform contravened federal children’s privacy laws, the department announced on Friday.
Regulators around the world have been ramping up enforcement against social media companies that contravene laws about protecting children’s data, privacy and safety. Chinese company ByteDance — which sold off a majority stake of its US entity earlier this year to avoid a ban by the administration of US President Donald Trump — is also named as part of the settlement.
It has a 19.9 percent ownership stake in TikTok US, US media reported.
Photo: AFP
“Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly,” the department said in a statement.
“[It is] one of the largest recoveries ever obtained” from a case involving the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the statement said.
The act bars Web sites from gathering the personal information of children younger than 13 without parental permission.
The justice department and US Federal Trade Commission jointly sued TikTok in 2024, alleging that it had placed the safety of millions of children in jeopardy by collecting their personal data without parental permission.
TikTok allowed children to use the app in addition to collecting and using personal data from young users without letting their parents know, they said.
Even accounts created in a “Kids Mode” intended for users younger than 13 gathered e-mail addresses and other personal information, the suit said.
In 2019, the US filed a COPPA lawsuit against an app called Musical.ly, which ByteDance bought in 2017 and then merged into TikTok.
TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
An ABC News report in May said that the Trump administration was considering using the funds for ongoing “beautification” projects, which have included resurfacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, renovating the White House ballroom and building an arch.
It was not immediately clear what the settlement funds would be used for.
The US settlement comes amid a growing global crackdown on the video app.
Brussels began a probe into TikTok in 2024 under the Digital Services Act (DSA) — a content law and major weapon in the EU’s boosted legal armory that it has deployed to rein in Big Tech over the past few years.
Last month, the EU accused TikTok of failing to protect children through account settings that could expose them to risks such as cyberbullying and predatory behavior, putting the company at risk of a large fine.
Minors’ accounts should only be visible to those they have given permission to, the EU said.
Children ages 13 and over can use TikTok.
“A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default,” European Commissioner for Digital and Frontier Technologies Henna Virkkunen said at the time.
Under the DSA, children’s account settings have, by default, the strongest safety and security protections.
“TikTok’s account settings fail to meet this standard, as they expose minors’ accounts and content too widely,” the EU said in its preliminary view.

South Korea makes billions, but takes home little
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

South Korea, home to the world’s two largest memorychip makers, is in the midst of an AI-fueled exports boom. Generating wealth and keeping it at home are not the same thing, however.
Korea Inc is making a staggering amount of money this year. Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc are among the world’s five most profitable companies, earning more than Alphabet Inc or Apple Inc. Thanks to soaring memorychip prices, gross domestic income, a measure of the nation’s purchasing power, increased by 15.6 percent in the second quarter, far outpacing the 3.7 percent gain in GDP.
However, chronic capital outflows, which have haunted successive governments, are not going away. A sizeable chunk of export revenue is kept offshore, according to consultancy Capital Economics, which looked at deposits data in South Korea’s financial account for clues (Offshore corporate deposits would show up under currency and deposits of other sectors — other than the central bank, financial institutions, or the general government — in the country’s financial account.). In June, the government asked major exporters to repatriate funds held overseas to stabilize the South Korean won.
The main factors that contributed to money leaving the country are still present. Retail investors have flocked to the NASDAQ, developing a taste that first took hold during the meme stock craze in late 2020. They briefly sold their overseas holdings earlier in the year, but re-entered the US market in June, piling into leveraged semiconductor exchange-traded funds.
While less risk-loving than mom-and-pop traders, South Korean companies continue to invest abroad. SK Group has promised to put in a “much, much bigger” amount than the US$35 billion it has committed to in the US, while Samsung Group is also expanding manufacturing capabilities there. Still, the White House is pushing for more.
At home, though, there are worries that retail traders will abandon the Kospi for good after last month’s rout, returning to a perception long-held before the AI fever hit that the South Korean market is a value trap. Meanwhile, business sentiment is fragile. Private-sector investments fell in 2024 and last year.
In other words, South Korea has the same kind of dilemma as its north Asian neighbors, Japan and China.
The vast wealth created from its industrial success is recycled overseas — through foreign direct or portfolio investments — and does not necessarily translate into deeper equity markets, higher asset valuations, or a broad-based economic boom at home.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s administration is certainly doing what it can to address structural problems. Vowing to make a “great leap forward,” the government has unveiled public-private partnership projects in the less-developed southwest region, with SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics each promising to deploy about 400 trillion won (US$288.22 billion) in new chipmaking factories. It is injecting fresh capital into sovereign wealth funds for strategic investments in AI infrastructure. Last month, Seoul introduced 24-hour trading of the South Korean won to facilitate transactions at a level comparable to G10 currencies. South Korea is one of the world’s largest exporters, but its currency accounts for only 1 percent of global foreign-exchange turnover, according to Deutsche Bank.
Big question marks remain, however. Economists worry about the day the AI boom runs out of steam. The strength of South Korea’s export revenue comes mostly from soaring prices rather than volumes, so what would happen if Chinese competitors flood the market and drag down the entire industry’s profitability? Will Korea Inc suffer from over-investment?
Nonetheless, the government is wise not to waste the big fiscal windfall on socialist wealth transfers, instead leveraging state money to tease out domestic investments. After all, South Korea is a functioning democracy and Seoul cannot take a page out of Beijing’s playbook, which simply cracks down on cross-border stock investments and traps its capital at home as a way to develop domestic equity markets. For South Korea, improving business sentiment is the only way.
Shuli Ren is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian markets. A former investment banker, she was a markets reporter for Barron’s. She is a CFA charterholder. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

China investigates comedian who altered song onstage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

One of China’s best-known comedians is under investigation and several of his shows have been canceled after he changed the lyrics of a revolutionary song during a performance.
Guo Degang (郭德?), the country’s most prominent performer of traditional xiangsheng, a form of Chinese comedic dialogue, is under investigation by Wuhan authorities, local media reported.
Guo’s show on Friday in Xi’an was canceled due to “venue issues,” a statement on ticketing platform Damai released by his promotion company showed.
Photo: AP
The company offered refunds for tickets as well as travel and hotel expenses. The exhibition center hosting the performance, which also cited “venue issues” on Wednesday, said the show had been “postponed,” without giving a new date.
Local media reports said several of Guo’s shows scheduled this month across cities were canceled.
The investigation highlights China’s stricter controls and censorship of the entertainment and arts industries, where performers and artists have to navigate an environment where “red lines” are often unclear and shifting.
Guo was reported to Wuhan’s culture and tourism authorities after he changed a lyric from “it is quiet along Weishan Lake” to “it is quiet in the Forbidden City” while performing at a show in the city last month, according to local media reports and videos on social media platforms.
The Forbidden City, once home to China’s emperors for hundreds of years, is now a museum that attracts more than 10 million visitors each year.
Guo’s performance had been approved in advance by Wuhan authorities, but the lyric change had not, which might have contravened regulations governing commercial performances, The Paper said.
The lyrics are from Playing My Beloved Pipa, a song from Railway Guerrilla, a well-known 1950s film about communist-led guerrillas fighting Japanese forces during World War II.
The pipa is a traditional Chinese stringed instrument, similar to a lute.
It is a popular song among the public. It was once played at CCTV Spring Festival gala in 1998, and was also selected in 2019 by the Chinese Communist Party’s Publicity Department as one of 100 songs recommended to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.
Guo is widely considered as the one who brought xiangsheng closer to the younger generation in China. The traditional art form was more regional and more popular among the older audience.
This is not the first time that performers face consequences over their work on stage. In 2023, comedian Li Haoshi (李昊石), known by his stage name House, sparked controversy after describing dogs chasing squirrels with a military slogan.
Xiaoguo Culture Media, the company he worked for, was later fined 14.7 million yuan (US$2.19 million), and Li has not appeared in public performances in mainland China since.

Printers’ group looks to future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

Once a major force for spreading knowledge, printing is now at a crossroads as digital reading reduces demand for traditional print. To adapt, one of Taiwan’s oldest printing associations is turning to artificial intelligence (AI), new markets and talent development.
Established 80 years ago, the Tainan City Printing Commercial Association is looking to the next 80 years with a focus on technology, talent and cultural preservation.
“AI adoption is only just beginning, and every industry is essentially starting from the same line,” the association’s honorary chairman Huang Chien-tung (黃建東) said on Sunday last week.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Church Press
The precision and commitment to quality developed by printing professionals provide a strong foundation for adopting AI, he said.
The association is promoting AI-powered design and intelligent production to address labor shortages, while developing AI training programs and seeking government support for digital transformation and talent development.
Pan Ching-chu (潘靜竹), head of the Fucheng Old Books Store, said Taiwan has about 10,000 publishers, but many new books have initial print runs of only 500 copies, compared with several thousand in the past. Rising production costs have pushed up book prices as demand falls, while large quantities of nearly new secondhand books are being sold for a fraction of their original prices.
Photo: Hung Jui-chin, Taipei Times
Still, Pan said printing remains essential for packaging, advertising and other commercial applications.
Huang Chin-yi (黃進益), a section chief at Academia Sinica’s Southern Branch Service Office, said books connect design, editing, paper, ink, machinery, binding, logistics and sales into a cultural and creative industry chain. Rather than mass production, print could increasingly focus on high-quality materials, sophisticated design and collectible value, he added.
The renewed popularity of independent publishing, zines, art books and photography books among younger creators also suggests that demand for print and its tangible qualities remains.
The association’s 80th-anniversary publication showcases that craftsmanship. Its cover combines Oxford paper, laser-foil stamping and die-cutting inspired by traditional Tainan window patterns, blending traditional motifs with modern printing techniques.
Printer Sun Wen-shan (孫文山) hopes Tainan can establish a printing-themed tourist factory combining cultural history, technology demonstrations and hands-on activities.
Companies are also demonstrating how the industry can adapt.
Chairman Lu Jung-ta (盧榮達) said that printing companies must understand how to adapt to markets and customer needs while maintaining expertise in design, production and service.
Chien Sheng Enterprise, the first printing company to establish a facility in the Tainan Technology Industrial Park, helped usher traditional printing into the technology sector through computerized equipment, digital typesetting and precision printing.
Manager Huang Chien-tung (黃建東) said that the global industry has moved beyond simple contract manufacturing toward digitalization and knowledge creation. With product life cycles shortening, companies must continually invest in research and development and incorporate new technologies to remain competitive, he added.
Chairman Cheng Chun-ming (鄭俊銘) said the company’s green transformation goes beyond upgrading equipment to incorporating sustainability into its products and operations.
Cheng also emphasized the importance of talent, saying that traditional industries face difficulties recruiting workers, and Taiwan has few printing-related programs. He said medium and senior-level professionals returning to the workforce, particularly those with management experience in the electronics industry, could become an important source of talent if given appropriate printing training.
From movable type to AI-powered manufacturing, Tainan’s printing industry is attempting to preserve its traditional expertise while adapting to a digital, increasingly automated and environmentally conscious economy.

Legislature loses ‘friendship’ travel funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

The legislature has suspended funding for overseas visits by lawmakers’ friendship groups after travel budget cuts, prompting mixed responses from the three major parties.
The central government’s budget for this fiscal year was delayed for 351 days before the Legislative Yuan finally passed it on Friday last week.
As part of across-the-board cuts, the budgets for overseas travel and training at central government agencies and their affiliated bodies were cut by 30 percent, with exceptions for legally mandated spending, Academia Sinica and the National Audit Office. Some agencies were subject to cuts ranging from 10 percent to 70 percent.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
In a letter sent to lawmakers, Legislative Yuan Secretary-General Chou Wan-lai (周萬來) said that after the cuts, the legislature’s overseas travel budget was insufficient to subsidize lawmakers’ visits organized by foreign parliamentary friendship groups, once existing expenditures and earmarked funds were taken into account.
Under Article 15 of the regulations governing parliamentary friendship groups with foreign legislators and other organizations, subsidies must be covered by the legislature’s budget.
The Legislative Yuan has stopped accepting applications for funding for overseas visits by parliamentary friendship groups, effective immediately.
“I think the legislature has only itself to blame,” Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus secretary-general Fan Yun (范雲) said yesterday, adding that the cuts ended up affecting the Legislative Yuan itself, leaving lawmakers without subsidies and forcing them to pay out of pocket for overseas parliamentary diplomacy.
DPP Legislator Michelle Lin (林楚茵), who also chairs the Taiwan-France Parliamentary Friendship Association and other friendship groups, said that there were 114 parliamentary friendship groups as of the end of June, 78 of which are cross-national groups focused on parliamentary diplomacy.
At a time when Taiwan is facing pressure from China, parliamentary exchanges with other democratic legislatures are an important way for the nation to engage internationally, she added.
The subsidy for overseas visits by parliamentary friendship groups is about NT$60,000 per person, Lin said.
While that amount may cover trips to some Asian countries, an economy-class ticket to Europe could cost more than NT$60,000, she said, adding that there are also accommodation expenses.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said the cuts apply to the Legislative Yuan, which shows that they were intended to rein in government spending, rather than targeting the Executive Yuan.
Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) said cuts have been made at a certain rate in previous years, adding that the 30 percent cut to overseas travel expenses was the version the three parties agreed upon during negotiations.
As DPP caucus whip Tsai Chi-chang (蔡其昌) signed off on the agreement, all government agencies would be able to adjust accordingly, Chen said.
TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said parliamentary diplomacy is necessary, and lawmakers should continue traveling overseas to seek international support and deepen ties with democratic partners.
However, the importance of parliamentary diplomacy does not mean every expense should be given unlimited leeway, he added.
Hung criticized some government officials for taking aimless overseas trips and submitting poorly written reports, only to invoke national security confidentiality as a cover when their conduct was exposed.
Such misuse of travel funds was the main reason for the cuts, he said, adding that the legislature’s parliamentary diplomacy budget was simply collateral damage.
Hung blamed ruling party officials for misusing public funds, saying that they dragged down the budgets of the legislature and government agencies.

EDITORIAL: The devil in the omissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:38 UTC
01:45:38 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) failure to win the previous three presidential elections has been tied to its tenacious approach to cross-strait relations, with polls showing that the electorate remain profoundly suspicious of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
At first glance, it might be confusing as to why a political party aspiring to return to power would continue to flog the pro-China horse. The answer is that continued engagement with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) makes sense, as long as one is willing to ignore some glaring omissions.
An editorial in a pro-China newspaper said that few could deny that China is overtaking other countries, including the US, in multiple metrics.
Many countries are engaging with China, while Taiwan continues to cling to the concept of “resisting China to protect Taiwan,” and the nation would lose by refusing to engage with the world’s second-largest economy in tourism, education, industry and technology, it said. It also warned against the assumption that the US military would handily defeat the Chinese People’s Liberation Army in the Western Pacific.
These are all fair points, which the article suggests are largely omitted from the pro-Taiwanese independence side. At the same time, it neglects to point out that, in Taiwan’s case, there is no possibility of a mutually beneficial economic exchange with China, nor does it concede that siding with Washington over the CCP is far more than an ideological preference. The devil is not only in the details: It is also in the omissions.
During an online interview on Friday last week, KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) told host Dennis Peng (彭文正) that “Taiwan has never been independent, nor has it ever been a country.”
Cheng is incorrect in that assertion, although it is perfectly consistent with the KMT’s stance. The omissions in her statement are highly complex.
Cheng’s expression of the KMT position in this case is that the name of the country is not Taiwan, it is the Republic of China (ROC), bound to the ROC Constitution. This is not controversial from the KMT perspective, although pro-Taiwanese critics would certainly take issue with it. To Cheng, Taiwan only exists because of the ROC Constitution, which she called a “one China” constitution, omitting the logical conclusion that must be drawn: From the CCP’s perspective, the ROC no longer exists, and its constitution is little more than a historical document, albeit linked to the PRC’s own.
On how this inconvenient contradiction is to be cleared up, and how the KMT envisages “peaceful unification” with China, Cheng said her ideas would “be truly introduced and implemented as policy once the KMT retakes power.” She wants Taiwanese to hand her the presidency first before they find out what she has in store for them.
Cheng mocked the Democratic Progressive Party for “not daring to hold a referendum on Taiwanese independence.” Yet she knows what the political jeopardy to the CCP and the KMT, and the risk of war, would be if such a referendum were ever held. The list of omissions goes on.
After her meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) in Beijing in April, questions about whether Cheng would stand as the KMT’s presidential candidate in the 2028 election started to surface. Despite being the party chair, it is not necessarily the case that she would be the first option. A week, let alone two years, is a long time in politics, and if she ran, she would potentially be vying for the candidacy with three other strong candidates: Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) — currently the party’s highest-ranked elected figure — and Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕).
According to an opinion poll released on Wednesday by the online media outlet Z.Media (震傳媒), when asked about who they thought would be the preferred KMT candidate for the 2028 presidential race, 20.4 percent of respondents said that they supported Chiang, 18.9 percent Han and 16 percent Lu. The differences are hardly insurmountable. Cheng only received 3 percent of the support.
In politics, omissions are to be expected, but the times also call for clarity and honesty.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

The underlying premise seems to be that as long as Taiwan projects an image of strength, there will be no cracks for China to exploit. When seen from Beijing’s perspective, the flaw in this logic becomes apparent. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) relies heavily on positive messaging and tightly managed information to maintain political stability. Taiwan simply cannot beat an authoritarian state at its own

Chiang Kung missile specifications released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:38 UTC
01:45:38 KST

The National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) yesterday disclosed technical specifications of the Chiang Kung missile, amid a legislative deadlock that cast doubt over the program’s future.
The Chiang Kung missile, also known as Tien Chien IV, is intended to serve as the principal high-altitude interceptor of the proposed “T-Dome,” an integrated air defense matrix for Taiwan proper.
The Ministry of National Defense has confirmed that it would seek to fund Chiang Kung missile production via a supplementary budget, since the program was not included in the special defense budget passed by the Legislative Yuan.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
According to the NCSIST, the state-run defense research and development group, the Chiang Kung air defense system uses a land-based vertical launch system to fire hypersonic weapons capable of intercepting ballistic missiles at mesospheric altitudes.
The interceptor missile uses vectored thrust to ensure speed and maneuverability in the low-air-density conditions of high altitudes, the institute said.
The warhead of the Chiang Kung missile is mounted atop a two-stage solid-propellant rocket housed in molded composite materials to enable large-scale production at a low cost, it said.
The Chiang Kung’s radar can identify different types of targets, engage multiple tactical ballistic missiles, and is hardened against electronic warfare countermeasures, the NCSIST said.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, a defense official said that the Chiang Kung system’s ability to intercept ballistic missiles at altitudes up to 70km is a significant improvement over the Tien Kung III.
The Chiang Kung features a mobile active electronically scanned array radar vehicle developed jointly by Taiwan and the US, which possesses formidable detection and is designed to operate under heavy electromagnetic interference and GPS jamming, they said.
The Chiang Kung missile is a crucial part of the planned “T-Dome” air defense network, which incorporates multiple types of interceptors under the control of the US-made Integrated Air and Missile Defense Battle Command System, they said.
This system’s importance stems from its high-altitude capability, which is absent in Taiwan’s arsenal and cannot be otherwise obtained through foreign procurement, the official said.
The ministry’s budget woes have impacted the Chiang Kung system acquisition timetable, which has negative ramifications for the entire “T-Dome” project, they said.
The military cannot integrate its patchwork of air defense missiles when key pieces are missing, the official said, adding that Taiwan can ill afford this problem as Chinese capabilities grow by leaps and bounds.
The uncertainty surrounding the funding of key weapon systems, including Chiang Kung, is highly worrisome to the military’s leadership, they said.

YouTube paying to keep creators amid Netflix push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:37 UTC
01:45:37 KST

YouTube is offering millions of dollars to popular channels if they upload their videos to the site exclusively for a certain period of time, in an effort to halt Netflix Inc’s pursuit of its biggest stars, people familiar with the conversations said.
The payment would come in a couple of different forms. YouTube has discussed directly financing some programs, and it has also offered to allot a portion of major brand deals to creators. Although YouTube has not finalized deals with any creators, it is close an agreement with several partners, said the people, who declined to be identified because the negotiations are sensitive and ongoing.
Creators who do sign deals with Netflix face consequences, YouTube has said, according to the people. YouTube would be less likely to feature them in marketing campaigns or at events if they release videos on Netflix at the same time. YouTube would also exclude those creators from collecting a share of proceeds from some major brand campaigns.
Photo: AP
Netflix has been pursuing agreements with dozens of prominent YouTubers, paying creators such as Alan Chikin Chow and Nick DiGiovanni to post their videos on YouTube and Netflix concurrently. The company remains in active conversations with dozens of other creators, channels and programs, such as Hot Ones, a celebrity talk show.
The Netflix deals appeal to creators, because they are a way to get paid millions of additional dollars for videos they are already making and expose their programming to new viewers. Netflix has more than 325 million subscribers.
Yet YouTube has told creators cross-posting on its platform and Netflix hurts viewership on YouTube and conveys the idea that channels are deprioritizing the streaming platform as their primary distribution outlet.
Photo: Reuters
Some creators have already decided not to work with Netflix. The service requires them to deliver videos days in advance, which is not how many creators operate. It has also asked creators to remove certain brand sponsorships from their videos.
YouTube and Netflix have been the leaders in streaming video for the past 20 years. For most of that time, they have been friendly competitors largely operating in separate universes.
Netflix was the king of subscription streaming, focused on more expensive, Hollywood-style films and TV shows. YouTube was the undisputed leader in user-generated content, birthing a new generation of stars that people primarily watched on mobile devices. Its past efforts to fund original programming failed to produce many hit programs. One of those shows, Cobra Kai, went on to be a big hit for Netflix.
Yet the line between the two sites has blurred in the past few years. YouTube prioritized getting people to watch on TV and now accounts for more viewership on those devices than any other service. It has chased TV advertising dollars and taken the rights to major live events such as the Academy Awards and the NFL.
Netflix, which has long promoted its titles on YouTube, licensed the rights to popular shows such as CoComelon and Ms. Rachel. It sees YouTube stars as a way to draw in younger viewers and boost the amount of time its users spend on Netflix.
The competition has intensified over the past year as Netflix has stepped up its pursuit of YouTube’s most popular channels.
YouTube has weighed whether to respond. Chief executive officer Neal Mohan has long said that creators who do deals with competitors, be they Instagram or Amazon Prime Video, tend to drive viewers back to YouTube. Few of these creators are leaving YouTube, which is still their primary distribution outlet. Funding any individual channel also risks aggravating the thousands of channels that do not get any cash.
YouTube still does not want to serve as a studio for creators, which would involve funding and providing creative direction. However, over the past few weeks, Mohan and his team have decided that the steady stream of creators now posting on YouTube and Netflix at the same time was a problem that needed to be addressed. It is harder to sell advertisers on the appeal and value of a video on YouTube if it is also available on Netflix.
This is not the first time YouTube has responded to competitors in this manner. It offered money to creators who did not do deals with Vessel, a start-up cofounded and formerly led by Jason Kilar that was trying to get social media creators to post on its app before YouTube. YouTube also created a product for short-form video to compete with TikTok.

====================================================================================================

Wildfires expose, detonate old explosives in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:35 UTC
01:45:35 KST

The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.
Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg Province in 1944.
Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict academic at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies.
Photo: AP
Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant.
“Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said.
Fires can ignite old munitions, and burn away the scrub and brush that hides them.
This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived.
Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, a World Weather Attribution study said last month.
As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent.
In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be WWII-era ammunition.
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Governor Herve Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area.
No fire crews were in danger, he said, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.
During WWII, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens.
In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said historian Bernard Collard, who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.
“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said.
He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry.
The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens.
The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 US and 28,000 German troops.
Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases and a human skeleton.
“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site.
Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.
Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires, because heat can trigger the explosives, North Rhine-Westphalia spokesperson Jonas Tepe said.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared with elsewhere in Belgium.
Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in WWI — call the annual tilling of the soil “ the iron harvest,” because it turns up so many war remnants.
Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tonnes of munitions left over from the world wars.
Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.
In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition.
Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from WWII emerged at its base in receding water.
As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb.
University of Arizona researcher Christina Greene, who wrote an article Njeri on Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change.
“It’s reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven’t had to deal with in a while in certain places,” Greene said.

Thousands of invasive fish taken from Sun Moon Lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:35 UTC
01:45:35 KST

More than 25,000 giant snakehead fry have been removed from Sun Moon Lake (日月潭) this year, marking a more than 30-fold annual increase from last year, the Nantou County Government said on Friday.
The county government has stepped up its effort to capture the invasive carnivorous fish species as its peak breeding season begins from this month.
The catch per unit effort ranged from 3,000 to more than 5,000 fry, it said, adding that a total of 4,808 giant snakehead fry were removed from the lake this week.
Photo courtesy of the Nantou County Government
While only slightly more than 800 fry were captured last year, this year’s catch via electrofishing has rapidly climbed to a cumulative total of 25,717 fry as of Friday, the county government said.
That is an annual increase of more than 30-fold from last year, it said, adding the annual total catch is projected to surpass 30,000 fry this year.
The giant snakehead, also locally known as “the bully of the lake,” came into the public eye in Taiwan about 20 years ago.
The fish species began to proliferate in Sun Moon Lake around 2020, requiring the county to conduct electrofishing removal in the summer of every year.
It is a carnivorous freshwater fish that hunts almost all kinds of aquatic life, including frogs, snakes, turtles and waterbirds.
A red devil cichlid — an invasive fish species commonly known as “the king of demons” in Taiwan for its aggressiveness — was found bitten when it was caught by a local angler at the lake on Thursday.
The angler, who has a Facebook page called “Sun Moon Lake No. 1” (日月潭一等高), posted a photo of the red devil cichlid showing that the bite left on its upper body was shaped like the mouth of a giant snakehead.
“Look who is the real underwater big boss of Sun Moon Lake,” he said.
“The bully of the lake can be so ferocious that it bit the king of demons even during Ghost Month,” the angler said, referring to this month of the lunar calendar.
Giant snakeheads can turn cannibal when their population grows too big in a single habitat.
While the giant snakehead’s breeding season could run through October, the county government said its removal effort might be coming to an end this year due to limited budgets.
The county government would provide guidance for local fishermen on how to capture giant snakehead fry balls, it said.
Fry balls are giant snakehead fry and juvenile fish merging into red-orange “balls” as they rise to the water surface to breathe or hunt small fry or shrimp.
Such fry balls have been nicknamed “death bubbles” by locals and have become a local specialty dish at restaurants around the lake, adding to local fishermen’s income.

China mulls bid to host 2028 UN climate talks: sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:32 UTC
01:45:32 KST

China is mulling a bid to host UN climate talks in 2028, two sources familiar with the matter said on Friday, as it seeks to burnish its reputation as a leader in the fight against global warming.
Beijing has not yet made a final decision regarding the proposal for the COP33 summit, the sources said, nor is there a clear timeline for doing so.
The host does not have to be decided this year.
Photo: Reuters
The UN’s annual climate gatherings rotate among regional blocs. This year’s COP31 is scheduled to take place in Turkey, followed by COP32 in Ethiopia next year.
The 2028 summit falls to the Asia-Pacific region.
In April, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 without specifying a reason. South Korea has previously expressed interest.
The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change secretariat said: “We have not been informed by the Asia-Pacific Regional Group on the nomination of the host country for COP33.”
“Regional groups hold consultations first to determine which country from their respective regions would offer to host on behalf of the group. Once agreed, the chair of that regional group formally sends an official nomination to the secretariat,” it added.
China has over the past few years positioned itself as a counterweight to the US.
Under US President Donald Trump, Washington left the Paris climate agreement twice while the administration seeks to boost fossil fuels.
Hosting UN climate talks could thus be an opportunity for China to boost its credentials as a climate leader.
The world’s second-largest economy also has an economic interest as the leading exporter of green technologies, including solar panels, electric vehicles, wind turbines and batteries.
However, hosting the gathering could also cast an unwelcome spotlight on China, which, with its population of 1.4 billion and massive manufacturing industry, is the world’s biggest greenhouse emitter, followed by the US, India and the EU.
Although it has pledged to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060, it is targeting only a modest 7 to 10 percent reduction in economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, compared with peak levels.
Another factor that China is considering is the US-China dynamic, one source said.
Climate cooperation had been a key feature of the bilateral relationship under former US presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, and COP33 could spur renewed collaboration if a Democrat is elected in 2028.
