TASA launches new sounding rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:32 UTC
01:45:32 KST

The Taiwan Space Agency (TASA) yesterday in Pingtung County launched the nation’s first independently developed sounding rocket under its orbital launch vehicle program, completing its end-to-end communication verification with a maximum speed of Mach 1.2.
The rocket, named Maraho (島脈), blasted off at the county’s Syuhai rocket launch site in its first test flight at 7:10am yesterday.
The launch operations, including rocket ignition, flight and parachute deployment, were successfully completed, the agency said yesterday.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Space Agency
The agency in 2023 initiated the orbital launch vehicle program with the goal of establishing indigenous satellite launch capabilities by 2034, it said.
The program involves the target of delivering a 200kg payload to low Earth orbit, the agency said, adding that the test flight of Maraho was part of the effort.
Maraho propulsed for 18 seconds and generated 1,500kgf of takeoff thrust in this test flight, reaching a maximum supersonic speed of about Mach 1.2, it said.
It peaked at an altitude of 8.1km with a total flight time of 432 seconds, the agency said.
The whole flight process was completed in accordance with the plan and the desired verification data were successfully obtained, it said.
However, the rocket body could not be recovered due to unfavorable sea conditions, the agency said.
The test flight was aimed to verify the operation of the overall Maraho rocket system in a real-world flight environment, it said.
One of the key targets was to build an end-to-end communication mechanism between the ground and rockets to receive data in real time, the agency said.
Flight verification was conducted on independently developed subsystems: propulsion, structure, avionics, communication, tracking, ground support and recovery, it said.
The acquired actual flight data would next serve as a basis for rocket design improvements and the following test flights, the agency said.
TASA Director Wu Jong-shinn (吳宗信) said that Maraho’s rocket design, manufacturing, assembly, integration testing and the test flight were carried out fully by the agency’s research team.
Multiple test flights would be conducted to repeatedly verify critical technologies, rehearse the mission procedures and accumulate team experience, he said.
That would help reduce the development risks for large rocket research and gradually improve Taiwan’s capabilities of developing indigenous orbital launch vehicles, Wu said.
National Cheng Kung University astronautics professor Wu Chih-yung (吳志勇) said that Maraho maintained stable communications with the ground during the whole test flight process and sent back effective flight data.
It has become a successful example of orbital launch vehicle verification, he said.
Feng Chia University aerospace engineering professor Yeh Chun-liang (葉俊良) said the filling process of 90 percent hydrogen peroxide for the hybrid propulsion system is highly complex.
The completion of Maraho’s test flight can be recognized as a successful launch, he said.
The agency said that Maraho was named after Taiwan’s endemic butterfly species, Papilio maraho, or the broad-tailed swallowtail butterfly.
The broad-tailed swallowtail butterfly is known as Taiwan’s national butterfly, featuring broad red tails that resemble the flames trailing behind a rocket during liftoff, it said.
The butterfly species’ specific epithet originated from mrhuw in the Atayal language, meaning “a respectable wise person,” the agency said.
The rocket is expected to help upgrade Taiwan’s independently developed launch vehicle technology, it said.

====================================================================================================

Interpretive autonomy required
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:31 UTC
01:45:31 KST

Over the past few weeks, domestic and international headlines have been dominated by reports of what was described as a “joint naval drill” between China and Indonesia in the waters east of Taiwan, following an announcement by the Chinese Ministry of National Defense on Tuesday last week.
The two countries conducted the activity the following day, involving the Chinese naval vessel Honghe and the Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai (332).
Beijing said that the exercise was intended to enhance the two navies’ operational capabilities, deepen practical cooperation and contribute to regional peace and stability.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council and Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the exercise, saying that China’s “reckless and irresponsible behavior” in repeatedly disregarding international norms and responsibilities continues to escalate regional tensions. The nation also sought clarification from the Indonesian government.
Indonesian officials — including the Indonesian Navy Information Service head and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ spokesperson — said that the activity was not a combat-oriented joint exercise, but rather a passing exercise. Such exercises are routine naval practices conducted when warships traverse a region, serving as a naval diplomacy, rather than a war-fighting drill.
The a passing exercise with China took place while KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai was returning home after participating in the joint exercise Orel-Garuda with Russia.
Technically, a passing exercise is a limited, short-duration exercise with a focus on non-warfighting exercises — in this case including communications drills and maritime replenishment — designed to build communication, trust, good relations and naval brotherhood.
A joint military exercise is normally more structured and deliberately planned, involving multiple phases and more complex scenarios such as simulated combat, amphibious operations or live-fire drills. Indonesia has also conducted similar a passing exercise activities with Japan and the US 7th Fleet, underscoring the routine, non-exclusive nature of these engagements.
Such naval interactions are consistent with Jakarta’s long-standing “free and active” foreign policy and its broader maritime diplomacy, which seeks to open cooperative avenues with a wide range of partners.
However, the concern here is not the technical content of the exercise, but its location. The waters east of Taiwan are geopolitically sensitive, sitting at the heart of cross-strait tensions.
Given this complexity, the combination of foreign participation and a flashpoint location inevitably carries geopolitical and strategic weight, even if it has no direct military impact on Taiwan. Indonesia’s naval presence in these waters, however routine, invites interpretations that transcend its operational intent.
What is particularly revealing is how the narrative around this a passing exercise has evolved, generating divergent readings across the international community. China described the activity as a naval navigation exercise; Taiwan characterized it an attempt to normalize Beijing’s presence in the waters to create a false international impression that China holds jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan; and Indonesia perceived it as a routine passing exercise in service of naval diplomacy.
Modern naval diplomacy is no longer simply about what naval forces physically do at sea. It is also about how those activities are framed, communicated and interpreted. Although Indonesia did not specifically intend to conduct an exercise only with China, the narrative that emerged around the low-intensity naval exercise could carry diplomatic risks and potentially affect Indonesia’s reputation.
This episode highlights a critical lesson: Indonesia must prioritize strategic communication before others define its actions and shape narratives that could misrepresent Indonesia’s intentions. Sensitivity to the operational details and the symbolic geography of any engagement should be carefully considered in foreign policy and defense decisionmaking.
At this level, strategic autonomy alone is insufficient. Indonesia must also cultivate what might be called interpretive autonomy — the capacity to proactively shape the narrative surrounding its actions to reduce misperceptions and maintain constructive relationships with various partners — without being boxed into narratives defined by others.
This is especially pertinent given the upward trajectory of Indonesia-China defense ties. Last year, the two countries held their inaugural 2+2 foreign and defense ministerial meeting, a clear sign of deepening strategic engagement.
Indonesia is also reportedly exploring defense industrial cooperation with China, including the potential procurement of 42 Chengdu J-10C fighter jets.
Under Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s administration, Jakarta has visibly expanded its defense cooperation beyond the traditional partner such as the US, reaching out to Beijing and Moscow.
The overarching message is clear: Even routine, low-level naval cooperation carries diplomatic weight when situated in contested waters.
Indonesia must ensure that its actions are clearly communicated — so that a standard naval interaction does not inadvertently entangle it in a diplomatic framing that distorts its true intentions.
Marina Ika Sari is this year’s Japan Foundation Southeast Asia Partnership visiting fellow and a researcher at The Habibie Center.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Taiwan in Time: Vanished on Qilai Mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:30 UTC
01:45:30 KST

Aug. 24 to Aug. 30
Three pairs of chopsticks, stuck upright in the ground like incense, have become one of the most curious details in the story of three university graduates who disappeared on Qilai Mountain (奇萊) in 1972.
The case remains unsolved today. Despite an extensive two-month search, the three men’s bodies were never found. The incident came just a year after five National Tsing Hua University students died on the mountain on July 25, 1971, after being unexpectedly caught in a typhoon, prompting serious concerns about hiking safety.
Photo courtesy of National Taitung Living Art Center
Tunghai University graduate Chiu Kao (邱高) and Fu Jen Catholic University students Lee Fu-ming (李福明) and Hu Te-ning (胡德寧) were reportedly experienced hikers with sufficient wilderness survival skills, and had with them a transistor radio. Chiu wanted to summit Qilai Main Peak, part of the notorious “Black Qilai” range, known for its treacherous terrain, mercurial weather, thick fog and frequent accidents.
Reports in Wilderness Magazine (野外) say that Chiu’s original application was for the Nengao Traversing Trail (能高越嶺步道), but the three men changed their route on their own and headed for Qilai Main Peak, which was not advisable without a guide.
This case gave rise to supernatural legends and rumors that the mountain was haunted, while a mysterious “ghost photo” taken in 1996 prompted another month-long search for the hikers’ remains.
Photo courtesy of Wilderness Magazine
While their fate remains unknown, reports show that the Chiu Kao Incident helped spur the development of mountain search and rescue in Taiwan. Permanent civilian rescue groups sprang up afterward, building their skills through training and operations.
MASSIVE SEARCH
The hikers began their ascent from the Lushan Checkpoint (廬山) on Aug. 23, reaching Taipower’s Tianchi Wiring Maintenance Station (天池保線所), where they spent the night in the lodge. They left the following morning. It was the last confirmed sighting of the trio.
Photo courtesy of National Central Library
Chiu’s father reported the three men missing to police on Sept. 4. However, another three young men had stayed at the Dayuling Lodge (大禹嶺) the previous night and descended the mountain the following day, leading authorities to believe they were Chiu and his companions. This mistake delayed the rescue operations until Chiu’s father, still waiting for his son to return, called the authorities again on Sept. 9.
On Sept. 11, police from Nantou and Hualien counties finally began searching for the three men, assisted by Indigenous guides. The Air Force also dispatched a plane from Hsinchu Air Base, but found nothing.
The search soon intensified. The Air Force sent two helicopters and four planes, while ground teams found two white undershirts. On Sept. 14, searchers discovered writing scratched into the ground with a rock past Kalulou Peak. Most of it was illegible, but it appeared to indicate that the hikers had passed the most dangerous section of the route.
Still, there was no sign of the men. The Army also joined the search, while civic mountaineering associations began sending teams led by veteran climbers. More than 300 people had taken part by then.
On Sept. 19, the Chinese Alpine Association (中華民國山岳協會) dispatched a team of 15 experienced mountaineers and 25 Indigenous guides, led by Tsai Ching-chang (蔡景璋), one of Taiwan’s famed “Four Heavenly Kings of Mountaineering” (see “Taiwan in Time: The making of Taiwan’s ‘100 Peaks Club,’” May 17, 2026). Fellow “Heavenly King” Lin Wen-an (林文安) was also on the roster. With seven teams of 75 people searching in the rain, they still came back empty handed.
UPRIGHT CHOPSTICKS?
Photo courtesy of the Taichung National Park Administration
Nearly two weeks into the search, there was finally a breakthrough on Sept. 24. The United Daily News reported that Tseng Lung-hua’s (曾龍華) volunteer search team first found half a piece of bread on the ground west of Qilai Main Peak. Upon closer inspection, they found four mountaineering-association membership cards, two spoons, a ticket to the Provincial Museum and three pairs of chopsticks stuck in the ground pointing toward the sky. The China Times reported the same.
However, the Central Daily News reported finding two pairs of chopsticks and did not specify how they were placed. Searchers also detected a suspicious odor in the area, but a few days later discovered that it came from a decomposing mountain goat. And the 2005 book, History of Taiwan Mountaineering (台灣登山史) by Lee Hsi-sheng (李希聖) makes no mention of the chopsticks. However, the detail appears in most modern articles discussing the incident.
The search continued to expand, drawing in more people. On Nov. 7, the United Daily News reported that Chiu’s father, who had spent the previous 60 days in Hualien and Nantou, was returning briefly to Taipei. Tseng reportedly told him, “As long as Mr. Chiu doesn’t give up, I’ll keep helping until we get some answers.”
However, winter soon arrived. The snow made the mountains inaccessible, bringing the search to an end.
THE AFTERMATH
In September 1995, the United Daily News ran an article about the impact of the Chiu Kao Incident. It noted that the search and rescue efforts were of an unprecedented scale, mobilizing thousands of people.
Jen Tie-gang (任鐵鋼), then-head of the Taiwan Mountain Rescue Association, said that prior to this, operations were focused on “rescue,” as in most cases they knew where the hikers were.
Tsai told the paper that it was extremely bizarre that such an extensive search had uncovered so few clues about what happened to Chiu and his companions. He suggested that the three chopsticks stuck in the ground were meant to signal, “Come save us!” Yet aside from that, he said, there was little trace of them anywhere else in the mountains.
Rumors circulated that the three men had been attacked by wild animals, killed by robbers or even faked their deaths and secretly left the country.
“The concept of mountain search and rescue took root from this incident,” the article stated. “Permanent civilian rescue organizations were subsequently established, while repeated experience and training gradually refined search-and-rescue methods.”
“All of this can be said to trace back to the Chiu Kao Incident.”
A final chapter in the saga came about 10 years later. A hiker took a photo on the grassy plain between Nanhua Mountain and Qilai South Peak that showed a mysterious human figure in the distance, standing at an improbable spot high on the mountain. Hu Te-ning’s mother reportedly recognized the jacket the figure was wearing as one she had bought for her son, prompting one final search mission — that still yielded no results.

An interesting essay in the spring issue this year of International Security by Kerby Davis and Eugene Gholz explores the possibilities and outcomes of simulated missile attacks by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) on Taiwan’s ports to carry out a blockade. “Substantively,” they conclude in Blockade by Fire: China’s Potential to Blockade Taiwan Using Missile Attacks on Ports, “our article raises serious concern about Taiwan’s vulnerability to Chinese military coercion. Even if Taiwan and the United States take steps to better prepare for a Chinese blockade, they face a greater threat from China than analysts previously believed.” The authors
The Tzu Chi Foundation, the globally known Buddhist charity, announced on July 21, 2021 that it had signed a deal to purchase 5 million doses of the Pfizer-BioNTech (BNT) COVID-19 vaccine. It said that the vaccine doses would be donated to the government’s COVID vaccine program. In October the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) made a public announcement thanking the Buddhist foundation and others for the 889,200 doses of the BNT vaccine they had collectively donated. Mentally ill prisoners need better options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:29 UTC
01:45:29 KST

There is a prisoner with a severe psychiatric disorder, exhibiting detachment from reality to the extent that they are unable to manage their own affairs, refusing treatment for nearly two years. Although this person continues to talk to themselves and experiences auditory hallucinations, paranoia and agitation, prison authorities can only place them in solitary confinement to prevent them from harming others.
This person with schizophrenia was sentenced to five years in prison for aggravated assault and other offenses, and is due to be released in a few months. From a psychiatrist’s perspective, it is simply absurd that a severely mentally ill person who has a history of aggravated assault cannot receive treatment in prison, leaving authorities to watch helplessly as they are released while still symptomatic.
This is not only a gap in the social safety net, but is unfair to people with psychiatric illnesses.
Correctional facilities are required to act in accordance with the law. Article 46 of the Mental Health Act (精神衛生法) states that “if correctional authorities, rehabilitation disposition facilities, and other institutions or facilities intended for detention and reformation have a patient or a person suspected of having the condition specified in Subparagraph 1 of Paragraph 1 of Article 3, they shall provide medical care or escort and assist such people in seeking medical care, and carry out the measures in a compulsory manner if necessary.” In this case, the correctional facility has provided psychiatric care, but the person has refused treatment. As they pose no risk of harming themselves or others, the facility has no legal basis to escort them to a hospital or apply for involuntary hospitalization.
However, the act actually provides a solution.
Article 54 of the act provides for compulsory “community treatment.” It states that if a severe patient “is not following medical advice, which is causing an unstable health condition or a risk of declining function, and the specialist doctor deems it necessary for the patient to receive community treatment, the local competent authority of the patient’s domicile or residence and the community mental health center must work together with the protector to help the patient access community treatment.”
The person in this case appears to meet the criteria for compulsory community treatment, and conducting that treatment while they are still in prison would be the most practical option. Medical personnel could make regular visits to administer medications, providing the most effective way to ensure continued care.
However, the authorities reportedly believe that a correctional facility is not a community, and therefore, compulsory community treatment cannot be applied for or carried out there. In my view, this is an unnecessarily restrictive interpretation of the law. In practice, compulsory community treatment is generally provided in people’s homes.
Article 5 of the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s guidelines for the home-based treatment of people with mental disorders (精神疾病病人居家治療標準) states that home-based treatment involves personnel providing professional services at a person’s residence or place of living. It does not restrict such treatment to a person’s own home.
In practice, people with mental disorders residing in nursing or residential care facilities also commonly receive home-based treatment.
I hope that the Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Health and Welfare and other government agencies would recognize the importance of treating incarcerated people with psychiatric illnesses and take steps to prevent these gaps in the social safety net.
Lin Jin-jia is a psychiatrist.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Lawmakers pass motion condemning the premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:28 UTC
01:45:28 KST

Opposition lawmakers voted on Friday to fast-track a motion condemning Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) following his refusal to countersign legislation on creating savings accounts for youth passed by the legislature, alongside other bills.
The motion, proposed by the Taiwan People’s Party, accused the Democratic Progressive Party administration of “repeatedly abusing authority under the Constitution” to invalidate legislation passed by the legislature.
“Not only does this exceed official authority and disrupt the separation of powers, but it also treats the legislature with complete disregard,” the proposal read.
Photo: CNA
With the support from the main opposition Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), the proposal skipped committee review and moved directly to a second reading, setting up a potential vote in as soon as a month.
Under the legal system, a legislative motion to censure the premier is symbolic only, with no binding force or statutory authority.
Cho announced on Monday last week he would not countersign the Youth Development and Future Account Act (台灣兒少成長及未來帳戶條例), a bill creating government-funded accounts for Taiwanese under the age of 18, and an amendment to the Cable Radio and Television Act, passed by the opposition-controlled legislation.
Article 37 of the Constitution of the Republic of China stipulates that laws passed by the Legislature must be countersigned by the premier before the president can formally enact them.
The opposition argues that this authority serves as a check on presidential power, not on the Legislature, and that the premier should request a re-vote if the government does not support a law.
No premier had ever taken such action to block a law passed by the Legislature before December last year when Cho first declined to countersign the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法).
Since then, Cho has refused to sign legislation seven times, including amendments to legislative governance rules.
Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) slammed Cho on Thursday for “weaponizing” his countersign authority, calling the move a mistake.
Responding to Han, Executive Yuan Secretary-General Xavier Chang (張惇涵) said on Friday that Article 37 of the Constitution requires Cho to take action to “uphold the constitutional order.”
The Executive Yuan refused to countersign the bill on constitutional and equity grounds, contending that the measure encroaches on its constitutional authority to manage policies and the national budget, that allowing corporate sponsorship of the accounts could widen the wealth gap, and that vague tax exemptions violate the principle of taxation by law, its statement said.

Tainan fire injures 15 and damages 68 homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:23 UTC
01:45:23 KST

A fire and subsequent explosion in a residential area in Tainan early yesterday injured 15 people and damaged 68 homes, the Tainan City Fire Bureau said.
The bureau said it received a report at 1:12am yesterday that a pile of waste in a vacant lot in Annan District’s (安南) Haidian Road had caught fire and exploded, adding that it dispatched 144 firefighters and 53 firetrucks to battle the blaze and evacuate nearby residents.
It took more than four hours to extinguish the fire, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Tainan City Government’s Environmental Protection Bureau
The incident damaged 11 privately owned vehicles, as well as eight fire engines, one ambulance and two disaster assessment vehicles, the bureau said.
The three homes closest to the blast site sustained the most severe damage, it added.
Twelve people and three firefighters were injured, sustaining cuts to the head or other minor injuries, the bureau said, adding that no one was seriously hurt.
The Tainan City Government’s air quality and pollutant sampling data showed no abnormalities after the incident.
A man surnamed Yang (楊) allegedly managed the land, allowing a Kaohsiung waste operator to illegally dump trash outside its jurisdiction in contravention of the Waste Disposal Act (廢棄物清理法), the bureau said, citing a police investigation.
The case has been referred to prosecutors, while the Kaohsiung Environmental Protection Bureau has been notified about conducting a joint investigation, it said.
Tainan Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲), who had been visiting Singapore, flew home after learning of the incident and arrived at the scene last night to assess the damage.
The city government would prioritize helping affected residents find temporary accommodation and restore their homes, he said, adding that lawyers would be hired to help them seek compensation and hold those responsible accountable.
The city government has activated emergency housing and relief measures for the 11 households that were most severely affected, Huang said.
Each household would receive NT$20,000 in emergency assistance, and civil engineers would be brought in to assess the structural safety of the homes to provide a basis for subsequent repairs and compensation claims, he added.

The Ciaotou District Court on Friday ruled that Chinese immigrant Zhou Manzhi (周滿芝) must serve an additional 18 months in prison for contravening the Anti-infiltration Act (反滲透法) after intervening in Taiwanese elections under orders from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Zhou had once been a member of the Shanxi Province Patriotic Volunteer Association and the China Patriotism Volunteer Association, groups whose core missions are to promote Beijing’s “united front” rhetoric, the ruling said.
The court accepted the argument that the associations were controlled by the CCP’s United Front Work Department, a ministerial-level agency reporting directly to the party’s Central Committee.
Photo: Taipei Times
The associations are legally defined as sources of infiltration, and Zhou followed the instructions of such organizations in founding the Kaohsiung New Immigrants Care Association and the Taiwan New Immigrants Care Foundation to promote the “united front” rhetoric, the ruling said.
During the 2024 elections, Zhou used her influence with new immigrants to garner votes for Labor Party legislator candidate Zhan Xiuying (湛秀英) at in-person rallies and online, the ruling said.
The collegiate bench presiding over the case found that Zhou intended to increase the number of Chinese spouses in legislative seats to raise the number of pro-China voices within the government.
Zhou obeyed orders from a foreign force despite knowing the CCP’s intentions to infiltrate Taiwan militarily, culturally and through diplomatic actions, the ruling said.
Separate charges against Zhou of accepting Chinese hospitality, spreading falsified polls and garnering votes for then-independent presidential candidate Terry Gou (郭台銘) were dropped, the ruling said.
Co-defendant in the case Hsu Wei-fu (徐維甫) was handed one year and 10 months in prison, while Wang Min (王敏), Hsu’s girlfriend, was given a sentence of one year of prison with a four-year deferral.
Taiwan New Immigrants Care Foundation secretary-general Kuo Yung-tsung (郭永聰) was found not guilty of related charges.
The ruling can still be appealed.

The idyllic beaches of the Greek islands have long been a draw for European holidaymakers, but now a new wave of US tourists is waking up to their charms, driven by stars such as Madonna, Katy Perry and Justin Bieber.
Madonna celebrated her 68th birthday on Corfu, sharing a whirl of parties and boat trips against the backdrop of the island’s landscape with her 20 million Instagram followers — earning her rapturous thanks from Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
Experts say the huge popularity of Christopher Nolan blockbuster The Odyssey would only fuel the trend — although holidaymakers would be hoping for an easier trip home than the one endured by Matt Damon’s eponymous hero.
Photo: Reuters
While Madonna partied in Corfu, singer Bieber took his family to the Peloponnese. Perry and her partner, former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, sampled the delights of Mykonos.
All of them chronicled their holidays on social media, giving the Greek tourism industry a massive hit of free advertising.
“Celebrities are voting for the Greek summer,” public broadcaster ERT said on Friday, devoting a report to these stars from across the Atlantic.
The newspaper To Vima hailed this “new wave” which “helps raise the country’s international profile.” It cited British singer and actress Rita Ora, who shared her holidays with “her millions of followers” on social media.
Paris Tsartas, professor of tourism development at Harokopio University in Athens, said the deluge of celebrity endorsements gave Greece a powerful boost as a summer destination — particularly with the lucrative US market.
After a decade of financial woes following the debt crisis of 2009, and the devastation of the COVID-19 pandemic, Greece has pumped money into the sector, which accounts for about 30 percent of GDP, according to the Association of Greek Tourism Enterprises (SETE).
About 1.55 million Americans visited Greece last year. They represent the third-largest source of tourism income, behind Germans and Britons, with an average spend per tourist of 1,120 euros (US$1,308), the SETE said.
To answer growing demand, the main US airlines have significantly stepped up services, American Airlines increasing its total available seat capacity by 30 percent compared with summer last year. This year Greece has had its highest-ever number of direct flights, with 103 connections a week between Athens and the US.
Some of the new enthusiasm is driven by the phenomenon of “set-jetting” — people traveling to a destination after seeing it in a movie or TV series.
In a study for online travel giant Expedia, 13 percent of American travelers said they had booked a trip after seeing a destination on screen. Greece is well acquainted with the trend, after hit musical Mamma Mia, filmed on the island of Skopelos, triggered a jump in US visitors.
Tsartas predicted The Odyssey would have a similar impact. Key parts of Nolan’s film, recounting the travails of Damon’s Odysseus as he seeks to return home from the Trojan war to his wife Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, were shot in the Peloponnese region of Greece. According to EasyJet Holidays, cited by ,
Bookings to Greece increased by 18 percent in the weeks following the film’s international release in last month, the Greek newspaper Kathimerini cited EasyJet Holidays as saying.
There is more small-screen exposure for Greece’s charms to come: Netflix had chosen the country for the sixth season of hit series Emily in Paris.
Lead actress Lily Collins and the rest of the production team were spotted this spring in Mykonos, Paros and Santorini.

Takaichi confronts her mentor’s mixed foreign policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:11 UTC
01:45:11 KST

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has inherited a lot of things from her mentor, the late prime minister Shinzo Abe: Her support base, conservative credentials, and even her favored slogan of “Japan is back.”
This is true of foreign policy, too. The sight of US President Donald Trump pulling the rug from under one of the US’ closest allies by ordering joint military drills with South Korea to be scaled back is but one reminder of the risks and rewards of Abe’s playbook in dealing with Washington. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to islands controlled by Russia but claimed by Japan drags up the late premier’s biggest international failure. And talk of summits with North Korea recalls an event that made Abe’s early career, before turning to bitter regret.
Takaichi should put a little distance between herself and her mentor, and work through a new foreign policy to decide what should stay and what should go.
Illustration: Tania Chou
Start with Trump. Japan’s leader can learn many of the right lessons from his relationship with Abe. Whatever Trump’s true reason for abruptly hamstringing the South Korea drills — his affinity for North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, Seoul’s supposed failure to help with Iran or, as reports suggest, the slow pace of investment in the US — the move has startled Tokyo. Officials are no doubt concerned that as in 2018, Trump will increase demands on Japan ahead of the midterm elections.
One of Abe’s greatest diplomatic achievements was showing the world how to engage with the capricious president. He understood earlier than most that dealing with Trump meant flattery, copious reciprocity, big promises of spending, and a willingness to hold one’s nose. Despite periodic calls for higher spending on US troops and increased imports of US cars, Japan remains one of the few traditional allies that has largely dodged his opprobrium.
Takaichi has mostly followed that model, and for now Tokyo looks better placed than Seoul. She has turned US demands for investment into an opportunity to secure rare-earth and energy projects that will boost economic security. And she understands that Trump does not care if these do not add up to US$550 billion — the official amount Japan agreed to invest during last year’s tariff war — so long as he gets a good headline.
There are lessons to take away from Abe’s dealings with North Korea, too, amid reports that the US president is looking for another summit with Kim. As a young politician, Abe made his career with his hardline stance during then-Japanese prime minister Junichiro Koizumi’s historic summit with Kim’s father, Kim Jong-il, in 2002, which paved the way for the return of some of the Japanese citizens that North Korea had kidnapped.
Abe also sensibly avoided being used as a tool by Pyongyang, a concern that does not seem to bother Trump. Japanese media reported following his assassination four years ago that Abe had rejected a 2014 proposal to repatriate just two of the abductees, something he deemed a bad deal. Yet he was never able to secure his own visit to Pyongyang as leader, and was sidelined by Trump’s overtures to Kim.
Takaichi must similarly balance the risks of being bypassed against those of being used as a political pawn. Having taken up the abductee issue herself, a summit with North Korea would be a potential political win.
The question is leverage: This is a very different state from the impoverished one in 2002. Arms sales to Russia and crypto thefts leave Pyongyang with a diminished need for assistance. Without tangible results, Takaichi should not lend legitimacy to the Kim regime in return for a mere photo op.
For all his clear-eyed vision on China, Abe had a terminal blind spot for Putin. He burned years of political capital seeking a deal to reclaim the territory Moscow calls the southern Kurils and Japan dubs the Northern Territories, seized by the Soviet Union in the dying days of World War II. It was the unfinished legacy of his own father, Shintaro, who as foreign minister believed he could break the impasse.
Shinzo Abe held summits with Putin, seeking “hot-tub diplomacy” at an onsen resort, while officials from a northern prefecture gifted the Russian president an adorable dog. All to no avail, with Putin stringing Japan on so long that the dog died of old age last year.
Any attempt to restart such talks should stay dead, too, but there are concerning signs that some around the prime minister want to return to this failed strategy, and re-engage with Moscow. Takaichi is notably the only G7 leader yet to hold a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. She must not make the same mistake Shinzo Abe did: allowing the ghosts of the past to dictate the present.
Shinzo Abe’s skill was in understanding that personal relations could create room for Japan where it might be militarily outmatched, but his mistake was sometimes to confuse relationships with actual results. Takaichi needs to know the difference.
Indeed, it is important to know when to change tactics when needed. That is what Shinzo Abe, at his best, would have done.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan and the Koreas. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. The challenges of Bilingual 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:10 UTC
01:45:10 KST

Jye Smallwood’s article on English-medium instruction (EMI) raises important questions about how Taiwan’s bilingual ambitions are being translated into classroom practice. In particular, he draws attention to a distinction that can easily become blurred: EMI is a teaching context, not a language-teaching method, and teaching a subject through English creates challenges that English proficiency alone cannot solve.
When assessing the challenges of Bilingual 2030, it is tempting to ask whether the policy is succeeding or failing. As a language educator, I wonder if there is a more constructive question: What has the experience taught us?
Language teachers navigate a similar problem every day.
During communicative fluency activities, students inevitably make errors. A teacher might be tempted to interrupt every mistake immediately. However, doing so can quickly disrupt the communication the activity was designed to develop.
Experienced teachers often do something different: We listen.
We observe what students are trying to accomplish. We notice which problems occur repeatedly, which interfere with communication and which are simply momentary slips. Then, after the activity, we address the patterns that matter most.
This is known as delayed correction. It is not about ignoring mistakes. It is about gathering enough evidence to make the subsequent intervention more useful.
Perhaps Bilingual 2030 has reached a similar point.
After years of implementation across Taiwan’s schools and universities, the policy has generated considerable experience with bilingual classrooms, EMI, teacher development and different approaches to supporting students. Inevitably, not everything has worked as intended. That is concerning, but it is also something valuable to learn from.
Smallwood’s observations highlight one important pattern. Deep subject knowledge and strong English do not automatically answer the pedagogical questions that arise when teaching a subject through English. Knowing economics, engineering or history and creating the conditions for students to learn those subjects are different forms of expertise.
This does not mean turning university professors into language teachers. As Smallwood said, EMI is a teaching context, not a language-teaching method.
However, that context places particular demands on teachers’ professional judgement: how to make complex ideas accessible without diminishing them, how to determine whether students have understood and how to create opportunities for students to engage with the subject rather than simply listening to it in another language.
Language education has wrestled with similar questions for decades. Communicative approaches shifted attention from simply presenting language toward creating conditions in which learners use it. The methods cannot simply be transplanted into an economics or engineering lecture, but some of the underlying lessons might transfer.
Effective teaching begins not only with what we intend to teach, but with careful attention to how these students are actually learning it.
The same principle can help with Bilingual 2030.
Delayed correction works because the teacher does not react to every error in isolation. The teacher observes long enough to identify patterns and then decides which interventions are most likely to improve the next attempt.
Taiwan has years of experience from which to do the same.
An initiative as ambitious as Bilingual 2030 was always going to test assumptions and reveal approaches that needed refinement. Identifying those weaknesses does not mean declaring the entire policy a success or a failure.
It provides an opportunity to ask which patterns have emerged, where students and teachers are succeeding, where they continue to struggle, and what support would make the greatest difference.
The value of delayed correction is not that mistakes become acceptable. It is that accumulated experience allows the teacher to respond more intelligently.
Bilingual 2030 has given Taiwan that experience. The important question is what we choose to learn from it.
Daniel Eyrich is director of English Studies at CenYing English in Keelung and has more than 15 years of experience in English language teaching, assessment and teacher development in Taiwan.

Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Average household income up 3.3%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:10 UTC
01:45:10 KST

Average total household income in Taiwan was NT$1,529,000 (US$ 48,009) last year, up 3.3 percent from a year earlier, the latest data from the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) showed.
Median disposable household income last year was NT$1,018,000, up 3.4 percent from a year earlier, the data showed.
Employee compensation was the main source of household income, although significant regional differences were evident, DGBAS said.
Graphic: CNA
Hsinchu City and Hsinchu County had average total household incomes of NT$2,042,000 and NT$2,007,000 respectively, the highest in Taiwan, it said.
They were followed by NT$1,857,000 in Taipei, NT$1,557,000 in Taoyuan and NT$1,506,000 in New Taipei City, it said.
Employee compensation accounted for more than half of household income in Taiwan’s six special municipalities, Hsinchu County and Hsinchu City, DGBAS said.
Hsinchu City and Hsinchu County reported significantly higher average household incomes, mainly because the high-paying technology sector dominates their economies, resulting in higher salaries, overtime pay and year-end bonuses, it said.
Other important sources included interest income, investment income and other property income, including rental income, DGBAS said.
Average household property income in Taiwan was NT$76,000 last year, with Taipei highest at NT$180,000, or nearly 10 percent of average household income in the city, it said.
The figures show that property income is a particularly important component of household income in Taipei, although DGBAS cautioned that its data do not sufficiently disaggregate rental income from other forms of property income to identify the main source.
Hsinchu City last year reported average household property income of NT$131,000, making it the only other administrative division where property income exceeded NT$100,000, it added.
Taiwanese stocks surged last year, especially shares in artificial intelligence companies, but gains from buying and selling stocks or funds are excluded from the agency’s household-income calculations because they are treated as changes in wealth rather than income, DGBAS said.

Defense budget proposal sending US signals: expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:07 UTC
01:45:07 KST

Taiwan’s proposed defense budget for next year sends a signal that should resonate with the White House, which has urged allies and partners to increase defense spending, a US academic said Friday.
The Cabinet on Thursday approved the central government budget proposal for next year, which would allocate NT$1.1225 trillion (US$35.2 billion) for defense, equivalent to 3.01 percent of GDP.
Michael Hunzeker, an associate professor at George Mason University who studies Taiwanese defense issues, said the proposed budget was a “very positive development” that showed that President William Lai (賴清德) remained committed to keeping defense spending above 3 percent of GDP and on track to reach 5 percent by 2030.
Photo: Cheng-Chia Huang, Reuters
Given the White House’s emphasis on urging allies and partners to increase defense spending, Hunzeker said that the proposal should send a signal that would be welcomed by the White House.
“It should likewise send a clear signal to Beijing that its increasingly aggressive actions have not caused the Lai administration to back down on its national security promises,” he added.
Hunzeker said a growing defense budget should give Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense and armed forces more resources to acquire better and more appropriate weapons, ammunition and spare parts, expand rigorous and realistic training, enhance resilience efforts, and attract and retain personnel for mission-critical frontline combat units.
“Of course, this proposal is just the start of a long process. Potential obstacles and challenges remain,” he added.
Hunzeker said that the proposal still needs to be reviewed by the legislature and could face scrutiny similar to that faced by this year’s budget, which lawmakers only passed this month.
He also pointed to opposition parties’ pushback against Lai’s proposed eight-year special defense budget, saying further scrutiny could be expected as parties prepare for upcoming elections.
A US Department of State spokesperson welcomed Taiwan’s proposal to increase defense spending to more than 3 percent of GDP, saying that it demonstrated Taiwan’s resolve to improve its self-defense capabilities.
The spokesperson said the US supports Taiwan’s acquisition of critical defense capabilities “consistent with the Taiwan Relations Act and more than 45 years of commitment across multiple US administrations.”
The spokesperson added that “the threat Taiwan faces from China has grown considerably.”

S Korean container to sail Arctic route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:05 UTC
01:45:05 KST

South Korea was yesterday to send its first trial container through the Arctic, as the Middle East war rattles global shipping, while environmental groups warned that the route could accelerate polar ice melt.
The Middle East conflict has roiled global shipping, sending governments and shipping firms scrambling to seek alternative routes.
Sailing from Busan New Port, container ship PanStar Acro would sail to Europe via the Arctic, testing whether a route opened by melting sea ice could be commercially viable.
Photo: AFP
“The ship will depart at 8pm today unless there are unforeseen circumstances, such as bad weather,” a South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries official said.
The ship would leave for Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland before returning, with the voyage expected to take about 45 days, the ministry said.
The voyage follows that of the Chinese container ship Dubai Tower, which left the eastern port city of Ningbo for Europe this month, heading north through the Bering Strait before turning west along Russia’s Arctic coast.
The usual maritime route between Asia and Europe runs through the Suez Canal, but traveling through the Arctic could cut the journey by about 7,000km and about 10 days, the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy said.
South Korean Vice Minister of Oceans and Fisheries Nam Jae-hon said the Arctic route was “bound to become an alternative” to Middle Eastern shipping lanes — as geopolitical risks and technological advances make it increasingly competitive.
Arctic University of Norway political science professor Marc Lanteigne said the voyage — coming soon after Dubai Tower began its own Arctic journey — showed that the Northern Sea Route was becoming normalized as a “secondary maritime transit corridor.”
A successful voyage would demonstrate South Korea’s interest in “developing alternative shipping sea lanes,” he said, adding that it could fall behind as Chinese firms expand regular services through the increasingly viable Arctic route.
Some experts warned that South Korean ships using the Arctic route could risk breaching Western sanctions on Russia, as they would receive Russian navigation and weather services involving payments, albeit small ones.
The South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs declined to comment about the concerns involving Russia.
The oceans ministry said this week that “consultations with key relevant countries and agencies” have been completed to “implement administrative procedures necessary” for the voyage.
University of Oslo Korean studies professor Vladimir Tikhonov said: “strictly speaking, US and EU sanctions are not international law, unlike UN sanctions.”
“And with continued uncertainty in the Middle East — itself driven in part by US actions — South Korea may have few alternatives if the Arctic route proves economically viable,” he said.
Lanteigne said China’s Northern Sea Route ambitions were more politically driven than South Korea’s, with Beijing viewing the polar regions as “strategic new frontiers,” raising Western security concerns.
Meanwhile, environmental groups warned growing traffic along the shorter route could accelerate Arctic sea ice loss already driven by global warming. Major carriers including CMA CGM, MSC and Hapag-Lloyd have pledged to avoid Arctic shipping routes.
The route is believed to be accessible only during the time of year when the ice is melted enough to allow transits without icebreakers.
“The Northern Sea Route has become increasingly viable as the Arctic warms about four times faster than the global average, leading to a sharp decline in sea ice,” South Korean environmental group Paran Ocean Citizen Science Center said in a statement last year. “But making the route commercially viable would require further warming, putting the policy at odds with efforts to combat climate change.”

Tropical depression threatens torrential rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:45:01 UTC
01:45:01 KST

The Central Weather Administration (CWA) yesterday forecast heavy rain for southern Taiwan today, saying tropical depression TD22 would strengthen southwesterly winds and bring more downpours.
The CWA said that in addition to torrential rain in southern Taiwan yesterday, mountainous areas in central and southeastern Taiwan also saw heavy rainfall, while northern and northeastern mountain areas were hit by short-duration downpours amid intense afternoon thunderstorms.
Tainan had experienced continuous rain since Friday night, with Yongkang District (永康) recording more than 132mm of rainfall in three hours and Rende District (仁德) nearly 100mm over the same period, the CWA said.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
By 3:20pm yesterday, Pingtung County’s Wandan Township (萬丹) had recorded 281mm of accumulated rainfall, the highest nationwide, followed by Majia Township (瑪家) with 263mm. Kaohsiung’s Siaogang District (小港) had recorded 254.5mm and Linyuan District (林園) 242mm, while Tainan’s Gueiren District (歸仁) had recorded 237.5mm.
The CWA said the most intense rainfall was expected from today through early Tuesday.
Southern Taiwan could see extremely heavy rain during that period, while Chiayi and eastern Taiwan could see localized extremely heavy rain and central Taiwan localized heavy rain, it said.
Taian, Kaohsiung and Pingtung County last night announced the cancellation of work and school today.
As of yesterday afternoon, TD22 was about 350km east of Taiwan. Although the Japan Meteorological Agency had upgraded the system to Typhoon Gaenari, the CWA continued to classify it as a tropical depression, saying its circulation and convection remained relatively weak.
The CWA said TD22 was expected to move northwest before turning west toward the Chinese coast. Even if it strengthens into a typhoon, its forecast track would take it more than 300km north of Taiwan, making a sea warning unlikely, although the system is expected to strengthen the southwesterly flow and bring heavier rain to southern Taiwan.
Typhoon Saudel was about 2,600km east of Taiwan at 2pm yesterday, with maximum sustained winds of about 137kph and gale-force winds extending an average of 180km from its center, the CWA said. It could strengthen into a strong typhoon today.
Saudel is forecast to move northwest before turning west-northwest toward the Ryukyu Islands, reaching the area on Wednesday or Thursday. It is then expected to slow and could track farther west, bringing it somewhat closer to Taiwan, although its path remains uncertain, the CWA said.
The typhoon’s outer clouds and circulation could bring increased rainfall to northern Taiwan on Friday and Saturday, with rain also possible in central and eastern Taiwan, it added.

South Korea helps Egypt expand Russian-built nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:36:58 UTC
01:36:58 KST

Breadcrumb
South Korea helps Egypt expand Russian-built nuclear plant
South Korea's growing role in Egypt's Russian-built El Dabaa nuclear power plant has helped Cairo shield the project from Western sanctions and paved the way for a major expansion of the site, according to senior Egyptian energy officials.
Electricity and Renewable Energy Minister Mahmoud Esmat said in televised remarks that Egypt was studying the addition of at least two more nuclear units at El Dabaa, with the possibility of eventually expanding the complex from four reactors to six or even eight.
Senior sources at Egypt's Ministry of Electricity and Energy told The New Arab that the proposed expansion reflected "a state of confidence" surrounding the project following South Korea's entry as a partner alongside Russia's Rosatom.
They said South Korean involvement had enabled Egypt to gain access to Western-linked technology while limiting the exposure of companies working on El Dabaa to US and European sanctions imposed on Russian firms following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to the sources, the South Korean government is expected to provide financial and technical support for future expansions of El Dabaa, alongside its existing role in completing control systems and turbine-related work.
The arrangement has allowed Russia to retain control of the project's nuclear core while South Korean companies handle major elements of its conventional power-generation infrastructure.
The sources said South Korea had taken on work that US company General Electric did not proceed with following the outbreak of the Ukraine war.
Egypt currently plans four Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors at El Dabaa, with a total capacity of 4.8 gigawatts.
The proposed expansion could eventually increase capacity to 9.6 gigawatts by 2040, according to the sources.
Nuclear energy experts said Esmat's remarks "open the door to transforming El Dabaa from a four-unit plant into a larger nuclear complex".
No cost estimate, reactor models or timetable have yet been announced for the additional units.
However, the experts said Cairo increasingly views El Dabaa as "the nucleus of a long-term nuclear programme, rather than a standalone project that ends with the operation of four reactors".
South Korea's involvement in the project expanded rapidly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine complicated Western-linked supply chains.
Experts at Egypt's Nuclear Energy Authority told The New Arab that Russian nuclear energy company Rosatom accelerated moves to bring Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power into El Dabaa as the key supplier for the turbine island and associated control systems for the four Russian units.
Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power signed a $2.25 billion contract with Russia's Atomstroyexport in Cairo on 25 August 2022, months after the outbreak of the war and the introduction of Western sanctions.
Russia nevertheless remained El Dabaa's general contractor and the supplier of its nuclear technology.
South Korea's Doosan Enerbility subsequently took on part of the turbine work under a contract worth around $1.15 billion, covering buildings and equipment associated with turbines, generators, cooling systems and water treatment, with implementation extending to 2029.
Sources said the Korean side consulted US authorities over the agreement to ensure that its involvement did not breach sanctions on Russia.
The resulting "hybrid" arrangement kept Rosatom responsible for the VVER-1200 reactors, primary-circuit systems and other main nuclear equipment, while South Korean firms handled turbines and control equipment used to convert the reactors' thermal energy into electricity.
Egyptian companies are also involved in civil construction and other supporting work at the site.
The expansion plans come as El Dabaa remains under scrutiny over its construction and safety record.
A Politico investigation previously raised questions over alleged construction defects and internal safety concerns at the site, citing internal documents.
Egypt's Nuclear Power Plants Authority and Rosatom rejected suggestions that the project was unsafe, saying any cases of non-conformity were subject to repair, inspection and approval before work progressed to subsequent stages.
Meanwhile, Egyptian Social Democratic Party MP Freddy Elbaiady submitted a parliamentary question on Wednesday to Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly and the electricity minister over concerns surrounding the project's construction, safety and timetable.
Elbaiady called on the government to provide "documented answers" and independent technical and regulatory evidence showing that the concerns had been addressed and would not threaten the project's safety or impose additional financial costs on the Egyptian state.

Hundreds of Palestinians under Israeli siege in Jordan Valley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:26:28 UTC
01:26:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Hundreds of Palestinians under Israeli siege, without water, in Jordan Valley
47 Palestinian families in the Jordan Valley area of the occupied West Bank are living under siege and without water, following the construction of a new settlement road.
They are facing extremely difficult conditions that seem to be meant to pressure them into leaving their homes and lands.
At the far eastern edge of the village of Atouf in the northern Jordan Valley, 70-year-old Lutfi Saeed Jabr and the families of his four sons are living under a blockade imposed by Israeli occupation forces and settlers. 
They have received no water for six days. 
Jabr told The New Arab that around 20 families in the northern Jordan Valley have been cut off from Atouf village following the construction of a concrete wall and iron gates, while another 27 families living about three kilometres away are experiencing similar conditions. 
Residents see this as an attempt to force all 47 families - more than 300 people in total - to leave.
Jabr fears that if he leaves his home to obtain water or food for around 30 members of his family, he may not be able to return. He told The New Arab that he owns around 700 sheep, as well as greenhouses growing vegetables, wheat and barley. 
His family depends on agricultural products which they grow themselves for their livelihood. For him, therefore, cutting off the water means “certain death or displacement,” which he vows not to accept.
He explained that his land lies in Area C, which covers over 60% of the West Bank, and is under full Israeli political and security control under the 1993 Oslo Accords.
He has documents proving ownership of the land, inherited from his father and grandparents. 
Settler incursions
However, he says the area is subjected to nightly incursions by armed settlers, who enter homes, threaten residents with burning of their homes and expulsion, and damage water pipes and block roads.
Farmer Abdullah Bani Odeh, one of the Palestinians threatened with expulsion, describes what is happening as a direct attack on the residents’ basic needs.
“The land is our only source of income. Taking parts of it away reduces our ability to farm and raise livestock. What is happening is not simply land being taken from us; it is our lives being taken from us.”
Bani Odeh describes the condition of the grazing land as a result of the Israeli blockade and incursions as “catastrophic.”
He says that Israeli authorities prevent residents from fully accessing their land, surround them and stop them from grazing livestock in areas their families have used for decades. This makes it difficult to provide food for their animals and ultimately leads to livestock losses.
A new separation barrier
Abdullah Basharat, head of the Atouf village council, says, “The repeated attacks on the water infrastructure, culminating in cutting off water supplies to families, are aimed at expelling the few remaining Palestinian communities in the area, alongside excavation work to construct the separation barrier known as the ‘Crimson Thread’ in the northern Jordan Valley.”
According to Basharat, the route of the barrier - which the Israeli army announced about a year ago - extends for approximately 22 kilometres, from the Ein Shibli area to the Tayasir checkpoint in the north. 
It passes through the lands of Khirbet Atouf, Ras al-Ahmar and other communities, cutting through agricultural land owned by Palestinians from Tubas, Tammun, Atouf and other areas. The route includes orchards, greenhouses, wells and water networks.
Basharat expects the barrier to isolate Palestinians from their land and enable the seizure of approximately 50,000 dunams of territory.
Since digging work to construct the barrier began in March 2026, Basharat says the area has suffered extensive damage, including the uprooting of hundreds of trees, destruction of crops and greenhouses, demolition of kilometres of water and irrigation pipelines, and damage to agricultural land on which dozens of Palestinians depend.
He added that Israeli authorities began by destroying the main water pipelines and then filled in three functioning artesian wells without prior notification. 
He describes the destruction of the wells as “a knockout blow to irrigated agriculture in the plain,” because it cut off water to around 4,500 dunams planted with grapes, olives and bananas.
Basharat warns that recent confiscation orders, together with plans to demolish a number of structures, will turn the area into “a genuinely barren place” and force families to leave under the pressure of poverty and targeting.
He says areas of the Jordan Valley surrounding Atouf, al-Baqi'a and the communities near Tubas have, in recent years, been turned into agricultural reserves for settlers, in addition to large areas converted into private grazing land for settlers and their livestock.

Trump’s trade war with Canada: A timeline of how we got here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:23:01 UTC
01:23:01 KST

Trump’s trade war with Canada: A timeline of how we got here
CHICAGO (AP) — President Donald Trump’s barrage of tariffs — and threats of even more — has strained the United States’ longstanding relationship with Canada.
Over the course of his second term in office, Trump has threatened Canada’s economy and sovereignty with steep new import taxes on its goods. He’s gone as far as suggesting that his northern neighbor could be “the 51st state.” That rhetoric — paired with volleys of on-again, off-again new tariffs — has outraged Canadians, whose government has responded with its own retaliatory measures. All the while, uncertainty for businesses and consumers across both sides of the border only grows.
Most recently, Trump followed through on a threat to impose 50% U.S. tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports. Those levies kicked in Saturday after last-ditch negotiations failed, and Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney quickly promised to match the new import taxes.
Here’s a timeline of how we got here.
January-March 2025: ‘Trafficking tariffs’ back-and-forth
On his first day back in office, Trump says he expects to put 25% tariffs on imports from Canada.
The president later signs an executive order to impose 25% tariffs on imports from Canada starting Feb. 4, 2025 — invoking this power by declaring a national emergency over undocumented immigration and drug trafficking. Outgoing Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau promises retaliatory levies.
But the tariffs soon get pushed back, cooling tensions at least temporarily. Trump first agrees to a 30-day pause, and more limited tariffs on Canadian imports kick in March 4. Within days, the U.S. rolls out an additional exemption for automakers and postpones the 25% tariff on goods that comply with the US-Mexico Canada Agreement, a trade pact from Trump’s first term.
Meanwhile, worldwide, Trump’s new steel and aluminum tariffs — which now tax imports of both metals at 25% — still go into effect. Canada imposes more retaliatory tariffs worth $29.8 billion Canadian dollars ($20.7 billion) on U.S. imports.
April-June 2025: More global levies
Trump announces his long-promised “reciprocal” tariffs on nearly all of America’s trading partners on April 2, 2025, but doesn’t unveil additional levies on Canada.
Trump soon faces legal challenges to these sweeping tariffs he invoked emergency powers to impose — which beyond “reciprocal” levies, include the 25% rate he slapped on Canadian goods earlier in the year. The U.S. Court of International Trade rules that Trump overstepped his authority in late May 2025, but a federal appeals court quickly halts that order temporarily.
Meanwhile, separate sectoral levies continue to pile up worldwide. Trump’s sweeping 25% tariffs on auto imports also begin in April 2025, and Canada’s Carney responds by matching the 25% rate with a tariff on non-USMCA compliant vehicles imported from the U.S.
Trump’s new 50% tariffs of nearly all foreign steel and aluminum later take effect in June 2025. Carney similarly threatens to impose new tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum starting in July, pending progress of trade talks. Negotiations hit a temporary snag after Trump takes aim at Canada’s plans to continue with a tax on tech firms, which Carney soon walks back on.
July-October 2025: Trade talks whiplash
Trade tensions bubble up again in the second half of the year. Trump threatens and then imposes a heightened 35% tariff rate on a range of Canadian goods starting Aug. 1, 2025. Globally, the U.S.’s new 50% levy on imported copper also kicks in the same day.
Later that month, Carney says Canada will drop many of its retaliatory tariffs to match U.S. exemptions for goods covered under the USMCA pact. Critics decry the move as capitulation to Trump, but the prime minister maintains Canada is in a good position and that such exemptions would jump-start further trade talks.
All the while, Trump imposes more tariffs worldwide in the coming weeks and months and ends the “de minimis” rule on Aug. 29 for low-value imports coming into the U.S.
In late October, Carney outlines plans for Canada to double its non-U.S. exports in the next decade, citing the affects of Trump’s tariffs. Separately, Trump’s anger over a television ad opposing U.S. tariffs leads him to pull the plug on all trade talks with Canada. Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose provincial government paid for the ad, later says he’ll pull it so talks may resume, although Trump still threatens an added 10% tariff.
November 2025-February 2026: Supreme Court ruling
Trump’s legal fight over the tariffs he imposed using emergency powers eventually makes it to the Supreme Court, with arguments in November. In February, a 6-3 decision strikes down those import taxes — including country-specific levies imposed on Canada. Trump quickly enacts a temporary 10% global levy using a different law.
U.S.-Canada trade relations had been souring ahead of that ruling. Notably in January, Canada’s Carney focuses on mending trading ties with China — and in a break from the U.S., soon agrees to cut Canadian tariffs on Chinese EVs. An angry Trump later threatens an (eventually unrealized) 100% tariff on Canadian goods that he says he will impose if Canada moves forward with a trade deal with China, but Carney says his country has no intention of pursuing a more sweeping agreement.
Trump at one point also threatens a 50% levy on Canadian aircraft sold to the U.S., but that similarly goes unrealized. He also later threatened to block the opening of a new Canadian-built bridge across the Detroit River.
March-present day: USMCA and latest 50% tariffs
Negotiations to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA, kick off in March — and ahead of the official July 1 review date, Canada calls for the pact to be renewed for 16 years.
But the outlook remains cloudy. And the U.S. eventually rules that it’s not ready to renew that pact for that length of time, leaving the current USMCA in effect until at least its 2036 expiration date.
Then later in July, Trump threatens to impose even steeper tariffs on Canada. He says the U.S. will slap 50% levies on many Canadian goods — including those previously-protected under the USMCA — while claiming that Canada unfairly discriminates against U.S. automobiles, alcohol and dairy products.
Those levies were originally slated to start kicking in Aug. 19. Trump declared the U.S. had reached a deal with Canada to delay the taxes until at least Saturday (Aug. 22), but its key terms weren’t disclosed, and when last-minute negotiations failed, the new tariffs kicked in just after midnight.
The 50% tariffs tax about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, including products that range from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Carney promises to match them “dollar for dollar” with retaliatory tariffs taking effect Sept. 8.

Chinese humanoid robots smash human records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:23:01 UTC
01:23:01 KST

Chinese humanoid robots smash human records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games
The five-day games, now in its second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the U.S. heats up, with 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and soccer. (AP Video: Olivia Zhang and Liu Zheng)
BEIJING (AP) — Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including beating Usain Bolt’s 100-meter sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday.
More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, the organizer said.
The five-day games, now in its second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the U.S. heats up, with 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and soccer.
The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week as Beijing held the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots.
China makes the majority of the world’s humanoid robots. The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from the country.
Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations.
At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination.
At a 100-meter sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009.
In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993.
Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid.
Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second.
Still, experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research — at least for now — and it will still take time to achieve mass real-world deployment.
Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities.
Humanoid robots are “evolving rapidly,” said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident.
“At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.”
“These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing,” said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator.
Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said that he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer.”
This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.
____
Chan Ho-him reported from Hong Kong. Olivia Zhang and Liu Zheng contributed to this report from Beijing.

Israel conducts fresh strike in Syria after US criticism
Israel carried out a fresh strike in Syria on Saturday and lambasted US envoy Tom Barrack for criticising an earlier attack on an air base in the northwest, which Israel has accused Turkey of seeking to use.
US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack on Tuesday slammed Israel's attack on the disused military air base that day as an "unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability".
On Friday, in an interview with influencer Mario Nawfal, Barrack said the strike may have been intended to provoke a conflict with Turkey, prompting Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz to hit back on Saturday, calling the remarks "full of inaccuracies".
Since the December 2024 overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and has sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that for decades had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan Heights.
Katz wrote on X on Saturday that Israel had passed on "intelligence information to the authorised parties in the United States" before the strike on Tuesday.
He added that Barrack's comments were "full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict the stance of US President (Donald) Trump himself regarding the Golan Heights", after Barrack called the territory "occupied".
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, in a move only recognised by the United States and, this month, also Colombia.
'Flagrant violation'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, commenting on the Tuesday strike, said Turkey, an ally of the new authorities in Damascus, had been looking to establish a military presence on the air base.
Ankara has denied any visit to the site.
Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have traded barbs since the incident, and Ankara announced it was seeking an Interpol red notice for Netanyahu, accusing him of "genocide" linked to the interception of a Gaza-bound aid flotilla.
Netanyahu's office called Erdogan an "antisemitic dictator" while Erdogan's office called the remarks "outrageous ravings" and accused Netanyahu's government of "seeking to evade accountability".
Also on Saturday, Syrian state television said a man was wounded when an "Israeli occupation drone" targeted a vehicle in the village of Beit Jinn, located southwest of Damascus near the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights, with the foreign ministry calling it a "flagrant violation" of its sovereignty.
Israel's military acknowledged the strike, saying that its forces "fired in southern Syria toward a terrorist who advanced terror attacks in the final stages of preparation", without identifying the target.
Israel has carried out repeated incursions into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
This week Israeli army chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir told troops in southern Syria that "we are monitoring the changes on the Syrian front. We will not allow hostile forces to establish themselves on our borders."
