Israel 'baited' Turkey with Abu al-Duhur airbase 'pre-election' strike, US Envoy Tom Barrack says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:26:02 UTC
20:26:02 KST

The Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur military base in Syria on Tuesday, which nearly led to a direct military confrontation with Turkey, may have been intended to provoke Ankara and could have been linked to political considerations ahead of Israel’s elections, US Special Envoy to Syria and Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack suggested on Saturday.
In an interview with Mario Nawfal on X/Twitter, Barrack stressed that this was only one possible theory, not an intelligence-based conclusion.
According to Barrack, one possibility is that “the Israelis were baiting the Turks,” partly against the backdrop of a previous incident in which Turkey shot down a Russian fighter jet that approached its border. He described a situation in which fighter jets operate near a border without coordination or warning as a “very dangerous game.”
Barrack directly linked this possibility to Israeli politics, saying that the strike may have been a “very aggressive but maybe a well-received pre-election concept.”
Later in the interview, Barrack discussed how domestic politics can shape the rhetoric of regional leaders.
“What you're hearing in rhetoric amongst the senior leaders of these countries is they have to, during a political campaign, which everybody is in, right?” he said.
“Prime Minister [Benjamin] Netanyahu is moving toward October," Barrack noted. "He knows what his constituency wants.”
Barrack: Erdogan may soon call early elections
He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is also approaching a decision on whether to call early elections and must consider his voters, who are particularly sensitive to developments in Gaza.
Barrack also presented a second theory regarding the circumstances that led to the strike: that Israel received intelligence indicating Turkish military personnel or military assets could be stationed at the Syrian base.
According to Barrack, Israel raised the concern with the United States about six days before the strike.
“We have some intelligence that there might be Turkish movement into this site, which we would be very concerned about,” Barrack said, describing the message delivered to Washington.
However, according to Barrack, the US reviewed the intelligence with relevant officials and received a clear response: “No, that's not happening.”
The comments come amid reports of behind-the-scenes contacts before the strike. According to Barrack’s account, the issue was examined through diplomatic channels, including a backchannel conversation lasting about two hours between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and the Mossad chief.
Despite those contacts, Israeli Air Force aircraft appeared and struck the base’s runways without Turkey receiving advance warning of the operation.
According to Barrack, the incident then escalated from another Israeli strike in Syria into a moment that could have triggered a far more dangerous regional confrontation.
Barrack emphasized that the Turkish military is strong, well-equipped, and possesses significant intelligence capabilities.
“When they see these jets coming towards the border, and they don't know what the purpose, direction, or intent is, they start to say 'we're going to have to scramble our own.'” he said.
Such a scenario could have led to a possible aerial encounter between Israeli and Turkish aircraft and a direct confrontation between Israel and Turkey, a NATO member and one of the United States’ most important allies in the region.
Barrack was asked whether such an incident could have escalated into “World War III.” He said that almost any unintended incident could lead to broader escalation, but stressed that, in his assessment, neither side intends to reach such a confrontation.
“Thank goodness, palm heads really came to the moment of the day, and we unwrapped it,” he said.
According to Barrack, it was one of those moments when “for many of us, our whole life went in front of us,” leading to the conclusion: “There's got to be a better way, guys.”
Barrack emphasized that, in his understanding, Ankara is not seeking a war with Israel.
“I know that the Turks, their intelligence agency, their hierarchy, their foreign minister, the president, the head of intelligence, all are concentrating on restraint,” he said.
“They're not predatory," he added. "They're not interested in attacking or even engaging in any kind of kinetic or adversarial relationship with Israel. It's not good for the region.”
Barrack said both sides are ultimately looking for a way to de-escalate, but that from Turkey’s perspective, the Palestinian issue is even more important than Iran. According to him, developments in Gaza are a major concern for both the Turkish public and the broader Muslim public.
Behind the immediate confrontation lies a much broader strategic struggle over the future of Syria following the fall of the Assad regime, according to Barrack.
Syrian territory provides Israel with 'a clear line of sight to Iran,' Barrack says
Israel wants Syria to remain free of military systems that could limit its freedom of action in the region, particularly against Iran. Barrack previously described Syrian territory as providing Israel with “a clear line of sight to Iran.”
Turkey, meanwhile, is expanding its military and political position in the new Syria. Barrack said Turkey’s growing influence as a regional power is raising concerns among other actors, but expressed hope the sides can maintain restraint.
According to Barrack, US President Donald Trump recently asked Erdogan why Turkey did not simply “take” Syria for itself, given the role it played in developments there.
According to Barrack, Erdogan responded: “Because we don’t want it. We want Syria to be a sovereign and independent country."
Barrack also addressed mutual concerns over territorial ambitions. According to him, maps are published in Turkey showing what is allegedly a vision of “Greater Israel,” while in Israel, maps appear warning of “Ottoman Empire 2.0.”
“We don't think any of those things are true,” he said.
Despite the severe crisis, Barrack revealed that behind the scenes there is also security cooperation between Turkey, Israel, and Syria over a shared threat.
“Every evening... we have coordination between Turkey, Israel, and Syria, hunting ISIS terrorists,” he said.
According to Barrack, the group is attempting to exploit the governing vacuum created in Syria to rebuild itself.
Barrack recalled that in the early 2000s, Israel and Turkey enjoyed a period of “honeymoon” relations and hoped the two countries could eventually return to a similar relationship.
However, this week’s incident highlighted how dangerous the path toward such a relationship remains. According to Trump’s envoy, Israeli aircraft approached the Turkish border without warning; Ankara began considering scrambling its own fighter jets, and for several moments two key US allies came close to a confrontation that, according to Barrack, neither side truly wants.
Defense Minister Katz: Barrack's statements 'full of inaccuracies'
After Barrack's statements, Defense Minister Israel Katz said they were "full of inaccuracies" and argued they contradicted US President Trump's positions.
"The attempt by opposition figures and parts of the media to paint the operation in Syria in political colors stems from a combination of ignorance, a lack of understanding of Israel’s security interests, and a constant desire to attack the government, and deserves every condemnation.
"The response of US envoy Barrack is full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump’s own position regarding the Golan Heights.”
Katz also claimed that the IDF issued a direct warning to senior Syrian officials before strikes on the Abu al-Duhur airfield "in an attempt to prevent the move."
"After the request went unanswered, the prime minister and I authorized the IDF to carry out the strike, and it was carried out successfully. Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down," Katz said.

The Middle East’s ‘peace architecture’ may be giving rise to an anti-Israel bloc - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:25:55 UTC
20:25:55 KST

Israel has always known how to deal with hostile governments one at a time.
What should worry it now is something more dangerous: a growing network of countries that increasingly act together, pressure together, and may soon help decide when Israel must withdraw, whether Hamas or Hezbollah have really disarmed, and when Israel is permitted to defend itself.
That danger became clearer this week.
Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Pakistan, and Indonesia issued a joint statement pressing Israel to move ahead with the latest Gaza framework and calling for continued American involvement to ensure Israeli compliance.
The problem is not diplomacy. The problem is the direction of the pressure.
Israel is being pushed to withdraw while Hamas remains armed.
Hamas can announce that it accepts a roadmap. That is not the same as surrendering weapons, dismantling tunnels, ending military command structures, and proving that it will not rebuild.
October 7 should have ended any illusion that Israel can afford to trade hard security for promises.
If Hamas is required to disarm, then disarmament should come first. Israel should not make an irreversible withdrawal while Hamas offers a reversible commitment.
Yet Turkey, Qatar, Egypt, and now the UAE are increasingly speaking through the same diplomatic framework and pushing Israel in the same direction.
That matters because these countries were never meant to function as a collective referee over Israeli security.
Egypt is the clearest example.
Israel and Egypt signed peace in 1979. For almost half a century, that agreement turned Israel's most dangerous military frontier into one of its most stable borders. It worked because it was bilateral.
Egypt acted according to Egyptian interests. Israel acted according to Israeli interests. The United States served as guarantor. Egypt did not need Turkey or Qatar to maintain peace with Israel.
Now Cairo is increasingly operating inside a wider Gaza mechanism together with Ankara and Doha, while the UAE is joining the same coordinated statements.
The danger is not that Egypt suddenly abandons peace. The danger is that a strong bilateral relationship becomes absorbed into a regional bloc where Turkey, Qatar, and others help shape the collective position.
Imagine the next crisis.
Israel discovers Hamas rebuilding tunnels, weapons depots, or armed units after an Israeli withdrawal. Israel acts. Turkey condemns it. Qatar condemns it. Other governments join them.
Egypt comes under pressure to align with the regional position. The UAE does too.
Suddenly, Israel is no longer dealing with one mediator or one peace partner. It is confronting a coordinated diplomatic front.
That is the risk we should be discussing now, before it becomes permanent.
The same pattern is appearing in Lebanon.
Britain, Italy, Switzerland, and Indonesia have been discussed as possible participants in a mechanism to verify whether Hezbollah has disarmed.
Again, the concept sounds reasonable; Israel needs Hezbollah disarmed.
But who gets to decide when Hezbollah has complied enough?
Britain has already shown a growing willingness to use sanctions and economic pressure against Israelis and Israeli policies in Judea and Samaria. Italy has created more distance in defense cooperation with Israel. Indonesia has long taken strongly pro-Palestinian positions.
Why should governments that are willing to pressure Israel become judges of whether Israel's enemies are sufficiently disarmed?
That is the larger issue.
The basic imbalance
Each initiative sounds harmless when viewed alone: a Gaza peace board. A stabilization force. Arab mediation. A Hezbollah verification mechanism. European sanctions. Reconstruction financing.
But together they form something much more powerful.
They create a network with money, military personnel, diplomatic recognition, economic leverage, and American backing.
That network can eventually influence whether Israel withdraws, whether it can strike, whether Hamas has complied, whether Hezbollah has complied, and whether Israeli actions in Judea and Samaria deserve punishment.
That could become more consequential than the United Nations.
Israel knows how to survive hostile UN resolutions. Most of them have limited practical effect.
These newer mechanisms are different. They can affect the battlefield. They can affect borders. They can affect sanctions. They can affect reconstruction money. They can affect Washington.
And there is a basic imbalance in all of this.
Israel is easy to pressure. It has banks, companies, diplomats, tourists, trade agreements, and international relationships.
Hamas does not.
Hezbollah does not.
A European government can sanction an Israeli. It cannot meaningfully sanction a terrorist hiding in a tunnel.
Turkey and Qatar can pressure Washington.
Hamas pays almost no price for rejecting international expectations until someone forces it to.
That means the democratic state becomes the easiest target.
We are already watching that happen.
Hamas remains armed, yet international pressure increasingly focuses on when Israel will withdraw. That is backwards.
Hamas started this war. Hamas carried out October 7. Hamas built the tunnels. Hamas took the hostages. Hamas created the military infrastructure that made this war possible. The burden should be on Hamas to prove that the threat is gone. Not on Israel to withdraw first and hope.
Peace requires partners, and Israel should continue strengthening peace with Egypt, expanding the Abraham Accords and building relationships across the Arab world.
But peace agreements should remain peace agreements. They should not quietly evolve into multinational structures that police Israel.
Egypt should be Israel's neighbor at peace. The UAE should be Israel's normalization partner. Turkey and Qatar can mediate when useful.
But none of them should be given a collective veto over Israel's security decisions.
The US should be building a regional architecture that restrains Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. It should not accidentally build one that is far better at restraining Israel.
The test is simple.
Before Israel is pressured to withdraw, Hamas should disarm.
Before Israel is told Hezbollah no longer poses a threat, Hezbollah should actually dismantle its military infrastructure.
Before international monitors tell Israel that the danger has passed, the danger should actually be gone.
Otherwise, we are not building peace. Instead, we are building a system in which Israel's enemies keep their weapons while Israel's friends gain the power to tell Israel when it may use its own.
That is not a peace architecture.
That is a bloc.
And Israel should recognize it before it is too late.
The writer is founder and CEO of the Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.

Hong Kong-built greenhouse gas tracker device ‘functioning well’ on space station
Tech minister Sun Dong says Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory has ‘successfully captured images with good clarity’
A greenhouse gas monitoring instrument developed by a university in Hong Kong is operating successfully aboard the Tiangong space station and is expected to contribute to sustainable development, the city’s technology minister has said.
Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong also revealed more details in a blog post on Saturday about the life of the city’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, who he said had a busy schedule at the space station.
The Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory (Musico), developed by a team led by scientists at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and funded by the city government, has been deployed to China’s space station.
“Musico is equipped with four sensors for detecting carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen, and aerosols. They have all successfully captured images with clear imaging quality and demonstrated good overall performance,” he said.
“Over the next two years or more, the instrument will provide autonomous, controllable, and highly accurate greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide and methane) emission monitoring data, contributing to efforts to address climate change and promote global sustainable development.”
Musico is considered the world’s first lightweight, high-resolution, high-precision synergistic observatory for carbon dioxide and methane.

====================================================================================================

Pine-cone grenades and planet-baking carbon: the French fires 170 years in the making – a visual guide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:00:32 UTC
20:00:32 KST

The ruinous fires that overran parts of France this summer have burned more land than ever recorded, forced more people from their homes than at any point since the second world war and caused what scientists suspect is the country’s first firestorm thundercloud. The smoke from France’s biggest inferno in nearly 80 years choked Limoges, a city 125 miles (200km) from the flames, with more toxic dust than Delhi residents inhaled on the city’s worst day of smog last year.
The blaze that tore through forests outside Bordeaux in late July took just a few weeks to reforge France’s relationship with fire, but the conditions behind it were centuries in the making.
In the 18th century, the coastal wetlands of south-western France were so swampy that shepherds used stilts to cross them in winter. When a 1857 decree from NapoleonIII forced landowners to drain the marsh and populate it with maritime pines, the water-logged landscape was converted into Europe’s largest human-made forest. It has since become a regional economic engine running on timber that employs 30,000 people.
It is also a firefighter’s nightmare. The pines that make up 90% of the trees in the Landes forest hold resin that burns like petrol, needles that carpet the ground with flammable material and cones that whiz in the wind like grenades, spreading flames across breaks in vegetation that should act as barriers. Without the diversity offered by broad-leafed species, which retain more moisture and have shady canopies that stop vegetation from drying, the dense monoculture can burn with fury when sparks catch.
That is what happened in 1949, when a blaze that began in a saw mill burned 50,000 hectares. Gorging on plentiful fuel and with few breaks to impede their spread, the flames killed 82 people, most of them volunteers racing to put out the fire. It remains Europe’s deadliest wildfire.
Firefighting capacity has vastly improved since, but the potential for disaster has continued to increase. Humanity has fouled the atmosphere with 1.85tn tonnes of planet-baking carbon since the 1857 decree, warming Europe by 2.4C and increasing the risk of hot and dry extremes that were once unthinkable.
A strikingly wet winter in western Europe this year helped plants grow tall, only for relentless heatwaves to later strip them of moisture, creating a large fuel surplus for fires to devour. By mid-July, temperatures across France had reached record highs and soil moisture had fallen to record lows, setting the stage for the Gironde inferno.
Not long after noon on 22 July, after three straight weeks of more than 30C heat, smoke rose from the tightly packed pine stands near Saumos, a village 20 miles west of Bordeaux. The source of ignition is under investigation, but workers contracted by Enedis, a utility company that manages France’s electricity distribution, were active in the area and reported having sparked a fire with a faulty machine. The Bordeaux public prosecutor, which has identified the machine as its leading line of inquiry, did not respond to requests for comment. Enedis declined to answer specific questions because of the continuing investigation.
Most wildfires are started by humans through actions such as dropping cigarette butts, failing to properly extinguish campfires or dispose of barbecues. Public awareness campaigns to discourage reckless behaviour are thought to have contributed to a fall in the number of fires in southern Europe since the 1980s but preventing arson is much harder. French police have arrested nearly 500 people on suspicion of starting fires since the start of the summer, about 70% of which are thought to have been deliberate.
Once a fire has begun, it is weather and geography that dictate whether it will quickly wither or morph into a hellish blaze. Outside Saumos, it was immediately clear that firefighters were facing the latter. The fire engulfed several hundreds of hectares in a matter of hours and reached the outskirts of La Porge, which would lose one in 10 homes to the flames in the days that followed. Within 24 hours of the initial spark, southerly winds had pushed the fire’s southern front to Cap Ferret, an upmarket peninsula known as the Hamptons of France, nine miles away.
Helping the fire’s rapid spread was its location in an area that had been flattened by a powerful storm in 1999 and then swiftly replanted, resulting in a uniform tree height that created a continuous fuel load. But the response in those crucial early hours has also been criticised. Local forestry workers told Le Monde that firefighters had rejected their recommendation to quickly set a controlled burn, while residents of La Porge claim resources were taken from their village to protect the wealthier Cap Ferret. The Gironde fire service, which did not respond to requests for comment, has said it had done all it could to stop the fire and rejected allegations that it abandoned La Porge.
Bruno Lafon, the head of the regional forest fire prevention service, an association of forestry workers who work with firefighters to prevent blazes, said he could understand that volunteers who saw their livelihoods go up in flames wanted more help to have come. But, he said, the powerful combination of drought, heat and wind made the initial spread extremely hard to stop. “The men on the ground did what they could, though I think it would have taken a greater number of planes from the beginning,” he said. The French government has also been criticised because maintenance work meant only seven of its 12 water-bombing planes were available at the peak of the fire.
As the fire torched more land, authorities acted quickly to get people to safety. The first evacuations began on the afternoon of 22 July, when 100 residents of the north-eastern quarter of La Porge were taken to shelter in a community hall. Overnight, that number rose to more than 10,000, and just a few days later it had reached nearly 220,000. Across France and neighbouring Spain, which was also battling extreme wildfires, evacuation orders covered more than 300,000 people, a peacetime displacement unprecedented in Europe.
Some residents returned to charred possessions, burnt-out homes and shells of cars, but the evacuations proved hugely successful. Not a single person died as a direct result of the Gironde fire, though four firefighters lost their lives tackling separate blazes across the country last month.
Among the evacuees was Hervé Jactel, a forest scientist at INRAE, a public research institute, who was forced to flee twice in two days. Watching Nasa maps with apprehension as the fire drew near, he lost a 20-year experiment investigating the diversity of forest trees as a result of burning biomass that jumped a cornfield. He said the fire had not come as a surprise.
“From an ecological and forest management point of view, everything was in place to increase the risk of a very large fire,” he said. “Not only because of the climate, but because of the amount and homogeneity of the fuel.”
Scientists suspect those conditions resulted in the extreme levels of energy that generated a firecloud, a powerful chimney of smoke stretching into the atmosphere that creates its own weather system. Known as a pyrocumulonimbus cloud, , it can spit lightning, and rain down burning embers that spark new blazes and spread the fire further. Nasa has described them as fire-breathing dragons.
The true danger, however, lay not in the apocalyptic fire cloud but in the pollutants that it dispersed.
Studies have found wildfire smoke to be responsible for 1.5 million deaths around the world each year, making it one of the deadliest environmental threats to human health. Initially, much of the smoke blew straight out over the Atlantic Ocean, but a shift in wind direction caused it to choke Bordeaux, which was nervously watching the approaching inferno, before drifting over Angoulême and Limoges.
It clogged the air with so much soot and ash that daily concentrations of airway-inflaming particles hit highs rarely seen, even in cities as polluted as Delhi.
A shift in the weather helped firefighters halt the advance of the blaze at 42,000 hectares of burned area at the end of July. In the days since, they have continued to put out small flare-ups and smouldering “zombie fires” underground that they say could continue to return for months.
Scientists fear for the forest’s short-term recovery. Fire can trigger outbreaks of bark beetles, which attack damaged trees and increase the fuel load for the next fire – a vicious cycle already well documented in California. The burned wood also attracts the invasive pine nematode, a microscopic worm that had arrived in south-west France in November. It blocks the flow of sap in trees, causing them to wilt and die within months.
The greatest threats to the forest, however, are yet to come. Fire weather is projected to become increasingly severe across Europe as carbon pollution continues to heat the planet. Without action to improve fire management, the burned area in Europe is predicted to rise by 39% even in a best-scenario scenario for cutting pollution. In a worst-case scenario, it could nearly triple.
Experts have called for rapid cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and better management of the land, such as breaking up continuous tracts of forest and diversifying tree species.

Dining across the divide: ‘I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

Joe, 41, Trafford, Greater Manchester
Occupation Press officer at a university
Voting record Historically, under Jeremy Corbyn, Labour; is a Green member now but was planning to vote Labour in the mayoral election
Amuse bouche Long-distance cycle touring is Joe’s big thing: he has been all over Europe solo, staying with families, trying to speak the languages, embedding himself with local people
Keith, 89, Cheshire
Occupation Retired – used to be a journalist, moved to Liverpool to edit a shipping newspaper and ended up owning it
Voting record Keith normally votes Labour. There was one occasion when he voted Conservative, for Margaret Thatcher
Amuse bouche Keith once went to Rio de Janeiro for the day. He was producing a magazine for British Airways Cargo and they wanted to promote the route to São Paulo
For starters
Joe I’d formed a view of what his character might be but he was really warm and friendly. It was like two old friends. It was just so comfortable.
Keith The first thing he said was, “Are you as nervous as I am?” I said I wasn’t nervous at all. I’m used to talking to people and it didn’t bother me.
Joe I had the prosciutto and melon, then chicken in breadcrumbs.
Keith I started with calamari, then gnocchi with prawns.
The big beef
Joe He was very set on the idea that the EU is anti-democratic. The arguments I had about the damage that leaving the EU has done to the British economy – how it has destroyed exports and left us isolated – he agreed with. But none of it mattered to him. He was a Brexiter from quite a leftwing perspective. I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”, but he wasn’t like that at all.
Keith I voted for Brexit for independence, not for the economy, although the economy could have been handled better by the prime ministers since. You had Theresa May – who was, I believe, a remainer at heart – trying to cobble together some sort of deal that looked like Brexit but wasn’t. Both she and Boris Johnson should share the blame because they let it drag on for so long. You should never be governed by people you can’t vote out of office.
Joe He said Nigel Farage sometimes says things that he agrees with – principally stuff about the European superstate. When he was talking about that, you couldn’t put a cigarette paper between him and Farage. But at the same time, he’s really anti-Trump, and really anti the rightwing position on migrants.
Keith There are 4,000 different edicts in the EU that we should have got rid of. I don’t feel we’ve taken advantage economically of the opportunities. Joe sort of saw that, but he believes too many small companies have lost business. I did point out that traders should have looked elsewhere for business. We were the sixth largest trading nation in the world before and we still are.
Sharing plate
Joe On the NHS, I don’t think we were miles apart. I’ve worked in the NHS in the past; the right wing dresses up overspending as back office stuff and equality and diversity, but all of that is a tiny drop in the ocean compared with PFI.
Keith He saw how the NHS is paying hundreds of millions in interest on PFI payments. PFI has been a bit of a disaster, but I’d be very open to other ways of bringing in private money.
For afters
Joe Drilling in the North Sea won’t make us more resilient as a country because it has all got to be sold on the international markets anyway. Is there any point doing damage to the environment when it won’t benefit British consumers? We could be spending that money and energy building renewable capacity.
Keith I’m all for going to renewables, I’m all for cutting pollution. I agree with all that, but I just don’t think we need to do it as quickly as people like Ed Miliband want us to. It’s impoverishing the country, we’re losing industry.
Takeaways
Joe As I was driving away, I did think I should have taken his email address, so we could have kept in touch.
Keith The only problem I was left with was that I’m never going to see him or hear from him again. He’s a long way away to go out for a casual drink.
Additional reporting: Kitty Drake
Joe and Keith ate at La Cantina in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire

Syria foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel

Syria foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
Asaad al-Shaibani urges Israel to seize ‘historic opportunity’ for diplomacy.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani says the door for diplomacy with Israel is open, urging it to seize a “historic opportunity”.
In an interview with the Reuters news agency, published on Sunday, al-Shaibani said he expects the talks over a security deal that would lead to Israel’s withdrawal from Syrian territory to resume soon.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Everything you need to know about the Syria – Israel deal in Paris
- list 2 of 3Analysis: Syrian airbase attack is an Israeli message to Damascus, Ankara
- list 3 of 3Syrian official says ‘no plans’ to establish Turkish military presence
He said negotiations over the security agreement were frozen at the start of the US-Israel war on Iran and that no date has been set for a resumption of talks.
Al-Shaibani also stressed that Damascus’s priority is to halt Israeli attacks, saying confidence-building steps were needed in this direction.
The United States has been trying to broker a security deal between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a new US ally in the Middle East, for more than a year. But an agreement has proven elusive as Israel has sent troops into Syrian territory and attacked government assets, citing threats to its security.
“We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn’t bring results, then we don’t need it,” al-Shaibani said. “We do not trust Israel currently.”
The Israeli prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
Al-Sharaa has said Syria poses no threat to other countries and that it is instead focused on rebuilding after 14 years of civil war.
Israeli officials have talked about a range of potential dangers in Syria, with several last year criticising the new government, even as al-Sharaa worked to strengthen ties with Washington.
In the days after the ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in 2024, Israel seized territory in southwest Syria, citing the need to safeguard its citizens against attack, and bombed dozens of Syrian military sites.
“Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force, and it hasn’t succeeded” anywhere, al-Shaibani said. “I believe negotiations will resume soon.”
He said the US is pressuring Israel to return to the dialogue table.
Asked how optimistic he was that talks would resume, al-Shaibani said: “It’s very hard to bet on Israel.” But Syria had “very great hope” of building stable relationships with its neighbours.
“Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy” and regional stability.
Israeli attacks cast doubt on will to make deal
Tensions over Syria were brought into focus last week when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase, saying Damascus was about to allow Turkish forces to deploy there. Syria and Turkiye denied the claim.
Al-Shaibani said Syria respected Israel’s security concerns but that it must also respect those of Damascus, instead of violating its airspace and conducting raids and arrests in the south of the country.
He said earlier this year, the two sides had “agreed on paper to almost everything” regarding a security deal that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and was tied to its withdrawal from territory seized after al-Assad fell.
That deal would include several security zones in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, including a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present, and others where Syrian forces would deploy in varying degrees of force.
However, he said, Israel had sought to evade implementation, adding: “We did not see they had the real will to reach an agreement.”
Golan Heights a sticking point
Syria and Israel have technically been in a state of war since 1948. Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria in the Six-Day War of 1967.
Al-Shaibani said the priority now is to “stop Israeli aggression even before reaching a security agreement”, and then “perhaps we can open the topics of peace and the Golan”.
Israeli officials have indicated they are not willing to return the Golan Heights to the al-Sharaa government.
US special envoy for Syria, Tom Barrack, said last week that Washington was working to establish a mechanism to prevent conflict among Israel, Turkiye and Syria.
Al-Shaibani said there was no agreement yet on the mechanism, which he said must stop attacks and pave the way for the security deal rather than “entrenching … Israeli occupation”.
The US Department of State did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Al-Shaibani said Israel had bombed Abu al-Duhur even after Syria conveyed a message that it would not be a Turkish base.
Syria draws on Turkish support in military training and cooperation, he said, noting that this was also the case with Jordan, Saudi Arabia and others.
Damascus was thankful for Turkiye’s support in rebuilding its military, “and we won’t forgo support”, he said.

Israeli politicians focus on foreign threats, ignoring spiralling debt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:46:52 UTC
16:46:52 KST

Israeli politicians focus on foreign threats, ignoring spiralling debt
Israel faces mounting debt pressures as wars and declining tax revenues collide with the emigration of its top earners.
Israel’s parliamentary election campaign is in full swing, with politicians talking up their ability to defeat the country’s opponents across the region.
But the focus on war and the perceived existential threat to Israel from those opponents masks that few of the most prominent contenders in October’s election are discussing the astronomical cost of the country’s multiple conflicts, and how they plan to deal with it.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Rights groups launch new legal challenge to Trump campaign against ICC
- list 2 of 4Can Trump keep his ‘irritation’ with Netanyahu in check?
- list 3 of 4Trump remarks on diminishing impact of pro-Israel groups in Congress
- list 4 of 4US diplomat calls Israeli settler siege of West Bank homes ‘act of terror’
Israel’s central bank estimated in its 2025 report that 350bn shekels ($118bn) had been spent on wars in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and elsewhere between 2023 and 2026, excluding the war on Iran that began in late February. In April, the Finance Ministry said that an extra 35bn shekels ($11.8bn) had been spent on that conflict.
Israel’s defence spending alone accounted for 249bn shekels ($84bn), according to the Bank of Israel’s report – and it is swallowing an ever-bigger share of the economy, almost doubling from 5.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2023 to more than 8 percent in 2024.
That has all contributed to Israel’s national debt soaring. The Finance Ministry said it is around 1.4 trillion shekels ($480bn), an increase from 1.07 trillion shekels ($365bn) before October 2023.
“Unfortunately, there just isn’t any electoral benefit in talking about the economy,” said Yossi Mekelberg, an Associate Fellow at Chatham House. “It wouldn’t move even a couple of seats. There isn’t really much of an understanding of how debt works, or even the massive costs of servicing that debt. Instead, politicians assume voters are just far more interested in hearing the typical jingoism and deliver that.”
War strains
Israel’s debt has been swollen by the government’s military campaigns and is being repaid by a treasury under increasing strain.
While tax collection hit a record 509.3bn shekels ($172.6bn) in 2025, up 12 percent on 2024, added together, the cost of defence and the cost of servicing Israel’s debt are rising faster still. The IMF warns that the 2026 budget’s deficit ceiling is too high to put debt on a downward path.
Compounding the strain on the economy is the growing share of Israel’s top earners who are leaving the country, with emigration among the top 10 percent of earners up 80 percent since 2019, according to tax authority data.
In lockstep with that flight is the intensely controversial issue of Israel’s growing ultra-Orthodox population. Exempt from military service and reliant on a generous state welfare system, ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, households receive a net average of almost 6,000 shekels ($2,000) a month from the state. Just over half of Haredi men are employed, well below the national average.
Non-Haredi households pay an estimated average of around 8,800 shekels ($2,980) a month more in taxes than they receive back.
Israel’s tax revenues must cover the rising cost of servicing the government debt – a burden governments have been trying to contain for decades. Since the 1973 war, after which debt climbed toward an all-time high of 284 percent of GDP by 1984, successive Israeli governments have striven to maintain a limit on their borrowing, said Michael Ben-Gad, a professor of economics at City St George’s, University of London.
“The long term projection for Israel’s debt [to GDP percentage] fluctuates between around 67 percent and 70 percent [compared to around 60 percent before October 2023], which is concerning,” he said. “As a result of the war it has been climbing, and the higher defence spending that is planned implies it will carry on growing unless we see higher taxes or cuts in civilian spending,” he said, “It needs to be capped, which it normally would be outside of an emergency,” he said.
Despite its enormous reserves, the Bank of Israel remained concerned, Ben-Gad continued. “It’s unsustainable,” the economist said, adding that, despite the overall growth in the economy, politicians would need to increase taxes to meet the cost of maintaining the debt.
However, few are showing any signs of doing so, Ben-Gad added, referring instead to spiralling defence projections to meet future threats.
“No one is really talking about the cost of that,” Ben-Gad said. “The only one who mentions the economy is [Democrats leader, Yair] Golan, but when he does he’s typically talking about the cost of living and reducing the wealth gap, rather than taxation.”
Despite the staggering cost of its wars, the Israeli economy is nonetheless expected to grow at 3.5 percent this year, with much of that attributable to Israel’s cutting-edge tech sector, especially investments in cybersecurity and its defence sector, which Ben-Gad described as not only benefitting from generous government contracts “but is also generating more and more export revenue, especially for anti-missile defence”.
Paying the bill
In April, the Israeli business daily Calcalist reported that, despite what appeared to be massive investment on paper, the Israeli government nevertheless owed the country’s private defence contractors $3.5bn.
“Companies like [Israeli defence giant] Elbit Systems are very right-wing and nationalistic, but at the end of the day they’re still companies with shareholders and investors,” said political economist Shir Hever, referring to the fall in the defence company’s share price after the scale of the government’s unpaid bills was revealed. “When the government starts talking about paying its debts in ten years’ time, that still hurts them.”
Hever also warned about the risk posed to Israel’s ability to service its debt through the sale of its government bonds in Europe. Given that Israel is outside the European Union, that had previously been managed through intermediaries, such as Luxembourg and Ireland. However, there is growing political pressure to stop the assistance due to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
“It may be that another EU state takes over as Israel’s intermediary,” Hever said, suggesting that Germany was most likely to step into the breach. “However, it may not, and the consequences of that would be dramatic. Essentially, Israel risks defaulting on its debt, at which point it stops being able to borrow money. Essentially, it would stop being able to pay for its weapons.”

'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:11:47 UTC
20:11:47 KST

'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Ukraine has launched a new operation targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers near its borders, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22, as Kyiv faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting ballistic weapons.
Zelensky said that Ukrainian military struck an Iskander ballistic missile launcher near Ukraine's borders on Aug. 22, without providing further details.
The strike was part of a separate operation to hunt down Russian missile systems positioned near Ukraine, which Zelensky described as an alternative tactic amid the dire lack of of anti-ballistic missile interceptors.
The Iskander is Russia's main surface to surface tactical ballistic missile system, with a stated range of around 500 kilometers.
Complemented with North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles and advanced Zircon cruise missiles, the Iskander has been the workhorse of combined mass attacks again Ukrainian targets in recent months.
When attacking Kyiv and other targets inside Ukraine, Iskanders are launched from mobile erector-launcher systems inside Russian territory, usually in border regions like Bryansk or Kursk oblasts.
With Ukraine's stocks of Patriot ballistic missile interceptor at or near empty, strikes against Iskander launchers have long been proposed as an alternative method of fighting the Iskander threat, but Ukraine has lacked options for quickly detecting and hitting launch sites.
"At one point (the Russians) were planning to launch an attack, but didn’t go through with it. This is no coincidence," Zelensky told journalists.
"In other words, we're working to prevent them from carrying out large-scale missile attacks. These are individual, complex operations, and we're now starting to see the first results."
Zelensky said Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually and currently has around 600–630 in stock. Moscow could eventually aim to produce around 100 ballistic missiles per month, he said, although it has not yet reached that rate.
Ukraine is also seeking more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter, Zelensky said, revealing that Ukraine had only received 264 missiles for the advanced surface-to-air system this year so far.
The Air Force has requested 360 missiles, up from an initial target of 300. According to the president, Kyiv hopes to secure 5–10% of U.S. stocks, with Ukraine prepared to pay for the missiles.
Zelensky also said Germany had agreed to provide 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027–2028, while negotiations with Washington over additional supplies continue.
Longer-term alternatives to the Patriot are also moving ahead, the president said, referring specifically to the Freyja project, a joint effort by European and Ukrainian defense companies to produce a new anti-ballistic missile system.
The project has moved from political discussions to the technical stage, with companies now beginning practical work, Zelensky said.
